UI_pzopt_text_optimizations_options_3879: A locked 60 fps on a 4-core CPU with an old GPU (Core i5-6300HQ / GTX 960M, 1920x1080, 2026-10-07): turns the master switch on, a render distance of 9 chunks (what the game itself picks for a small window: the native lighting thread, the chunk bakes and every arriving chunk's setup grow with it, and they were what broke 60 on four cores), no chunk worker pool (its threads took the game thread's core), trees baked only while walking, and on the Display page vsync on with the frame limit at 60, lighting updates 10/s, the UI redrawn 30 times a second and texture compression (keeps a 4 GB card from spilling into system memory). Everything else goes back to the build's default. Walking through town 1.3 %% of the screen's refreshes repeat a frame (stock 29.9 %%), a 60 km/h drive 6.3-6.8 %% (stock 36.8 %%). Zombies, cars and sounds are simulated 36 tiles around you instead of 76. See docs/findings-low-end-mode-2026-10-07.md.

UI_pzopt_tip_actionConditionFast: A rule comparing a true/false or integer animation variable reads it directly; stock printed the value to text and parsed it back for every rule of every zombie every frame. Same outcomes.
UI_pzopt_tip_actionEvalParallel: Each zombie's action-state transition rules (dozens of variable tests per zombie per frame) are evaluated on worker threads after the object loop; the state changes, the animator and the model update then run on the game thread in the stock order. Rules that call Lua, and zombies mid-grapple, stay on the game thread.
UI_pzopt_tip_actionGroupCache: Every zombie asked the engine for its action group by name twice a frame, which copied the name into a new lower-case string and probed a map for a group loaded once at startup. It is held instead.
UI_pzopt_tip_actionSnapshotFilter: Before a zombie's transitions are evaluated on a worker, the game thread reads the variables whose engine callback has a side effect. It used to resolve every variable of every transition to find out which those are; the answer only depends on the variable's name, so it is now decided once per state. Same values.
UI_pzopt_tip_aimHoldMs: The game starts aiming only after the right button has been held this long, so a quick right-click still opens the context menu. Shorter aims sooner; at 0 every right-click aims for a moment. Applies on the next launch.
UI_pzopt_tip_ambientOcclusion: Soft shading where surfaces meet: floors darken a little along the base of walls, in room corners, under and around furniture, fences, stairs and bushes, so buildings and objects sit on the ground instead of floating on it. Computed from the game's own depth when a chunk's picture is drawn and baked into it. Characters and vehicles keep their own shadows. Windows, Linux and macOS (on a Mac with "macOS: OpenGL 4.1" on, the default; on OpenGL 2.1 it stays off). Changing an ambient occlusion setting redraws every chunk picture over the next few frames.
UI_pzopt_tip_animBatchAsync: The bone math batch starts after the zombie updates and runs on the workers while the game thread carries on with the rest of the frame's logic; it is joined where the game itself would wait for animation, right before drawing (anything touching a zombie's bones earlier waits for it first).
UI_pzopt_tip_animBonesParallel: After the object update loop the zombies' animation blending (bone, twist, model and skin matrices) runs on worker threads and is joined before rendering; off, it runs inline like stock.
UI_pzopt_tip_animClipCache: Imported animation clips are written under Zomboid/pzopt/anims and read from there on later boots. The first boot after an update or a cache wipe imports them as stock does and fills the cache.
UI_pzopt_tip_animalLosFast: An animal's line-of-sight update walks every zombie in range even when it is too far to change anything; those calls are skipped with the same bookkeeping applied afterwards (bit-identical numbers), and players are never skipped. Matters on farms and near hordes.
UI_pzopt_tip_animatorParallel: After its decision rules, each zombie's animator (which animations play and how they blend), its turn and move speeds and its animation clock run on worker threads; the sounds, footsteps and state hooks those animations trigger are replayed on the game thread in the stock order. A zombie whose animator fires such an event this frame finishes on the game thread.
UI_pzopt_tip_animatorPipeline: The workers run the decision rules and the animators alone while the game thread applies each zombie's result as soon as it is ready, instead of taking a share of the batch and then applying everything.
UI_pzopt_tip_aoContextParallel: With ambient occlusion or sun shadows on, every chunk the game redraws also gathers which squares hold grass, trees, walls and roofs around it. Those reads are done for all the chunks of a frame at once on the worker threads, instead of one by one inside each redraw. Same shading.
UI_pzopt_tip_aoRadiusPct: How far from a wall or an object the shading reaches, in tiles. Longer reach is softer and wider.
UI_pzopt_tip_aoScalePct: The resolution the shading is computed and kept at, per axis of a chunk picture. Lower is softer.
UI_pzopt_tip_aoStrengthFloorPct: How dark the shading gets on floors and flat ground where it is strongest: along the base of walls, in room corners, under furniture and around what stands on them. 0 leaves floors unshaded. The three strengths replace the single strength of earlier versions, whose value they take until you set them.
UI_pzopt_tip_aoStrengthObjectPct: How dark the shading gets on everything that is neither floor nor wall nor tree nor plant: furniture, counters, fences, stairs, crates. 0 leaves them unshaded.
UI_pzopt_tip_aoStrengthPlantPct: How dark the shading gets on bushes, hedges, tall grass and flowers where walls, fences, furniture and the ground close them in (their own leaves do not shade each other). 0 leaves them bright; the contact shading where a bush meets the floor follows the floor strength. Until you set it, it takes the value of the trees' strength (one strength for all vegetation in earlier versions).
UI_pzopt_tip_aoStrengthVegetationPct: How dark the shading gets on trees and the soft shade their crowns cast on the ground straight below them. 0 leaves trees bright and removes the dark patch under them. Bushes, grass and flowers have their own strength below.
UI_pzopt_tip_aoStrengthWallPct: How dark the shading gets on walls: where they meet the floor and each other, and behind furniture standing against them. 0 leaves walls unshaded.
UI_pzopt_tip_aotCache: The game records a Java warm-start cache (AOT: the classes it loads and how its methods ran) on one launch and starts from it afterwards, so the menu and every world load begin with warm code. Changes the launcher config (backed up once); off puts it back.
UI_pzopt_tip_audioLimiter: The game mixes in 5.1 at 32 kHz and has no limiter: a gun fired next to you over alarms and a horde went over full scale and the sound card clipped it (about 6,000 clipped samples in 25 s in the test scene). FMOD's own limiter now sits at the very end of the mix; below its ceiling it changes nothing. Applies on the next launch.
UI_pzopt_tip_audioLimiterCeilingDb: The highest level the mix may reach, in dB below full scale. -2 leaves room for the conversion to your sound card's rate (the game mixes at 32 kHz). Applies on the next launch.
UI_pzopt_tip_audioLimiterStereoFold: On headphones or stereo speakers the system mixer folds the game's six channels into two by adding them up, after the game, where nothing could stop the sum from clipping. With this on the game does that fold itself, just before the limiter, so the limiter sees what you hear. 5.1 and 7.1 devices keep their surround. Applies on the next launch.
UI_pzopt_tip_bakeBudget: Never-baked chunk-level textures made in one frame; the rest wait for the next frame. Used only while One prioritized bake budget per frame is off, and during a zoom's bake flood. 0 = unlimited, stock.
UI_pzopt_tip_bakeBudgetAdaptive: The bake budget halves after a frame that used more than 90 % of the frame-rate cap's time and grows by one after frames under 60 %, between 2 and the budget above.
UI_pzopt_tip_bakeFrameBudget: The most chunk-level bakes a frame (the highest the adaptive budget goes); changes to objects in a texture next to you and up to four new chunk levels always come on top.
UI_pzopt_tip_bakeMipLevels: The smaller copies of a chunk texture made after each bake; the widest zoom only samples the first ones, so 3 gives the same picture. 0 = stock, all 11.
UI_pzopt_tip_bakeScheduler: Every chunk-level bake of a frame (new chunks, cutaways, strong light, redraws, lighting drift) shares one budget, granted by urgency and distance, instead of each kind having its own; a level waiting past its kind's longest wait goes first, and changes to objects next to you always bake at once. Driving through Rosewood at 120 km/h the worst frames drop from 37 to 16 ms. Replaces the per-kind budgets below: they apply only while this is off and during a zoom's bake flood.
UI_pzopt_tip_bloodAppend: A new blood splat is drawn into the chunk textures it lands on instead of re-baking the chunk's floor, and into the neighbours' textures within a tile of a chunk edge, where stock cut it off until they re-baked. Hidden by the Blood Decals option: nothing happens at all (stock re-baked for it anyway). Where grass, a body or an item lies under it, or ambient occlusion or sun shadows touch that texture, the floor re-bakes as stock.
UI_pzopt_tip_bloodAppendPlants: Where grass or bushes grow under a new splat, the splat is drawn into the finished texture under those plants, the way the game's bake draws them after the blood (same light, same wind sway), instead of re-baking the whole floor. Bodies, items and flattened grass still re-bake.
UI_pzopt_tip_bloodAppendVegetation: Also draw new splats into finished textures where grass, a body or an item lies under them (the blood then covers them; stock bakes them over the blood). Off (default) = those floors re-bake.
UI_pzopt_tip_bloodBake: Blood on the floor is baked into the chunk textures. Stock walks up to 18,000 splats of the chunk and its eight neighbours on every bake and sets the shader, depth test and blend for each splat it draws. gpu (default): each chunk keeps its splats sorted once and a bake draws them in one instanced draw per chunk, with the same position, colour, age and light (pixel-identical to stock; on macOS it runs as cpu). cpu: the same list drawn as sprites, on any computer. off = stock.
UI_pzopt_tip_bloodFadeFix: Stock keeps drawing the splats pushed out at 1,000 per chunk: they were meant to fade out, but in chunk textures their fade only runs down one step per bake, so they stay for as long as the chunk is loaded. On: they go at the chunk's next bake. Off = stock.
UI_pzopt_tip_bloodGlintPct: With HDR output: how bright the highlights above white are.
UI_pzopt_tip_bloodRebakeCoalesceMs: A new splat on grass, a body or an item still re-bakes its floor (see above); it waits this long first, so the splats one hit throws over the next few frames share a single re-bake. 0 = at once, as stock.
UI_pzopt_tip_bloodReflectPct: How much of the sky and the scene the film mirrors (100: a liquid film's own amount, a few percent of the sky, more of what stands in the pool).
UI_pzopt_tip_bloodSettleSec: Some seconds after the first splat drawn into a finished texture, that floor re-bakes once in stock's exact order (blood under anything flat on the floor that the depth test cannot tell from it). 0 = never.
UI_pzopt_tip_bloodSheenPct: How bright the sun and lamp highlights on the pools' rims are.
UI_pzopt_tip_bloodWet: Fresh blood on the floor is a film of liquid until it dries: the rims of the pools catch the sun and the lamps, the sky and (with Reflections on) the zombies and walls standing in them are mirrored at the film's own angle, and with HDR output the highlights go above white. The film's shape comes from the splat itself (flat pools, bright edges) and it dries from the edges in. Walls, tables and bodies in front of the floor hide it. Windows, Linux and macOS (on a Mac with "macOS: OpenGL 4.1" on, the default).
UI_pzopt_tip_bloodWetMinutes: How long a splat stays wet, in game time.
UI_pzopt_tip_boneIndexCache: The head and feet bone indices the shadow asks for by name every frame are cached per skeleton.
UI_pzopt_tip_bootFileThreads: How many file threads decode while the boot pump runs; the pool shrinks to "File threads in game" at the world load. Default: cores - 6, at least 4.
UI_pzopt_tip_bootPump: A thread drives the game's file loading during boot, so texture pages and animations decode before the main menu instead of only once the menu starts drawing frames.
UI_pzopt_tip_borderlessFullscreen: KWin, Mutter and gamescope only switch variable refresh on for fullscreen windows; the stock borderless window is just a screen-sized window, so a G-SYNC / FreeSync display stayed at its fixed refresh (0 % of the time in VRR vs 100 % with this on, desktop KDE test). The window is held as a fullscreen window at the desktop's own resolution (no mode switch) and stays on screen when you switch away.
UI_pzopt_tip_cameraScreenPixels: Zoomed in closer than 100 %, stock moves the world in whole pixels of the zoomed image: 2 screen pixels at 50 %. On: in whole screen pixels, so the scroll is twice as fine at 50 % and every tile still lands exactly on a pixel. No change at 100 % and out.
UI_pzopt_tip_centerFirstLoad: The chunks around you load and light first and the world appears as soon as they are ready; the rest streams in around you.
UI_pzopt_tip_charDrawPrep: The draw data of every zombie model on screen (its lights, one render record and matrix palette per body and clothing model, the depth and light setup) is built on worker threads before the game thread queues the draws in the stock order; stock built it one zombie at a time on the game thread. Same pixels.
UI_pzopt_tip_charDrawThreads: Threads of the zombie draw-data pool; the data has to be ready before the zombies are queued. More than cores - 2 is clamped.
UI_pzopt_tip_chunkGridFollowView: The camera looks at you from above, so on an upper floor the ground in the middle of the screen is 3 tiles north and 3 tiles west of you per level. With a render distance wider than vanilla the grid then moves with that ground point, so the screen corners stay filled upstairs as on the ground floor (25 at 5120x2160 up to level 8). You always stay at least as far from every grid edge as in vanilla; a grid no wider than vanilla never moves. Off = the grid stays centred on you and the top corners go dark from the second or third floor at the widest zoom. Single player only. Applies on the next launch.
UI_pzopt_tip_chunkGridWidth: How many chunks (8 tiles each) per side are loaded, simulated, lit and drawn around you. Vanilla picks it from the screen size but stops at 19 (152 tiles), sized for 1080p: on a 4K or ultrawide screen the world ends before the screen corners at the widest zooms. Auto picks the smallest grid that fills your screen at the widest zoom, never less than vanilla (21 at 3840x2160, 25 at 5120x2160, vanilla at 1080p). Smaller than vanilla helps CPU-limited setups (4 cores, heavy mod lists, NPC mods), with the world ending nearer the screen edge. Larger simulates zombies, vehicles and sounds further out and moves every resource below the other way. Only the grid size changes; zombie AI, streaming and culling are untouched.
UI_pzopt_tip_chunkHandoffDivisor: How many freshly loaded chunks join the world per frame: at most 1 + queued/divisor instead of stock's up to 4, so a chunk row arriving at once is spread over a few frames instead of one long one. 0 = stock.
UI_pzopt_tip_cloudOpacityPct: How much of the sun a thick cloud holds back (100: all of it, so the shade under it is as dark as a building's shadow).
UI_pzopt_tip_cloudScalePct: The size of the clouds (100: fair-weather cumulus, their shadows a hundred to two hundred tiles across).
UI_pzopt_tip_cloudShadows: The shadows of the clouds drift over the sunlit (or moonlit) ground, walls and roofs with the wind: as many as the weather's cloud cover, changing shape as they go, lying where the sun ray through each cloud meets the ground. Under a cloud the sunlit outdoors takes exactly the shade of a building's shadow, and the shadows the sun casts fade there; characters and cars walking into one are shaded too. Full overcast has no cloud gaps and so no shadows. Windows and Linux. Applies on the next launch when sun shadows or cloud shadows were off when the game started (the game's own shaders stay untouched then).
UI_pzopt_tip_cloudSpeedPct: How fast the cloud shadows travel, % of the wind at the clouds' height (they follow the game's clock: they stop when it is paused and race with fast-forward).
UI_pzopt_tip_colorGrading: The picture is colour graded by time of day and weather, like a film: nights shift towards the desaturated blue-green your eyes see in the dark (the Purkinje effect) while lamps and fires keep their colour, dawn is pink and cool in the shadows, the hour before dusk golden, overcast and rain greyer and cooler, storms dark and cold, fog soft and flat. Clear daylight is unchanged. The game's own screen filter and the grade become one colour lookup per pixel (the game's invisible film grain is left out). Custom looks: .cube files named base, night, dawn, dusk, overcast, rain, storm, fog or snow in Zomboid/pzopt/luts. Windows, Linux and macOS (on a Mac with "macOS: OpenGL 4.1" on, the default).
UI_pzopt_tip_colorGradingNightPct: How much dark places at night lose their colour and turn blue-green, like human night vision. 0 keeps the night's colours.
UI_pzopt_tip_colorGradingPct: How strong the grade is. 0 would be the game's own colours.
UI_pzopt_tip_corePlacement: On CPUs with fast and efficient cores (the Ryzen AI 300 series' Zen 5 + Zen 5c, Intel's P + E core chips, Apple silicon), which cores the game's threads run on. Linux put the game's lighting, compiler, audio and loader threads on the fast cores as often as not. Auto (the default) keeps all of that on the efficient cores and moves the game and render threads to the fast cores only while they would otherwise miss the frame cap. Efficient puts every thread on the efficient cores; Performance keeps the game and render threads on the fast cores and the rest on the efficient ones. Off = stock: the operating system decides. Linux sets the cores directly; macOS gets the matching quality-of-service classes. Applies on the next launch.
UI_pzopt_tip_cursorLatch: With "Lock cursor to window" the game draws its own cursor where the mouse was when the frame started, so it trails the hand by the whole frame pipeline. With this on it is moved to the newest pointer position just before the frame is drawn. The OS cursor (lock off) has no such lag. Applies on the next launch.
UI_pzopt_tip_curtainDepthNudgePct: Closed curtains draw this much nearer the camera than their tile geometry says, so a baked window never shows through them (north windows sit 0.017 tile in front of their curtain in the game's tile geometry).
UI_pzopt_tip_cutawayFast: When walls are cut away around you, the game tests every square of every chunk level on screen to find the squares that hide others. A chunk level that has not changed now replays the mask it stored last time. Same picture.
UI_pzopt_tip_cutawayInvalidateChanged: Each cutaway visit re-flags every cut-away wall square, and stock re-bakes every chunk holding one on every visit, which runs almost every frame while you move through a town. Only the chunks where a square's cutaway flag actually changed are re-baked. Same picture.
UI_pzopt_tip_cutawayRadius: The wall cutaway only visits the chunks within this many chunks of the camera instead of every chunk on screen. 0 = stock (every chunk on screen).
UI_pzopt_tip_cutawayVisitPrefilter: A cutaway visit only walks the squares of walls that occlude a cut-away room, belong to a collapsing building or may hide a window being peeked through; the others are skipped before their squares are looked up. Same result.
UI_pzopt_tip_darknessFloorBasements: Basements and everything below ground get the darkness floor too. Off: below ground stays as dark as the game makes it.
UI_pzopt_tip_darknessFloorPct: No place you have already seen gets darker than this: pitch-black rooms and nights keep a faint, cool light, so you can make out the floor, walls and furniture instead of a black void. Lamps, fires, torches and daylight are unchanged; places you have never seen stay black. Basements stay pitch black unless you tick the next box. Applied to the game's own light values.
UI_pzopt_tip_dlssOutputFilter: How a DLSS output smaller than the screen (the size above) is brought to the screen.
UI_pzopt_tip_dlssOutputPct: The size DLSS writes. Writing less than the screen and letting a cheap filter (below) finish the upscale is what makes DLSS faster than no upscaler on a 4K screen, and with the sharpen finish the picture is sharper than full-size DLSS with the default model. At DLAA (native) the output is always the screen size.
UI_pzopt_tip_dlssPreset: Which DLSS network runs. The transformer models (DLSS 4: k, j, m, l and NVIDIA's default) reconstruct the most detail; the older convolutional models e and f are a little softer, and e leaves no trails in this game (recommended). m and l are too heavy for a 4K screen.
UI_pzopt_tip_dlssSharpen: Asks DLSS for its mild extra sharpening pass on top of the super resolution; off is the plain reconstruction.
UI_pzopt_tip_dlssWaterCurrent: DLSS blends each frame with the previous ones; the water's ripples move in place with no motion vectors, so that blend slowed them to half speed. On: the water pixels show the frame just drawn, so rivers and lakes flow like the stock game. Off = DLSS's own image everywhere (an A/B).
UI_pzopt_tip_dlssWaterHistoryPct: With the water from the current frame, how much of the previous frame's water is mixed in. DLSS shifts each frame by a fraction of a pixel; one frame of history evens that out so the ripples do not shimmer, without slowing them.
UI_pzopt_tip_driveCameraLate: Stock places the camera inside the player's update; when the game updates the player before the car (it depends on the save), the camera sits one physics step behind on most frames and catches up on the others: the car jumps back and forth by ~20 pixels, 20 times a second (the rubber band). On: the camera is centred on the driver after every update of the frame. Included in the setting above whenever that is on.
UI_pzopt_tip_driveLookSmooth: The camera looks ahead of a moving car. Stock moves that look-ahead in whole pixels, paced by a millisecond clock, so the car creeps across the screen in uneven steps. On: fractional, paced by the nanosecond clock (the car moving backwards on screen: 4.2 to 1.0 % of frames at zoom 1).
UI_pzopt_tip_earlyModels: Models and the animation queue register right after the scripts load instead of later in boot, so the boot pump has about 2 s more for the 2,209 animations.
UI_pzopt_tip_earlyTilePacks: The tile texture packs and depth maps start decoding before the boot Lua load instead of after it, so the world load does not wait for them.
UI_pzopt_tip_ecsLookupFast: Every state-machine, action-context and animation-variable access of a character went through a class walk, a map probe and a reflective cast; the answer is now remembered and zombies keep their component in a field. Same results.
UI_pzopt_tip_emitterDefer: With entity updates on other cores, a zombie's per-frame sound work (FMOD parameters, position, tick) is queued instead of run on the worker, and the game thread runs the queue right after the batch in the stock order - same frame, before anything renders. The workers no longer wait for each other at the sound locks.
UI_pzopt_tip_emitterIdleSkip: A zombie that is not making any sound skips its three sound emitters entirely; a flag set when it starts a sound brings it back. Same sounds.
UI_pzopt_tip_emitterParamSkip: A character's sound parameters (the floor material under its feet, the room it is in) are recomputed only while it actually has a sound playing or about to start; stock recomputed all of them for every zombie every frame and wrote them nowhere. Same sounds.
UI_pzopt_tip_enabled: Off = the game runs stock: every override takes its original code path and the settings below are ignored. On = the settings below apply. The Tools are not affected: the performance overlay works either way.
UI_pzopt_tip_enhancementsEnabled: Off = the picture is the stock game's: upscaling, sprite filtering, HDR output, ambient occlusion, sun shadows, reflections, car glass, the darkness floor, remembered places, colour grading, per-pixel lighting, god rays and foliage sway are all off, whatever the settings below say (they are kept for when you switch it on again). On = the settings below apply. HDR output, per-pixel lighting, reflections and car glass switch on the next launch.
UI_pzopt_tip_entityUpdateParallel: Calm zombies run their update on the worker threads instead of one after another on the game thread, with the stock four-step sequence per zombie kept. Players, animals, vehicles and busy zombies stay on the game thread; Lua events fired from a worker are replayed on the game thread in the stock order; a zombie that fails on a worker turns the batching off for the rest of the session. The batched zombies see each other where they stood at the start of the batch (like the separation pass), and their random rolls come in a different order. In a 2,700-zombie horde: 67 to 95 fps; the horde behaves the same in the brawl check (2026-10-13). On by default.
UI_pzopt_tip_entityUpdatePipeline: With zombie updates on other cores, the workers run the frame's zombies while the game thread updates the animals, vehicles and busy zombies, instead of the game thread waiting for the batch. The frame-timing multiplier each zombie reads is captured per bucket, so timings stay right. Only active while the setting above is on.
UI_pzopt_tip_entityUpdateSafeStates: With entity updates on other cores, only zombies that are idle, walking or following a path, with no player within 12 squares, nothing physical going on (no bullet hit being tracked, no ragdoll, not falling, not burning, not grappled) run on the worker threads; everything else updates as in the stock game. Without it the worker threads crashed the game when zombies were shot. On by default.
UI_pzopt_tip_fileInflight: How many file tasks are handed to the file threads at once. Default: 4 per file thread; stock 16.
UI_pzopt_tip_fileThreads: Worker threads of the game's file loading (texture decoding, model and animation import, depth maps), in game and during the world load. Stock: 2 on up to 4 cores, else 4; default here: half your cores, at least 4.
UI_pzopt_tip_fliesToggleFix: The corpse-flies update cleared and set the same square's flies every few frames while driving, and each toggle re-baked the chunk texture next to you at once; the clear is now skipped when the square stays the same. Same result.
UI_pzopt_tip_fmodAsync: The sound system and its 12 sound banks start on a thread of their own during boot, alongside the rest of the start-up, instead of first thing on the main thread.
UI_pzopt_tip_fogMaskFrames: The fog rows are built from per-chunk masks of the squares that take fog instead of reading every square each frame; a mask is refreshed this many frames after its last refresh, so a newly built room reaches the fog within that many frames. 0 = read every square every frame.
UI_pzopt_tip_fogPass: EXPERIMENTAL. Heavy fog is drawn in one batch into a smaller buffer, tested against the scene's depth and blended over it once, instead of up to twelve layers per pixel. Same look; on the 5K desktop the 120 km/h drive in heavy fog runs at about 340 instead of 220 fps (447 in clear weather). Known issue: power lines can flicker slightly in fog while the camera moves; disabling this removes it (stock fog).
UI_pzopt_tip_fogScalePct: The fog pass's buffer size per axis as a percentage of the screen. Fog is soft, so the smaller buffers look the same, and edges where fog meets walls or wires are resolved against the real depth. 100 = full resolution.
UI_pzopt_tip_foliageSway: Grass, bushes and trees bend and sway in the wind: they lean with it, gusts roll across fields and tree crowns, each plant swings at its own pace (grass quick, trees slow) and leaves flutter. The plants stay in the game's cached chunk pictures; their pixels are moved by the wind as the pictures go on screen. The game's own "Wind sprite effects" option (off by default) does this by drawing every plant every frame instead. Windows, Linux and macOS (on a Mac with "macOS: OpenGL 4.1" on, the default).
UI_pzopt_tip_foliageSwayPct: How far the plants bend in the wind.
UI_pzopt_tip_foliageSwayTaps: How the moving plants cover what is behind them: 1 moves each plant's pixels inside its own outline only; 2 to 4 also let the plant's edge move out over the ground behind it, looking 1 to 3 steps upwind.
UI_pzopt_tip_frameClockSmooth: Each frame simulates the time the previous one took; with vsync or a frame cap the frames reach the screen on a fixed grid, so a frame that started half a millisecond late moves the world by that much more than the screen shows. On: frames close to the grid step exactly one (or two...) refresh periods and the difference to the real clock is fed back slowly, so game time never drifts.
UI_pzopt_tip_frameStartGate: When the render thread is still busy with the previous frame, the game waits for it before it reads input rather than after building the new frame on older input. Only matters when the render thread or the GPU is the limit. Applies on the next launch.
UI_pzopt_tip_frameThreads: Threads of the per-frame zombie batches (bone math, decision rules, lighting reads; the game thread joins in). More than cores - 1 is clamped. Default 8, or on a CPU with fast and efficient cores and more than nine cores one per core besides the game thread's, at most 11.
UI_pzopt_tip_fsrSharpnessPct: The contrast-adaptive sharpening (RCAS) after the FSR 1.0 upsample; 80 is AMD's usual default.
UI_pzopt_tip_gameThreadProfileHz: Higher resolves short phases sooner. 25 (the default) gives 125 samples over the overlay's 5 s window. Sampling only runs while the overlay is shown or its log is on, and only when the tree, the flame graph, the detailed verdict or the log needs it.
UI_pzopt_tip_godRays: Sunlight (and moonlight) falls through windows and open doorways into rooms as shafts of light in the dust, with sunlit patches on the floor, tables and walls where it lands, cut exactly by the window frames; outdoors, in fog, rain and morning mist, the shadows of buildings and trees stretch through the haze; torches, headlights and lamps glow in the dust and fog around them. Walls, roofs, upper floors, curtains and barricades block the light; tree crowns let it through their gaps. Windows, Linux and macOS (on a Mac with "macOS: OpenGL 4.1" on, the default).
UI_pzopt_tip_godRaysDustPct: How dusty the air in rooms is: the more dust, the brighter the shafts through the windows (0: only the sunlit patches).
UI_pzopt_tip_godRaysHazePct: How hazy the open air is: fog, rain and the mist of the hours after sunrise add to it, and the shadows of buildings and trees stretch through it as rays. A clear midday has almost none (and costs nothing).
UI_pzopt_tip_godRaysLocal: Torch beams, headlights, street lamps and fires glow in the dust of rooms and in fog and rain, their cones shaped by the light's reach and direction.
UI_pzopt_tip_godRaysLocalPct: How strong the glow around torches, headlights and lamps is.
UI_pzopt_tip_godRaysPatchPct: How bright the sun lands on the floor, furniture and walls where a shaft reaches them (0: the shafts only).
UI_pzopt_tip_godRaysStrengthPct: How bright the shafts of light and the sunlit patches are.
UI_pzopt_tip_gpuMaxFrames: After each frame the render thread waits until at most this many frames are waiting for the GPU (the driver's "low latency mode"). Helps a GPU-bound game; with vsync the low-latency mode above does more and should be used instead. Applies on the next launch.
UI_pzopt_tip_gpuPstate: AMD Radeon on Linux only. At a frame cap the Radeon driver runs the GPU at its top clock and highest voltage for a few milliseconds a frame and then idles it. Auto (the default) measures the GPU time of every frame and holds the lowest fixed clock level that keeps the cap, stepping up the moment it does not. Standard holds about 1 GHz, min_sclk the lowest shader clock (about 640 MHz). The level applies to the whole GPU while the game runs and is released when it exits (a crash included). Off = stock: the driver's automatic clocks. Applies on the next launch.
UI_pzopt_tip_gridStackInterval: While the camera's square and facing stay the same, the scan of which buildings stand in front of you (and which of their floors to hide) runs only this often; a new square, a turn or the game's own request rescans at once. 0 = every frame, stock.
UI_pzopt_tip_guardedCallbacks: Eight zombie rules (has a target, should sprint, should attack, thump, lunge, attack a car, passenger exposed, eat a body) only change something in rare cases (a target that died, a door that is out of reach, a body next to it). They are now read on the worker threads, and the rare case falls back to the game thread before anything changes.
UI_pzopt_tip_hdr: Turns HDR on even when the automatic check finds no HDR screen. The game is shown as HDR: the menus and the HUD stay at your desktop's white, lamps, torches, headlights, fires and lightning go above it up to your screen's peak. Needs an HDR screen with HDR switched on in the desktop settings; on Linux the game then runs as a native Wayland window. On a Mac the lights and lightning go above the screen's white (the other HDR settings below are Linux only for now); an XDR display (MacBook Pro 14/16, Pro Display XDR) has the most room above it. Without an HDR screen, or on Windows for now, nothing changes. Applies on the next launch.
UI_pzopt_tip_hdrAuto: On by default: when the game starts on an HDR screen it is shown as HDR by itself (Linux: a Wayland desktop with HDR switched on; macOS: a display with HDR headroom, e.g. a MacBook Pro's XDR screen), on an SDR screen nothing changes. Untick it to keep the SDR picture on an HDR screen. Applies on the next launch.
UI_pzopt_tip_hdrBloomPct: The light the HDR highlights add also spills a little into the dark around them, the way a bright lamp glows in the eye. Linux only for now.
UI_pzopt_tip_hdrGlintPct: The sun glitters on rivers, lakes and puddles above the desktop's white, the sky reflects in them, and at night lamps, torches and headlights glint on the water. Linux only for now.
UI_pzopt_tip_hdrItmPct: At night, pixels that are already near white (lit windows, bright signs) are also pushed above the desktop's white. Off in daylight. Linux only for now.
UI_pzopt_tip_hdrLightPct: What makes it HDR: every square the game lights with a lamp, a torch, a headlight or a fire is shown brighter in proportion to how much light falls on it, up to the screen's peak, with its colours intact; the dark stays dark.
UI_pzopt_tip_hdrPaperPct: The brightness of the world's ordinary (unlit by lamps) surfaces relative to your desktop's white. Lower leaves more room above it for the highlights: they look brighter by contrast. Linux only for now.
UI_pzopt_tip_hdrPeakNits: Caps the brightest highlight below what the screen can do, if the peaks are too much. Linux only (macOS gives no nits).
UI_pzopt_tip_hdrSaturationPct: A little more colour saturation, using the wider colour range of HDR screens. Linux only for now.
UI_pzopt_tip_hdrSunPct: On a clear day the sunlit outdoors is shown brighter than the SDR picture by this much, less with the sun low or behind clouds; shade and interiors stay as they are. Linux only for now.
UI_pzopt_tip_hdrUiNits: The brightness of the menus and the HUD. By default the desktop's own white, so switching windows does not change brightness. Linux only (on a Mac the screen brightness sets it).
UI_pzopt_tip_headOnWorker: The start of each zombie's animation step (which way it faces, its aim angle, whether it is turning, turning 90 degrees or turning around) runs in its decision-rule task on a worker thread instead of on the game thread; a zombie starting or re-aiming a 180-degree turn, whose event must go through the game thread first, is left to it.
UI_pzopt_tip_hearingHoist: When a zombie looks for the loudest noise around it, its own hearing and the square it stands on are now looked up once per search instead of once for every noise in the list. Same answer.
UI_pzopt_tip_hotsaveIntervalSec: Minimum seconds between the saves of the meta grid, game time, world map and entities that follow every drained chunk-save queue. Default 30; 0 = stock, after every drain.
UI_pzopt_tip_hotsaveStaged: The periodic hot save writes the meta grid and the other systems one part per streamer update instead of all in one frame. Off by default: the parts of one save are then written at different moments, so the meta-grid files could disagree with each other.
UI_pzopt_tip_hotsaveWarmup: Dropping or looting items makes the game save the map's building, room and zone records on the next save pass, on the game thread. The first time in a session that code ran cold: a stutter a moment after the first transfer. It is now run three times into a scratch buffer on the loading screen, so that first save runs warm.
UI_pzopt_tip_inputLatch: The game polled input once, right after the previous frame was shown, and used that until its next frame started (the frame limiter's idle time later). With this on, the game asks for a fresh poll the moment its frame starts: mouse and controller reach the game in ~2 ms instead of ~5.5 at 240 fps, and up to a frame sooner at low frame caps. Applies on the next launch.
UI_pzopt_tip_itemParamSwitch: Item script fields dispatch through a switch instead of a chain of 361 text comparisons per parameter.
UI_pzopt_tip_jitSteady: Java's optimising compiler leaves out the branches a method never took while it was being profiled; when the game later takes one (a new street, a different zombie state) the compiled code is thrown away and compiled again. With this on the compiler keeps every branch, and since 2026-10-15 it no longer bets on the types a method was seen with either (-XX:-UseTypeSpeculation: about 45 such bets failed on the Louisville route, one of them in the player's sight check at the horde's first sight). The game runs as fast. Written into the game's launcher file for the next launch; the uninstallers take it out again.
UI_pzopt_tip_keyboardFresh: The game read the keyboard one frame behind the mouse and the controller: it filled its key table from the previous poll and swapped the new one in afterwards. With this on it reads the new one. One frame less for every key (4 ms at 240 fps, 17 ms at 60). Applies on the next launch.
UI_pzopt_tip_lazyPose: Every animation track searched the keyframes of all 60 bones every frame; the search now happens when a bone is first read. A zombie drawn as a far sprite reads one or two bones, a modelled one reads them in the bone batch on the workers. Same poses.
UI_pzopt_tip_lightInfoChunkGate: Before refreshing the 64 squares of a chunk level about to be re-baked, one question to the lighting engine says whether any of them changed; a square that was never read is always read. Same picture.
UI_pzopt_tip_lightInfoOncePerFrame: The per-square light-info call into the lighting engine is skipped when the same square was already refreshed this frame (a chunk level that needs both a re-bake and a lighting refresh asked twice). Same light.
UI_pzopt_tip_lightSwitchCheckFrames: Each light switch reuses its has-electricity answer for this many frames, so a power change (the grid going off, a generator) reaches a lamp up to that many frames late. 0 = every frame, stock.
UI_pzopt_tip_lightingBudget: Chunks whose square light info is refreshed in one frame; the rest continue next frame, and nothing still queued is lost when the next lighting pass arrives. 0 = unlimited, stock.
UI_pzopt_tip_lightingFlush: Chunks the per-frame lighting refresh budget still holds are refreshed just before the next lighting pass rewrites their dirty bits; off, they keep stale light until it changes again (chunk-sized dark patches in a headlight beam).
UI_pzopt_tip_lightingGlobalDeltaPct: A lightning flash or a fast dusk moves the whole scene's light at once; past this per-frame move the lighting re-bakes stay spread over frames instead of landing at once.
UI_pzopt_tip_lightingReadParallel: When a lighting pass lands, the per-square light reads of the queued chunk levels (two engine calls per visible square) run one chunk level per worker thread; the room-discovery hooks then run on the game thread in the stock order. Same light.
UI_pzopt_tip_lightingRebakeBudget: Textures dirtied only by a lighting change (daylight drift, a lightning flash) re-bake at most this many per frame. Used only while One prioritized bake budget per frame is off.
UI_pzopt_tip_lightingRebakeMaxFrames: A lighting-only re-bake lands after at most this many frames; a lightning strike or a fast dusk spreads over this window instead of one long frame.
UI_pzopt_tip_lightingRebakeMs: A chunk texture dirtied only by a small lighting change (daylight drift) is not re-baked more often than this. 0 = stock.
UI_pzopt_tip_lightingStrongBudget: How many chunk textures with a strong light change re-bake in the same frame; the rest keep the lighting-only re-bake hold. A torch or headlight beam touches a few per frame; turning moves the out-of-sight fade over every exterior tile. Used only while One prioritized bake budget per frame is off. 0 = no cap.
UI_pzopt_tip_lightingStrongDelta: A square whose light moved by this much since its texture was last baked (a torch or headlight beam sweeping in) re-bakes now, like stock; smaller drift keeps the lighting-only re-bake hold. Held, a moving beam showed as a patchwork of past angles, one per chunk. 255 = hold everything.
UI_pzopt_tip_lightingStrongFrameMs: A game-thread frame longer than this many milliseconds halves the number of strong-light re-bakes allowed next frame (it grows back on fast frames). Stops the slow frame, more re-bakes, slower frame loop of a big downtown horde. Used only while One prioritized bake budget per frame is off. 0 = fixed budget.
UI_pzopt_tip_lightingSyncPark: The lighting thread updates 15 times a second (the Lighting FPS setting). Between updates it now sleeps straight to the next one instead of using LWJGL's timer. Applies on the next launch.
UI_pzopt_tip_limiterSleep: While the game waits for its next frame under a frame cap, the stock limiter keeps one core busy spinning. This sleeps until 0.2 ms before the frame (1.5 ms on Windows, where a sleep wakes on the 1 ms timer tick) and spins only that: same frame timing. On by default except on Windows.
UI_pzopt_tip_loadWorkers: How many threads recalculate the first chunks around you while a world loads (361 at the vanilla render distance); afterwards the pool shrinks back to "Chunk worker threads". Default: half your cores.
UI_pzopt_tip_loaderCpuFixes: Lot headers, vehicle zones and room ids resolve once per cell instead of repeatedly while a world loads; identical results.
UI_pzopt_tip_losLightPrefetch: The squares the player's sight check reads have their light refreshed on the worker threads first. Off by default: measured slower than reading them one by one.
UI_pzopt_tip_luaChecksumExempt: When joining a server the game lists every Lua file under media/lua to the server; the pzopt files (this tab and its search index, the frame cap combo, the key binding, the update item) only exist on clients and a server without them refused the join with "File doesn't exist on the server". They are skipped like the game skips SandboxVars.lua. Applies on the next launch.
UI_pzopt_tip_luaIndexCache: A Lua method looked up through a class chain is remembered until any class changes. Exact; no measurable change on the UI scenes.
UI_pzopt_tip_luaInternConstants: Text constants of every Lua file are shared, so table lookups compare them by identity first. Exact; no measurable change on the UI scenes.
UI_pzopt_tip_luaPrecompile: Every Lua file is compiled on a thread pool during boot; the game takes the compiled code from that cache instead of compiling each file when it first runs it (at boot, and the server Lua and map zones at Continue).
UI_pzopt_tip_luaSkipEmpty: A window's draw, update or mouse handler that is an empty Lua function is not called. Exact; no measurable change on the UI scenes.
UI_pzopt_tip_macPresent: OpenGL frames on a Mac are shown on the 120 Hz grid, so a cap like 90 fps alternates 8 ms and 17 ms frames. Presented through Metal, a ProMotion or Adaptive-Sync display shows frames at any multiple of 4.17 ms in fullscreen: the frame cap is snapped to what the panel shows exactly (120, 80, 60, 48, 40 fps) and every frame is held on screen for exactly that long. It adds input delay: a frame is shown one panel step after the one before it.
UI_pzopt_tip_mapStreetCache: While the map is not moved or zoomed the whole street-label layout is reused.
UI_pzopt_tip_mapStreetMemo: The world map measured every street, translated every street name for every letter and sorted the visible streets with a list search in every frame. Lengths and names are now kept per view and language.
UI_pzopt_tip_mapVisitedFast: The map's dark / explored overlay was rebuilt pixel by pixel, re-computing the row width for every pixel; the first map open after loading rebuilds all 16 million. It is now built a row at a time, the same pixels.
UI_pzopt_tip_memoryLightPct: How bright rooms you have seen stay once they are out of sight (the game fades them to black).
UI_pzopt_tip_memoryTint: What you cannot see right now (behind walls, behind you) is drawn like a memory, desaturated, dimmer and cooler, with a soft edge, instead of darkened; rooms of a building you walked out of keep a dim remembered light and their furniture instead of going black. Zombies and other characters out of sight stay hidden as always. It replaces the view cone's own darkening in the same pass. Windows, Linux and macOS (on a Mac with "macOS: OpenGL 4.1" on, the default).
UI_pzopt_tip_memoryTintPct: How strongly what you cannot see is desaturated and dimmed. 100 turns it fully grey.
UI_pzopt_tip_mipmapArrays: Texture mipmaps and alpha premultiply are built row by row on byte arrays; same pixels as stock.
UI_pzopt_tip_modelLockPerInstance: The engine's model update lock was a single text constant shared by every character, so the worker threads queued behind each other on it. Each model now has its own lock; stock only ever updates a model from one thread.
UI_pzopt_tip_moonShadowPct: How dark a full moon's shadows are compared with the sun's.
UI_pzopt_tip_moonShadows: At night the moon casts the same soft shadows when it is up: where it really is for the game's date and hour, as strong as its phase allows (a full moon high in a clear sky casts clear shadows, a thin crescent barely any, a new moon none), once the sky is dark. The game's own night brightness already follows the moon's phase.
UI_pzopt_tip_noClickToStart: The loading screen goes straight into the world when loading is done instead of waiting for a click or A.
UI_pzopt_tip_noIntroWait: A new game shows click-to-start as soon as it is loaded instead of after the 33 s intro text; the lines still play behind it.
UI_pzopt_tip_noLoadFade: The main menu and the loading screen no longer fade to black before the world's own fade-in.
UI_pzopt_tip_noLoadingScreen: Single player: a plain black frame while the world loads and no fade from black into the world; with "Show the last view while loading" that view instead of the loading screen. The stock screen still appears for errors, a world-version dialog, a map download or a save conversion.
UI_pzopt_tip_occlusionGrantedOnly: The pass that finds which chunk levels are hidden behind buildings looks only at the levels baked this frame, not every one still waiting.
UI_pzopt_tip_occlusionSkipLightingOnly: The grid of squares hidden behind walls and the per-level counts of drawn squares are rebuilt only when a visible chunk level changed for a reason other than lighting drift. Lighting changes none of their inputs, so the result is the same.
UI_pzopt_tip_overlay: Frame rate, frame-time tail (p99, p99.9, max, 1%-low, jitter, spikes), GPU busy share, game and render thread load, and a frame-time graph. The key (F9) or L3 + R3 on a controller toggles it any time.
UI_pzopt_tip_overlayCorner: Where the overlay sits: top-left, top-right, bottom-left, bottom-right.
UI_pzopt_tip_overlayFlame: The last 5 s of stack samples as a flame graph: root (GameWindow.frameStep) at the bottom, callees above, width = share of the time, biggest first from the left; update green, render blue, lighting amber, pzopt frames magenta. Off by default. harness/flamegraph.py draws a whole run as an SVG.
UI_pzopt_tip_overlayFlameDepth: How many call levels above GameWindow.frameStep the flame graph shows.
UI_pzopt_tip_overlayFont: The UI font the overlay text uses. auto follows the screen height: CodeSmall under 1000 px, CodeMedium under 1800, CodeLarge above. Whatever the font, the panel fits the screen: the frame graph shows fewer frames, the flame graph keeps up to a third of the width (hints and legend are cut to the rest) or moves under the frame graph and long lines are cut when it would not.
UI_pzopt_tip_overlayFpsBlueAbove: Uncapped, or with follow-cap off: blue above this many fps.
UI_pzopt_tip_overlayFpsCapBluePct: At or above this share of the cap counts as at the cap. The limiter rarely lands exactly on it, so 100 is stricter than it looks.
UI_pzopt_tip_overlayFpsCapGreenPct: Green from this share of the cap up to the blue threshold.
UI_pzopt_tip_overlayFpsCapYellowPct: Yellow from this share of the cap up to the green threshold; red below it.
UI_pzopt_tip_overlayFpsColor: The fps number takes one of four colours by how close it is to the target; off = white like the rest of the line.
UI_pzopt_tip_overlayFpsColorBlue: Named colour, or a RRGGBB hex value typed into Zomboid/pzopt/options.ini.
UI_pzopt_tip_overlayFpsColorGreen: Named colour, or a RRGGBB hex value typed into Zomboid/pzopt/options.ini.
UI_pzopt_tip_overlayFpsColorRed: Named colour, or a RRGGBB hex value typed into Zomboid/pzopt/options.ini.
UI_pzopt_tip_overlayFpsColorYellow: Named colour, or a RRGGBB hex value typed into Zomboid/pzopt/options.ini.
UI_pzopt_tip_overlayFpsFollowCap: On: with a framerate cap the thresholds are percentages of it (the three "% of the cap" values). Off, or uncapped: the three fixed fps thresholds apply.
UI_pzopt_tip_overlayFpsGreenAbove: Uncapped, or with follow-cap off: green from this many fps up to the blue threshold.
UI_pzopt_tip_overlayFpsYellowAbove: Uncapped, or with follow-cap off: yellow from this many fps up to the green threshold; red below it.
UI_pzopt_tip_overlayGraph: A bar per presented frame (green under 1.1x the cap budget, amber under 2x, red above; GPU time in blue) with ms ticks and the budget line.
UI_pzopt_tip_overlayGraphHz: With "Draw the overlay as one texture" on, the frame-time bars are redrawn into that texture this often instead of drawn as ~480 sprites every frame. 0 draws them every frame.
UI_pzopt_tip_overlayLog: Writes Zomboid/pzopt-overlay.out, one CSV row per frame in MangoHud's column names, for harness/analyze.py. Harness runs log regardless.
UI_pzopt_tip_overlayPower: A line with the watts the machine draws while you play and the energy each frame costs (J/frame = watts / fps): CPU package, GPU board power, an AMD APU's socket, or the whole machine while a laptop runs on battery. Read from the counters the system exposes: NVIDIA GPUs through the driver (Windows and Linux), AMD GPUs and APUs, and on Linux the CPU's RAPL counters, which only root may read on most distributions (the line then says CPU n/a). While the frame log is on it also writes Zomboid/pzopt-power.out twice a second.
UI_pzopt_tip_overlayRefreshMs: How often the overlay's numbers, game-thread tree and verdict are recomputed and its texture redrawn. The frame-time graph has its own rate.
UI_pzopt_tip_overlaySampling: Records every presented frame, times the GPU with GL timer queries and samples the CPU load twice a second on a background thread. Off by default: without it F9 (or L3 + R3 on a controller) only shows a notice. "Show the overlay from boot" and "Log every presented frame" turn it on too.
UI_pzopt_tip_overlayStats: The lines at the top of the overlay.
UI_pzopt_tip_overlayTexture: The overlay's text, tree and flame graph only change four times a second, so they are drawn into an offscreen texture then and each frame shows that texture plus the live frame-time bars. Off draws every letter and box as its own sprite every frame (thousands of quads).
UI_pzopt_tip_overlayTree: What the game thread is doing, from its call stack sampled on a background thread: the phases (update / render / lighting) with their share of the time, under each the biggest sub-phases (chunk bakes, zombies, UI draw, frame hand-off...) with a bar, the wait share in red and the hottest methods. Also logged per second to Zomboid/pzopt-gamethread.out for harness/analyze.py.
UI_pzopt_tip_overlayVerdict: What is holding the frame rate below the cap.
UI_pzopt_tip_packIndex: Texture packs keep their page offsets under Zomboid/pzopt/packs, so the reader jumps to each page instead of scanning the packs at every boot.
UI_pzopt_tip_parallel: Chunk recalculation (collision, pathfinding and sight for every square of a freshly loaded chunk) runs on a pool of worker threads instead of the one streamer thread. Chunks are handed to the game in the same order with the same result. Off = the stock single-threaded pass.
UI_pzopt_tip_parallelDepthMaps: The 218 depth-map tilesets (how deep each pixel of a tile lies, for drawing order) decode at the same time instead of one at a time under one lock.
UI_pzopt_tip_persistentVbo: Sprite ring buffers use persistently mapped buffer storage instead of an orphan and re-map per batch. Matters most uncapped and zoomed out, where the render thread is the limit.
UI_pzopt_tip_persistentVboFrameSync: The persistent sprite buffers are fenced once per frame instead of per 64 KB batch, and a buffer last used 8 frames ago is reused without asking the driver.
UI_pzopt_tip_persistentVboSlots: Each persistent sprite buffer holds this many batches before it wraps, so a wrap rarely meets one the GPU still reads.
UI_pzopt_tip_physicsDefer: With entity updates on other cores, the two physics engine calls a zombie's update can make queue instead of running on the worker, and the game thread makes them right after the batch in the stock order - same frame, before anything renders. They are the bullet hitbox of a zombie you have a gun aimed at, and the contact test between a ragdolling zombie and a car. The physics engine is not safe to call from several threads at once, and a crash inside it cannot be caught and turned off the way a Java error can, so leave this on: without it, shooting into a horde with entity updates on other cores ends the game process. Only active while entity updates on other cores is on.
UI_pzopt_tip_physicsStepHz: The fixed rate Bullet runs the vehicles at. Matching the display (120 at 120 Hz) makes one step per frame, but only at exactly that frame rate; the drawing between steps above does the same at any rate and keeps the physics stock. For comparison.
UI_pzopt_tip_physicsStepMode: Frame steps make every frame advance the cars by exactly its own time, at the price of physics that change a little with the frame rate. For comparison.
UI_pzopt_tip_pixelLight: The world's light is drawn per pixel instead of being painted into the chunk pictures square by square. The game's own lighting still decides how much light every square gets and what walls hide; the picture follows it smoothly between squares instead of in blocky steps, and a torch or headlight beam is drawn from its own cone, so it has straight edges and follows your aim every frame. Nights look a little darker than stock: stock spreads every lit square's light half a square into its neighbours, even through walls. Windows, Linux and macOS (on a Mac with "macOS: OpenGL 4.1" on, the default). Applies on the next launch.
UI_pzopt_tip_playerLosFast: The list of everything you have spotted since the last quiet moment is searched once per spotted object per frame; stock walked it end to end each time, so in a horde the cost grew with the square of the zombies in view. The search is one hash probe now, and the sneak modifier zombies ask for is computed once per frame. Same list, same order.
UI_pzopt_tip_poolStatsBatched: Every reuse of a pooled engine object bumps shared statistics counters; the worker threads now count in private tallies and add them once per batch. Same totals, no fight over one memory line.
UI_pzopt_tip_pplAnalytic: Torches and headlights drawn from their cone, lamps and fires from their round falloff, pixel by pixel. Off: the game's per-square light only, smoothed between squares.
UI_pzopt_tip_pplNormals: Walls and objects turned towards a torch, a headlight or a lamp catch more of its light, those turned away less (the direction of every surface is read from the game's depth picture). Floors are unchanged.
UI_pzopt_tip_pplPackParallel: With per-pixel lighting, the light of every changed piece of the screen is packed on the worker threads, each piece into its own slot, instead of one after another on the game thread. Same light.
UI_pzopt_tip_pplPointLights: Lamps and fires drawn from their round falloff, pixel by pixel. Off: their light is the game's per-square light, smoothed between squares, and the chunk pictures they reach are drawn with the light-free program.
UI_pzopt_tip_pplShadows: Posts, fences, furniture, stairs and walls cast shadows into your torch's beam in their own shape: a shadow map of everything round the torch, built from the world's own depth (also what is off screen or hidden behind a wall), in the same frame, so the shadows move with the torch. Applies at the next launch.
UI_pzopt_tip_pplSmooth: The light changes smoothly from one tile to the next (no faint diamond pattern where its slope changes). Off: straight blends between tile centres.
UI_pzopt_tip_pplSpecPct: How bright the glints on wet ground are.
UI_pzopt_tip_pplTorchFeetGlow: A torch in your hands also lights a small circle round your feet, behind and beside you. Off: only the beam in front of you is lit. Applies at once.
UI_pzopt_tip_pplTorchNearChunk: With per-pixel lighting, whether a torch reaches a square is first decided for the whole 8x8 chunk; only a chunk a torch can reach tests its squares. Same result.
UI_pzopt_tip_pplWetSpecular: While the rain wets the ground outdoors (and while it dries), torches, headlights and lamps glint on it.
UI_pzopt_tip_pplWrapPct: Higher softens the effect of the surface direction: the sprites already carry painted shading, so a strong effect can shade them twice.
UI_pzopt_tip_preloadAnimSets: The player and zombie animation sets (XML) are read on a boot thread while the menu loads, instead of on the loader thread after you press Continue.
UI_pzopt_tip_presentPacing: The game samples its time at an even rate, but each frame takes a different time to update and draw, so on a variable refresh display the gaps between frames on screen wander around the game-time steps: judder. With this on each frame is held until a steady time after its game moment. At a 100 fps cap on a 165 Hz G-SYNC display frames landed on average 3.1 ms off their game-time step (54 % of them more than 2 ms off); held, 0.95 ms (13 %), for about 5 ms more input delay. On a fixed-refresh display it evens out when frames leave the game: driving through Rosewood at 240 Hz, frames off their slot 28 to 11 %, frame-to-frame jitter 1.3 to 0.4 ms, for ~1.7 ms more delay on average (~2.6 ms typical, less than one 240 Hz frame).
UI_pzopt_tip_profilerEnabled: Off = no performance overlay, no measuring and no frame log: the overlay's samplers never start and the toggle key only says the profiler is off, whatever the settings below say (they are kept for when you switch it on again). On = the settings below apply.
UI_pzopt_tip_profilerThreadMemo: Every performance probe in the game asks twice whether it is on a profiled thread, and the engine answers by scanning a list of thread names. The answer per thread is remembered. The game asks this whether or not its profiler is recording, so it helps in normal play.
UI_pzopt_tip_puddleCache: Rain puddles keep their prepared vertices per chunk level and only refresh the light, the camera offset and the depth each frame, instead of filtering, lighting and packing every wet square again. Same picture.
UI_pzopt_tip_puddleCacheFrames: A cached puddle batch is rebuilt with the stock code after this many frames at the latest; bakes and cutaway changes rebuild it at once. 1 = rebuild every frame (the cache does nothing).
UI_pzopt_tip_puddleEarlyZ: The puddle shaders take their depth from the vertex instead of writing it per pixel, so wet ground hidden behind walls, roofs and objects is skipped before the puddle shader runs. Same picture.
UI_pzopt_tip_puddleVbo: Each chunk level's cached puddles stay in their own buffer on the graphics card and are sent again only when a light changed, the camera crossed a chunk edge or the batch was rebuilt; nothing is copied per frame. Same picture. Works on top of the puddle cache above.
UI_pzopt_tip_ragdollCorpseGuard: When a shot zombie's ragdoll settles and it turns into a corpse, the game builds a second, invisible ragdoll for the corpse in the same frame from the animation left over, and nothing ever owns it: it stays in the physics world, counts against the maximum number of ragdolls, and quitting while one is there crashes the game on the way out. With this on no ragdoll is made for a character that is already a corpse. On by default.
UI_pzopt_tip_ragdollQuitSweep: Just before the physics world is destroyed on the way out of a game, any ragdoll still in it is removed first; the physics library destroys the world before its ragdolls, and a ragdoll left over then crashed the game at quit. A safety net behind the fix above. On by default.
UI_pzopt_tip_rainSplashesFast: Rain splashes start from a cheap local random generator: one draw per splash instead of one roll of the game's random generator per idle square per frame. Same chance, timing and sprites.
UI_pzopt_tip_rainTiles: Rain and snow repeat one particle cell across the screen. The cell is now prepared once and the graphics card draws it at every screen position, instead of every copy being prepared on both CPU threads. Same picture.
UI_pzopt_tip_rebakeBudget: Textures dirtied only by lighting drift or a redraw keep their previous image for a few frames past this many re-bakes a frame (object, tree and cutaway changes always re-bake). Used only while One prioritized bake budget per frame is off. 0 = unlimited, stock.
UI_pzopt_tip_rebakeMaxFrames: A held re-bake (a redraw) lands after at most this many frames. Used only while One prioritized bake budget per frame is off.
UI_pzopt_tip_reflectionPuddles: Puddles mirror the scene too once the rain has made them big enough (the rain's rings blur them).
UI_pzopt_tip_reflectionStrengthPct: How strongly the water mirrors the scene. Real water seen from the game's camera angle reflects little (a few percent, more on the side of a wave); higher is more of a mirror.
UI_pzopt_tip_reflections: Buildings, fences, trees, lamp posts, cars and characters are mirrored in rivers, lakes and puddles, rippled by the waves and the rain, sharp where they meet the water and softer further out, stronger at grazing angles of the waves. Characters' reflections are one frame behind. Windows, Linux and macOS (on a Mac with "macOS: OpenGL 4.1" on, the default; there the water finds its reflection by a slower search up its column). Turning it on applies on the next launch (the game's water and chunk shaders are only patched when it starts with reflections on; off, they stay exactly the game's own).
UI_pzopt_tip_reflexBoost: At a frame cap the GPU is idle most of each frame, so the driver lowers its clocks and the frame it does draw takes longer, which the input waits for. This holds the driver's "prefer maximum performance" setting while a world is loaded, what Reflex's On + Boost does. The driver drops it again when the game exits, even after a crash. Uses more power; NVIDIA only. Applies on the next launch.
UI_pzopt_tip_reflexCapFps: With vsync on, a game that runs a hair faster than the screen refills the queue the low-latency mode drained. Auto caps the frame rate at refresh - refresh x refresh / 3600 (157 at 165 Hz, 224 at 240 Hz), what Reflex does with vsync. On a fixed-refresh screen one frame in ~20 is shown twice. Applies on the next launch.
UI_pzopt_tip_reflexSleep: What NVIDIA Reflex does, built with OpenGL (Reflex itself has no OpenGL version): each frame measures how long it waited in the queue to the screen (the hand-off to the render thread, a vsync swap that blocks, the driver's queue), and the next frame starts that much later so it arrives just in time, carrying newer input. With vsync on and an uncapped game, together with the cap below: 25-28 ms from input to screen became 5-10 ms. Does nothing when nothing queues (a frame cap below the refresh, vsync off). Applies on the next launch.
UI_pzopt_tip_relief: The fine relief the art paints (mortar between bricks and stones, gaps between planks and floor tiles, roof shingles, cobbles) catches the light that moves: a low sun or the moon rakes it and the grooves fall into shade, a torch, headlight or lamp sweeping along a wall brings the stones out. Floors and walls only: furniture keeps its painted shading. Sun and moon: needs Sun shadows. Torches, headlights and lamps: needs Per-pixel lighting. Windows, Linux and macOS (on a Mac with "macOS: OpenGL 4.1" on, the default). Applies on the next launch.
UI_pzopt_tip_reliefDepthPct: How deep the grooves between bricks, planks and tiles are.
UI_pzopt_tip_reliefSunPct: How strongly the sun and the moon bring the relief out (the part of their light that reaches the surface directly: none in shade).
UI_pzopt_tip_reliefTorchShadowSteps: The grooves also fall into the shadow of their own edges in torch, headlight and lamp light (each lit pixel follows the light a few texels across the relief). The sun and the moon always have it (baked).
UI_pzopt_tip_renderChunkTopUp: Keeps this many empty chunk textures ready for the current zoom, made two a frame, so a burst of new chunks never waits for texture creation. 0 = stock: made when first needed.
UI_pzopt_tip_renderPrepParallel: Every character on screen asks the sun shadows how much sun reaches it (a walk through the buildings towards the sun) and the reflections whether water is near it. Both answers only read the world, so they are worked out on the worker threads while the game thread draws the ground; the characters then take them ready. Same picture.
UI_pzopt_tip_resumeShot: Quitting keeps the view around you (see Last view detail); Continue shows it while loading, its chunks appearing the way the world loads, and the world builds over it. Saves without it show the normal loading screen.
UI_pzopt_tip_resumeShotDetail: What the last view keeps when you quit: floors = the ground only; buildings = floors, walls, doors and furniture; world = everything that does not move, trees included; full = the frame as you left it, zombies and cars too. Taken at the next quit.
UI_pzopt_tip_roofHideDebounceFrames: A carport or pergola roof is hidden or shown only after the decision has held for this many frames, so a player on its edge (or pushed by zombies) does not make the roof flicker every frame.
UI_pzopt_tip_schedulerClassifyParallel: Every frame the game decides how often each zombie, animal and car is updated (distance, visibility, what it is doing); the worker threads compute it and the game thread files the results in the same order. Same schedule.
UI_pzopt_tip_scriptParserFast: Script comments are stripped in one pass and tokens parse without copying the rest of the file each time; identical output.
UI_pzopt_tip_separateFast: The pass that pushes overlapping zombies apart skips the half of the engine's version that only ever applies to the player, and the grid answer 'is my square walled off from that neighbour' is computed once per square per frame instead of once per zombie. Same positions.
UI_pzopt_tip_separateParallel: That push-apart is computed for the whole horde on worker threads before the update loop; the game thread applies each zombie's result at the same point in its update as before, so the collide events and window climbs keep their order. The neighbours' positions are read at the top of the frame instead of as the loop advances.
UI_pzopt_tip_shaderCache: A model takes a shader an earlier model already created instead of asking the render thread for its own and waiting a loading-screen frame for it.
UI_pzopt_tip_shadowPrep: The shadow blob under a zombie (head and feet projected to the ground) is computed right after its bones on the worker instead of in the render pass; same numbers.
UI_pzopt_tip_skinPalettePrecompute: The same worker also stores those matrices in the layout the shader reads, so the draw data copies one block instead of sixteen numbers per bone.
UI_pzopt_tip_skinTransformsPrecompute: The worker that blends a zombie's bones also multiplies them into the skin matrices of the body and clothing models it wore last frame, so the render pass finds them ready.
UI_pzopt_tip_skipIdChecks: A log-only check over every building and room of the map (six walks per load) runs in debug mode only; the game never uses its result.
UI_pzopt_tip_sleepCheckMemo: The game asks whether all players are asleep on the way into every character update, and a zombie asks several times per update; the answer cannot change inside a frame, so it is computed once.
UI_pzopt_tip_soundTickHz: How often per second the ambient-object sounds, the wall emitters, the room and weather sound parameters and the sound parameters of zombies making noise are refreshed. The sound engine applies them every 20 ms, so above ~60 fps stock recomputed them several times for every change you could hear. Below this rate nothing changes. 0 = every frame, stock.
UI_pzopt_tip_soundZoneCache: The ambient sounds (forest, farm, town and others) measure your distance to the map's zones in an 80x80 area. The answer is now reused while you stay on one square, for at most 30 frames, instead of scanned every frame. Same sound.
UI_pzopt_tip_spriteFilter: How the world's art is scaled to your zoom. The game draws it sharp at 100 % and 50 %, soft at 75 % (a linear blur) and when zoomed out (a blend of the full picture and a blurred half-size copy: the blurry look while driving). Sharp: zoomed in, every texel of the art stays a hard square and only the one screen pixel an edge crosses is blended by how much of it the texel covers, so edges are crisp at any zoom and do not crawl while the camera glides; zoomed out, a few samples per pixel from a sharper copy of the art keep fences, window frames and road lines sharp without shimmer. At 100 % the picture is the game's own. Nearest: hard pixels at every zoom-in step (75 % included), no blending. Off (stock) = the game's own filtering. Windows, Linux and macOS (on a Mac with "macOS: OpenGL 4.1" on, the default); with per-pixel lighting on it applies on the next launch.
UI_pzopt_tip_spriteFilterMin: How the sharp filter shrinks the art when you zoom out. The game blends a half-size and a quarter-size copy of the art (soft); the sharp filter reads the one copy that fits the zoom. Adaptive spreads two (or four) samples as the zoom approaches the next copy, where fine lines would otherwise shimmer; one sample is the sharpest with a little grain; four fixed samples is the steadiest and softest.
UI_pzopt_tip_spriteFilterSharpnessPct: 100 blends each texel edge over exactly one screen pixel, the smoothest motion. Higher narrows the blend: harder edges, a little more crawl while the camera glides.
UI_pzopt_tip_spriteFilterSprites: The tiles the game draws every frame instead of into the chunk pictures (open doors, items, things near the cut-away walls) get the same filtering, so they match the rest of the world.
UI_pzopt_tip_stateParamMemo: The per-character scratch values the AI states keep were looked up through two maps and allocated a throwaway object on every read. Same values, one probe, no allocation.
UI_pzopt_tip_sunShadowAnimals: Farm and wild animals cast sun shadows too.
UI_pzopt_tip_sunShadowCharacters: Characters cast the shadow of their body onto the ground, walls and furniture around them, drawn every frame, and a character standing in a building's or a tree's shadow is shaded too. Only characters drawn with a model (the ones near enough to animate); the far ones drawn as flat pictures cast a simple upright shape.
UI_pzopt_tip_sunShadowMeshes: Each character, animal and vehicle is drawn once more, as the sun sees it, into a small shadow picture of its own, and its shadow takes that shape: arms, legs, hair, clothes, backpacks and weapons; an animal's legs, head and tail; a car's body and wheels. How often the pose is renewed: "Sun shadows: update rate". Off: a simpler shape of rounded pieces.
UI_pzopt_tip_sunShadowRate: How often the true-shape shadow of a character, animal or vehicle takes its new pose. Every frame: the shadow is drawn in the same frame as the character, so arms and legs move in step with it; in big crowds at most 32 are renewed a frame (your own every frame), the rest in turns. 15 times a second: each pose is kept for several frames and shown a frame late, which reads as a slightly choppy shadow next to a smoothly animated character; the shadow still follows the character's position every frame.
UI_pzopt_tip_sunShadowSoftnessPct: How quickly a shadow's edge blurs with the distance from what casts it (the size of the sun's disk). 25 is close to real sunlight: a tree's shadow keeps its branches and leaves, a character's its arms and legs; 100 and more blur every shadow into a soft shape; 10 is as sharp as the real sun.
UI_pzopt_tip_sunShadowStockFadePct: Where a character or a vehicle casts a real sun shadow, the game's own round shadow under its feet fades by this much (it was a second shadow beside the sun's). Overcast, at night and indoors it stays.
UI_pzopt_tip_sunShadowStrengthPct: How much of the daylight a full shadow takes away on a clear day. Clouds, rain and fog lower it further.
UI_pzopt_tip_sunShadowTorches: At night (and in dark places), characters caught in a torch beam or in headlights cast long soft shadows away from the light. The one holding the torch does not shadow their own beam.
UI_pzopt_tip_sunShadowTreeCards: A tree casts the shadow of its own picture, trunk, branches and leaves, in one piece from its foot to its crown, turned towards the sun so it never thins to a line. Off: a soft oval for the crown.
UI_pzopt_tip_sunShadowVehicles: Cars and trucks outdoors cast a sun shadow of their body.
UI_pzopt_tip_sunShadows: By day, walls, trees, fences, cars parked in the world's pictures and furniture outdoors cast soft shadows of the sun onto the ground and onto each other: sharp where they touch the ground, softer further away, like real sunlight. The sun stands where it really does over Kentucky for the game's date and hour (high and short-shadowed in summer, low and long in winter, rising in the north-east in June and the south-east in December), so the shadows turn and lengthen through the day; rain and fog thin them out and they fade away at dusk. Indoors stays as it is (rooms have a roof). Characters, animals and cars cast and take shadows too (the settings below). Windows, Linux and macOS (on a Mac with "macOS: OpenGL 4.1" on, the default).
UI_pzopt_tip_texCompress: Only matters with the game's own "Texture compression" option on (the low-end preset and the Steam Deck defaults). Stock hands every texture to the graphics driver uncompressed and lets it compress; Mesa (Linux AMD and Intel) does that on the CPU inside each upload, so after boot the main menu stutters for several seconds. Auto: the file threads prepare each texture and the GPU builds its mip levels and compresses it where OpenGL 4.3 compute runs, else as Worker. Worker: the file threads also compress them, the GPU does no compression work. Driver = stock. Applies on the next launch.
UI_pzopt_tip_textureBufferMb: Decoded texture bytes that may wait for the render thread before the decoders pause. 50 = stock and the default.
UI_pzopt_tip_tileDefPreload: The ~60k tile sprites are built on a thread while the main menu loads; Continue only binds their textures instead of parsing the tile files again.
UI_pzopt_tip_translucentLightsPerFrame: Translucent light fixtures that have a lit sprite (ceiling lights, lamps) are drawn every frame as in the stock game, so a lit ceiling light never shows through the floor or roof above it (a gas-station canopy's tubes did).
UI_pzopt_tip_translucentOrderCache: Objects drawn every frame (windows, doors, wind-blown plants, items) are put in drawing order level by level, every frame. That order only changes when the level changes, so it is kept and reused until then. Same order, checked against the recomputed one over a whole drive.
UI_pzopt_tip_translucentTilesInChunkText: Fences, railings, wall decorations and overlays (16,476 tile kinds carry the game's Translucent flag) bake into the chunk textures instead of being drawn every frame; the ones fading near you stay per frame.
UI_pzopt_tip_treeAppend: A newly loaded chunk's trees that reach into an already baked neighbour texture are drawn on top of it instead of re-baking the whole texture. Same picture.
UI_pzopt_tip_treeBakeDirect: Baked trees go through the plain sprite path; the game's batched path dropped the largest (jumbo) trees near buildings. Used only while Trees: crowns across textures, depth by height is off.
UI_pzopt_tip_treeBakeMaxChunksPerSec: While chunks stream in faster than this (walking loads about 9 a second, driving at 60 km/h about 32, at 120 km/h about 72), new chunk textures are baked without their trees and the trees are drawn every frame instead: a texture that lives only a second or two while driving is not worth baking trees into. Textures already baked keep their trees until they re-bake anyway. 0 (default) = always bake; the Low-end hardware preset uses 24.
UI_pzopt_tip_treeBakePass: Baked trees are drawn by their own pass: into every chunk texture the crown reaches (a jumbo tree is up to 7 tiles wide) and with a depth that rises with the crown like walls do. Off = trees are clipped at their chunk texture's border and cut by upper-floor walls behind them (issue #5).
UI_pzopt_tip_treesInChunkTexture: Static trees are drawn once into the chunk textures instead of every frame; only trees that fade around you, sway in the wind or carry an effect stay per frame. Off = stock (every tree every frame).
