UI_pzopt_tip_floorDecalsPerFrame: Translucent tiles that lie on the ground (manhole covers, drains) are drawn every frame as in the stock game, over the rain puddles. Baked, a manhole cover in a puddle flickered in stripes while you walked, most visibly zoomed out.
UI_pzopt_label_gcHeap: Java memory for the game (heap size)
UI_pzopt_tip_gcHeap: The most memory the game's Java objects may use. Auto (the default) gives the game 4 GB, or 8 GB when 30 or more mods are enabled (in the main menu or in the save you played last), never more than half your RAM; the game ships with 3 GB. When the heap is full Java stops the game to clean it up, and a big horde or a long mod list fills the game's 3 GB. With a big mod list pick 6 or 8 GB; the larger sizes are for very large mod lists (the most any test needed was 4.7 GB, with 132 mods). A size over half your RAM is lowered to half (64 GB needs a 128 GB machine). From 32 GB up Java stores every object reference in 8 bytes instead of 4, so a 32 GB heap holds less than a 31 GB one would and every collection walks more memory: go past 24 GB only if you need far more than that. Auto never lowers a larger heap you set yourself in ProjectZomboid64.json, and a size you edit there by hand stays yours until you pick another one here. Written into the game's launcher file for the next launch; the uninstallers put the game's own value back where the mod's value still stands.
UI_pzopt_label_luaGcNoop: Ignore mods' requests for a full memory clean-up
UI_pzopt_tip_luaGcNoop: Some mods call Lua's collectgarbage() to "free memory". In this game that is a full stop-the-world collection of all of Java's memory, which Java does on its own anyway when it needs to. With this on (the default) such calls return at once; asking how much memory Lua uses still works. Off = stock.
UI_pzopt_label_gcHeapFixed: Reserve the whole heap from the start
UI_pzopt_tip_gcHeapFixed: The heap starts at its full size instead of growing as the game needs it (Java's -Xms equal to the heap size), so it is never resized while you play. Off by default. Applies on the next launch.
UI_pzopt_label_gcPreTouch: Touch the heap's memory at boot
UI_pzopt_tip_gcPreTouch: Java writes every page of the heap at boot (-XX:+AlwaysPreTouch) so the system never has to hand out a page while the game runs. Best together with "Reserve the whole heap from the start". Off by default. Applies on the next launch.
UI_pzopt_tip_gcMode: The game ships with ZGC, which collects alongside the game on its own threads. G1 (the default) pauses the game for a few milliseconds a few times a minute instead. Auto: G1 on 4 cores or fewer, the game's own above. Applies on the next launch.
UI_pzopt_tip_gcPauseMs: The longest pause G1 aims for. Auto (0, the default) is 5 ms together with "G1 tuned for steady frames" and G1's own 200 ms target without it. With 200 ms the pauses in a horde were 50-75 ms long; with 5 ms and the tuned settings they are typically 3-5 ms. Applies on the next launch.
UI_pzopt_note_17ff0e4f73: 4 GB, 8 GB with 30 mods or more (default)
UI_pzopt_note_17f4b27180: 32 GB: Java's references double in size from here
UI_pzopt_note_f4de30bdd5: G1 on 4 cores or fewer, the game's own above
UI_pzopt_tip_entityShadows: The player, zombies, animals and cars take the shadows of buildings, walls, roofs and trees where they stand, part by part: a zombie half behind a wall has its legs in the shade and its head in the sun, a car under a porch roof is dark under the roof only. With Sun shadows turned on during a game, part by part from the next launch (one shade for a whole character until then). Off: one shade for a whole character, none for cars.
UI_pzopt_tip_entityShadowFormPct: How much the side of a body facing the sun is brighter and the far side darker. The overall brightness stays the same. 0: flat, as the game draws them.
UI_pzopt_label_entityShadowCasters: Shadows on characters: from other characters and cars
UI_pzopt_tip_entityShadowCasters: Characters and cars also shade each other: a zombie standing in a car's shadow, the player in a crowd's.
UI_pzopt_label_entityShadowSelf: Shadows on characters: their own shadow
UI_pzopt_tip_entityShadowSelf: A character's or a car's own body shades itself: an arm on the chest, a hat brim on the face, the cabin on the hood. For the 16 nearest characters, when zoomed in enough to see it.
UI_pzopt_tip_entityShadowImpostors: Zombies drawn as flat pictures (far away, big hordes) take the shade of where they stand too, one shade for the whole body.
UI_pzopt_label_entityShadowTorches: Shadows on characters: torches and headlights
UI_pzopt_tip_entityShadowTorches: At night (and in dark places), a character standing in another character's or a car's shadow from a torch or headlights is shaded too, as the ground there: a zombie behind another in your torch beam stays dark. With "Shadows from torches and headlights" this matches the shadows on the ground.
UI_pzopt_label_entityShadowAoPct: Shadows on characters: from the bodies next to them (%)
UI_pzopt_tip_entityShadowAoPct: Characters standing close together, or against a car, hide part of the surrounding light from each other: the sides that face each other are a little darker, so a packed crowd has depth instead of every body lit the same.
UI_pzopt_tip_entityShadowClouds: With cloud shadows on, a cloud's soft shadow crosses characters and cars as it crosses the ground: a car half under a cloud's edge is half shaded, and a character's head can be in the sun while their feet are not (the shadow falls along the sun). Off: one cloud value for each character or car.
UI_pzopt_profile_lowEndLookTip: The Low-end hardware set above plus the Visuals that cost nothing on that laptop, measured one by one walking and driving at the locked 60, then together: sharp sprite filtering, colour grading, god rays, remembered places tinted, and mirrors and windows that reflect (town walk: 2.1 %% of the screen's refreshes repeat a frame, 1.3 %% without them). Every other Visuals setting goes back to off: ambient occlusion doubled the missed frames while driving (it is baked into every arriving chunk), water reflections cost the render thread while driving, sun shadows, per-pixel light and zombie outlines cost the lock while walking. Mirrors apply on the next launch. See docs/findings-low-end-mode-2026-10-07.md.
UI_pzopt_tip_shaderWarmup: Shaders that were built the first time something needed them, in the middle of play, are built ahead: every model shader the game's scripts name during the loading screen, and the Visuals' own programs (foliage sway, god rays, wet blood) as the world appears. Matters most on the first launch after an update, when the graphics driver has none of them cached. Applies on the next launch.
UI_pzopt_tip_mirrorsWallMirrors: On: wall mirrors, mirrored medicine cabinets and dressers, and the gym's wall mirrors reflect the room in front of them and the people in it. Off: they look as in the game (a plain mirror texture), and only the windows and glass props reflect: for window reflections without the mirrors. Applies on the next launch.
UI_pzopt_tip_ripples: Anyone walking or running through a puddle, zombies, animals and you, rings it at every step, and car wheels leave trails of rings behind them. The rings are real water: each one a train of waves that spreads and fades (the longer waves run ahead), they cross and add up, and they bend whatever the puddle mirrors (the sky, and with Reflections on the zombies and the buildings). Only puddles big enough to show do it, outdoors, only where someone steps. The rain rings puddles and wet ground with real drop rings instead of the game's grid of half rings, and cars leave a continuous wake. Windows, Linux and macOS. Turning it on applies on the next launch, the rest at once.
UI_pzopt_tip_ripplesStrengthPct: How much the rings tilt the puddle's surface (how strongly they catch the light and bend the reflection).
UI_pzopt_tip_ripplesVehicles: Moving cars ring the puddles under their wheels too.
UI_pzopt_label_ripplesPerSec: Puddle ripples: rings a second at most
UI_pzopt_tip_ripplesPerSec: A horde walking through flooded streets would start hundreds of rings a second; past this many, each footstep makes a ring by chance (your own always do), so a crowd still churns the water but costs no more than a few walkers. Higher: busier water in hordes, a little more work.
UI_pzopt_tip_ripplesMode: How the rings are drawn; all but sim look the same. alu: each part of the screen looks only at the rings that reach it, the wave shape computed (the cheapest, most on weak GPUs). tiled: the same, the wave shape read from a table (the exact simulation's). world: the rings sorted once for their whole life instead of every frame (least work for the game, more for the GPU). sim: the water is simulated on the GPU, so the rings also bounce off the puddle's edges (needs OpenGL 4.3). field: the rings drawn once into a texture the puddles read (needs OpenGL 4.3). loop: every puddle pixel looks at every ring (slow, for comparison).
UI_pzopt_tip_ripplesRain: The rings the rain makes on puddles and wet ground. The game's own (stock) draw a grid of half rings that pulse in place; these are real drop rings at random spots, each a small train of waves that spreads and fades, filtered so they never shimmer when zoomed out. cells: worked out per pixel (no textures). texture: drops read from a small texture (Lagarde's technique from Remember Me). flipbook (default): a precomputed loop of the whole rain field. field: drawn once a frame into a small texture the puddles read (needs OpenGL 4.3). sim: the water simulated on the GPU, rings crossing each other for real (needs OpenGL 4.3). none: no rings at all.
UI_pzopt_tip_ripplesRainPct: How strongly the raindrops' rings catch the light.
UI_pzopt_tip_ripplesWake: What a car leaves in the puddles it drives through. trail: two tyre grooves that fill back in and a wave running out of each, a continuous wake however fast you drive. kelvin: the V-shaped wake of a boat. particles: each tyre sheds little waves to both sides as it moves (wave particles). sim: the wheels push the simulated water (the footsteps then run in that simulation too; needs OpenGL 4.3). rings: a ring at the rear wheels every few squares (the first version). trail, kelvin and particles need OpenGL 4.3 (else rings).
UI_pzopt_section_40229551b8: Puddle ripples (footsteps, raindrops and car wakes)
UI_pzopt_label_bakeNoSync: Bake passes never wait for the graphics driver
UI_pzopt_tip_bakeNoSync: The ambient-occlusion and foliage-sway passes that run inside a chunk bake keep their own record of the GL state and take object names from a ready pool, instead of asking the graphics driver. Matters only with those Enhancements on. Same picture.
UI_pzopt_label_separateMemo: Zombie crowding: each answer once per frame
UI_pzopt_tip_separateMemo: When zombies push each other apart, every zombie asks of each neighbour whether it counts as solid (its state, sitting, ragdoll) and whether a wall stands between their squares. While that pass runs nothing in the world changes, so with this each neighbour's answer is worked out once per frame and each worker thread remembers the wall answers it already found. Same answers. Off by default: the Louisville horde ran no faster with it.
UI_pzopt_label_nearVehicleGrid: Find nearby cars from one map per frame
UI_pzopt_tip_nearVehicleGrid: Every zombie asks each update whether a car is within four squares; stock looked up the 16 chunks around it and their car lists one by one. One table of which chunks hold a car, built once per frame, answers "none" for most of them; when a car may be near, the stock search runs. Same answers.
UI_pzopt_label_ragdollGate: Skip the ragdoll question when nothing is a ragdoll
UI_pzopt_tip_ragdollGate: The engine asks 'is this character a ragdoll?' about 60,000 times a frame in a big horde (every zombie's push-apart asks it of each neighbour), and each answer looked up the character's body model first. While no character is ragdolling the answer is no without looking at anyone; a character with no ragdoll in its animation player says no from that player. Same answers.
UI_pzopt_tip_bodyModelCache: Every request for a character's animation player first worked out its body model (male, female, skeleton) from its descriptor and compared it with the player's. The answer is kept on the character and dropped exactly when one of its inputs changes (descriptor, gender, skeleton, the body models, the player itself). Same players.
UI_pzopt_label_entityUpdatePlayerFirst: Entity updates: players and cars before the batch
UI_pzopt_tip_entityUpdatePlayerFirst: With the overlap above, your character and the vehicles update before the zombie batch starts instead of beside it. Your line of sight tells the zombies it sees that they saw you, and a moving car marks the zombies it touches; doing that while those zombies were updating on the workers lost part of it (in the brawl check the horde closed in noticeably slower), and the car's polygons are brought up to date before the workers read them. On by default.
UI_pzopt_tip_entityUpdateMoreStates: With zombie updates on other cores, zombies sitting against a wall or resting in their default state also update on the worker threads; their state does nothing of its own in single player, so their update is the same one the idle zombies already run there. In downtown Louisville that is about 300 zombies a frame.
UI_pzopt_tip_postupdateParallel: After the updates, each calm zombie's move for the frame (its push, the walls and fences it slides along, the stairs, the square it lands on) is computed on the worker threads; the game thread only moves it to its new square, in the stock order. A zombie near a car, against a fence or touching a special object moves on the game thread as before. Checked against the stock movement: 0 differences in 692,000 moves.
UI_pzopt_tip_hordeBatch: The game draws every 3D zombie on its own: a full GL state save and restore, a shader switch, ~25 settings and a 60-matrix skeleton upload for each of its ~4 models. Batched, the render thread works out the same values, puts them in buffers the graphics card reads, and draws a run of zombies with one shader and one draw call per model. 'exact' keeps the stock drawing order (same pixels, checked pixel by pixel); 'defer' draws all of a frame's 3D zombies at the end of the moving objects, as if the game had listed them last (a semi-transparent edge where a zombie overlaps a flat sprite can blend the other way round). Needs OpenGL 4.3; elsewhere the stock path stays.
UI_pzopt_label_hordeBatchUpload: Zombie batches: how the data reaches the GPU
UI_pzopt_tip_hordeBatchUpload: mapped: buffers the GPU reads straight from (OpenGL 4.4), written once. subdata: a copy per batch through the driver.
UI_pzopt_label_renderLastFast: Skip the empty per-character inventory walk
UI_pzopt_tip_renderLastFast: After drawing, every character looked through its whole inventory each frame for items that draw something then; none of the game's items do. Off when Java mods are loaded. Same picture.
UI_pzopt_label_zombieLodFixed3d: Zombie detail: a fixed number of 3D zombies
UI_pzopt_tip_zombieLodFixed3d: Instead of following the frame cap, always draw this many of the nearest zombies as 3D models and the rest as flat sprites. 0 = follow the frame cap (the setting above).
UI_pzopt_label_zombieLodHysteresis: Zombie detail: places a 3D zombie keeps its model
UI_pzopt_tip_zombieLodHysteresis: A zombie already drawn in 3D keeps its model while it ranks up to this many places past the 3D count; a zombie that is a flat sprite needs a place inside the count. The edge of the 3D group then does not flip between model and sprite while zombies walk or the view turns (it can hold this many more models).
UI_pzopt_label_zombieLodSpriteLight: Zombie detail: flat zombies in the light
UI_pzopt_tip_zombieLodSpriteLight: The game draws its flat zombie sprites as black silhouettes. With this they take this share of their square's light, closer to the lit 3D zombies beside them. Without "Zombie detail follows the frame cap" (or a fixed number) only new zombies waiting for their 3D model are lit ("new zombies start as sprites"); the far sprites stay as the game draws them.
UI_pzopt_tip_zombieLodFadeMs: A zombie switching between its 3D model and the flat sprite fades from one to the other over this long instead of popping. During the fade both are drawn.
UI_pzopt_label_postupdateNoopSkip: Zombie movement: skip square moves that change nothing
UI_pzopt_tip_postupdateNoopSkip: A zombie that ends its move on the square it was already listed on no longer re-checks that square's list in the movement loop. Same lists.
UI_pzopt_label_postupdateEligibleOnWorke: Zombie movement: eligibility checked on other cores
UI_pzopt_tip_postupdateEligibleOnWorker: Which zombies may compute their move on the worker threads is decided in each zombie's own task instead of in a pass over every zombie on the game thread. Same zombies.
UI_pzopt_label_postupdateVehicleOnWorker: Zombie movement near cars on other cores
UI_pzopt_tip_postupdateVehicleOnWorker: A zombie whose move comes within reach of a car resolves the car on its worker thread (the game's own collision, under its lock) instead of moving entirely on the game thread. Same moves.
UI_pzopt_label_postupdateFuse: Zombie animation decisions under the movement loop
UI_pzopt_tip_postupdateFuse: A zombie with no target starts its animation-state decision on the worker threads while the game thread is still moving the others; when nothing changes it also runs its animation there. The game thread then finishes every zombie in the stock order. Same states and animations.
UI_pzopt_label_postupdateClean: Zombie movement loop skips finished zombies
UI_pzopt_tip_postupdateClean: A calm zombie with no target whose whole movement step needs nothing of the game thread finishes it on its worker, and the game thread's loop passes over it without reading it. Same results.
UI_pzopt_label_separateEdgeCache: Zombie crowding: wall answers shared between cores
UI_pzopt_tip_separateEdgeCache: When zombies push each other apart, whether a wall stands between two squares is worked out once per frame and kept on the square for every worker thread; before, each worker asked again. Same answers.
UI_pzopt_label_luaSilentSkip: No per-zombie Lua event when nothing listens
UI_pzopt_tip_luaSilentSkip: Each zombie update raised a Lua event that the worker threads recorded and the game thread replayed; while no Lua function listens to it (none in the base game) it is not recorded. A mod that listens gets it as before.
UI_pzopt_label_randPerWorker: Zombie dice rolls: one random stream per core
UI_pzopt_tip_randPerWorker: The zombie work on the worker threads drew every random number (spotting, lunges, groans) from the game's one generator behind a lock. Each worker thread now draws from its own generator of the same kind: the same odds for every roll, but not the same sequence of numbers as the stock game.
UI_pzopt_label_uiVerify: UI: changes shown the frame they happen
UI_pzopt_tip_uiVerify: A window kept from an earlier frame is now checked every frame against exactly what its drawing read the last time (the Lua fields it used, the item names, stats and conditions it asked the game for, the mouse position) and drawn again in the frame any of them changes, instead of after a timer of up to a second. Measured at 240 fps with the ground-truth rig (every window drawn every frame for comparison): items renamed or worn in an open inventory late on 43 % of frames before, 0.4 % now; skill XP arriving 61 % to 0.7 %; mouse over inventory rows and a 200-item stack 25-29 % to 0 %.
UI_pzopt_tip_uiAnimate: A window whose picture is changing (smooth scrolling, an item being dragged, a fade) is drawn on every frame while it moves instead of 60 times a second. Wheel scrolling through a 200-item stack showed an out-of-date list on 58 % of frames before, 0 % now. Uses only the time the frame has left before the frame cap (see the next setting); never draws less often than before.
UI_pzopt_label_uiSlack: UI: extra redraws only in the frame's spare time
UI_pzopt_tip_uiSlack: The redraws for mouse movement and animation are done only when they fit in the time the frame has left before the frame cap (measured each frame), so the frame rate does not drop for them; a window that has waited the stock 1/60 s is drawn anyway (never later than before). Uncapped they get a fifth of the frame.
UI_pzopt_label_uiMoveReplay: UI: dragged windows moved, not redrawn
UI_pzopt_tip_uiMoveReplay: While you drag a window that draws the same thing wherever it is, its kept picture is moved to the new place every frame (what a desktop compositor does with a window) instead of running its Lua again; it is still redrawn 60 times a second, so a change during the drag shows at the old rate at the latest.
UI_pzopt_label_slackWork: Deferred work in the frame cap's spare time
UI_pzopt_tip_slackWork: With a frame cap, the time left in a frame before the limiter waits is used for queued game-thread jobs: freshly loaded chunks joining the world, far loot rolls and far zombie spawns run one at a time while each one's learned cost still fits, instead of all at once in the frame they arrive. Without a cap nothing changes.
UI_pzopt_note_78e8c99c5f: stock: every zombie its own little scene
UI_pzopt_note_7f4d7009d7: fastest; zombies drawn after the other moving objects
UI_pzopt_note_672d81f51d: follow the frame cap (the setting above)
UI_pzopt_note_3b0f681301: stock: the nearest win every frame
UI_pzopt_label_bakeBudgetGpu: One budget: count the GPU's time too
UI_pzopt_tip_bakeBudgetGpu: The adaptive budget above judges a frame by the time the game and render threads took. With this it also counts how long the GPU kept drawing after the frame was handed over (the frame queue's GPU timestamps), so a frame whose GPU ran long, such as a horde coming into view, also halves the next frames' bakes. Only changes when chunk pictures bake, never what they show. On by default.
UI_pzopt_label_lookupMemo: Remember clothing and animation name lookups
UI_pzopt_tip_lookupMemo: Dressing a new zombie looks up dozens of clothing and animation names in tables that ignore upper and lower case, so each lookup compared strings letter by letter all the way down the table. The exact names already asked are remembered, so the same name again is one hash probe. Same answers: 3.1 million lookups compared on the Louisville horde, none different.
UI_pzopt_label_playerLosParallel: Player sight: each zombie's checks on other cores
UI_pzopt_tip_playerLosParallel: Every frame the game checks every zombie, animal and car against your sight: how far it is, whether its square is in view, whether it is climbing through a window. Those reads are made on the worker threads, and the game thread then applies the results one by one in the usual order (fade, spot roll, counters). A zombie nobody can see is finished on the worker. Same result, checked object by object. Single player only.
UI_pzopt_label_hordeBatchVao: Zombie batches: one vertex setup per mesh layout
UI_pzopt_tip_hordeBatchVao: Batched zombies drew each body and clothing mesh through its own vertex setup, made the first time that mesh was drawn, which made the render thread wait for the graphics driver, about 250 times on the Louisville route, mostly in the frames a horde comes into view. 'format' keeps one setup per vertex layout (two on that route) and points it at each mesh's buffers per draw. Same pixels (checked pixel by pixel). Needs OpenGL 4.3, like the batches.
UI_pzopt_tip_atlasBatch: Zombies too far for a 3D model are small pre-rendered sprites, about 1,100 a frame in a Louisville horde, each drawn with its own state change and draw call. They are now queued and drawn in runs, in the stock order and with each sprite's own state, from a vertex buffer the graphics card reads directly. Same pixels (checked pixel by pixel). Needs OpenGL 4.4; elsewhere the stock draws stay.
UI_pzopt_label_hordeBatchOrder: Zombie batches: models and sprites in two groups
UI_pzopt_tip_hordeBatchOrder: In a horde the 3D zombies and the far zombies' sprites alternate in the drawing order, and every switch ended a batch. With 'window', the models and sprites between two other objects are drawn as two groups; one may move ahead of the other only where their screen rectangles do not overlap, so every pixel is drawn exactly as before (checked pixel by pixel). Works with the sprite batching above.
UI_pzopt_label_hordeBatchUnits: Zombie batches: textures bound 16 at a time
UI_pzopt_tip_hordeBatchUnits: Each batched zombie model bound its texture before its draw. Now a batch binds up to 16 of its textures at once and each draw picks its own. Same pixels (checked pixel by pixel). Needs OpenGL 4.3, like the batches.
UI_pzopt_label_renderPrewarm: Prepare the horde's drawing while the world loads
UI_pzopt_tip_renderPrewarm: The first zombie drawn in 3D made the render thread set up the zombie batches' shaders and buffers, the far zombies' sprite buffer and the first clothing pictures (a new framebuffer and about 11 textures), so the moment a horde came into view stuttered. These are now made once at the first frame of the world, during loading. The same objects, made earlier: nothing drawn changes.
UI_pzopt_label_bodyAtlasPrewarm: Prepare the far zombies' body sprites while you play
UI_pzopt_tip_bodyAtlasPrewarm: Far zombies are drawn as flat sprites made from 128 generic body pictures, which the game drew in the frames a horde first came into view. They are now drawn two a frame from a second after the world appears, so the horde's first sight finds them ready. Same pictures, made earlier.
UI_pzopt_label_renderPrewarmOutlines: Prepare the outline passes while the world loads
UI_pzopt_tip_renderPrewarmOutlines: The first outlined character or object (a highlighted zombie, an item under the mouse) made the render thread set up the outline passes: three screen-sized framebuffers and their shaders. With the prepare option above they are made at the first frame of the world instead. Same pixels.
UI_pzopt_label_hordePaletteMismatch: Zombie batches: palette compare in one step
UI_pzopt_tip_hordePaletteMismatch: Zombies whose bone palettes are identical share one upload; the compare read the two palettes eight bytes at a time through a call that is slow until the Java compiler has optimised it. Now one memory compare of both ranges. Same answer (checked over 228,114 compares).
UI_pzopt_label_zombieFirstSightSprite: Zombie detail: new zombies start as sprites
UI_pzopt_tip_zombieFirstSightSprite: When a horde comes into view, a few hundred zombies take their 3D model within a second and each first makes its clothing picture on the render thread, up to about 90 in one frame. With this on, those pictures are spread over the next frames, nearest zombies first, within the budget below; a zombie still waiting is not drawn yet (as the game does while a picture is not ready) and waits at most a quarter of a second (more pictures a frame when needed). A zombie that was already drawn with its clothes (hit, hat falling off, killed, dragged) never waits. With "Zombie detail follows the frame cap" on, a waiting zombie is that option's flat sprite instead and its model fades in over it. It only changes what you see for a moment: a new zombie in a horde appears a few frames later.
UI_pzopt_label_zombieCompositeBudgetUs: Zombie detail: clothing pictures per frame (us)
UI_pzopt_tip_zombieCompositeBudgetUs: The render-thread time a frame may spend on new zombies' first clothing pictures when new zombies start as sprites (at least one picture a frame).
UI_pzopt_label_zombieCompositeMaxPerFram: Zombie detail: clothing pictures per frame (count)
UI_pzopt_tip_zombieCompositeMaxPerFrame: When new zombies start as sprites, at most this many first clothing pictures a frame. Each one also costs about 0.2 ms of GPU time, which the render-thread budget above does not see.
UI_pzopt_label_schedulerFillParallel: Update schedule: the whole sort on other cores
UI_pzopt_tip_schedulerFillParallel: With the update schedule computed on other cores, the rest of that step moves too: the worker threads also make the per-object checks the game thread still made, read each zombie's current behaviour from a remembered reference instead of a table lookup, and the game thread files the results in the usual order from what the workers read, without going back to each zombie. Same schedule, checked list by list. On by default since 2026-10-15.
UI_pzopt_label_zombieSpawnSpread: Zombie creation queue: new zombies spread over frames
UI_pzopt_tip_zombieSpawnSpread: When a chunk next to a horde loads, the game turns dozens of zombies real in one frame, each one dressed and given its animations. With this on they are created from a queue within a small time a frame (the frame's spare time under a frame cap), so they appear a few frames later; a zombie within 25 squares of you is still created at once, the first 3 seconds of a load create everything at once as the game does, and none waits longer than the longest wait below, so the horde is never thinned. Changes only when zombies appear, not which or where. On by default since 2026-10-15.
UI_pzopt_label_zombieModelAddBudgetUs: Horde first sight: 3D models given per frame (us)
UI_pzopt_tip_zombieModelAddBudgetUs: A zombie that gets its 3D model builds the model and every piece of its clothing in that frame; when a crowd comes into view or the view turns, many do it at once. With a budget, the zombies past it stay their flat sprite a frame longer (lit, with "new zombies start as sprites") and get their model in the next frames, nearest first. On by default since 2026-10-15 (500).
UI_pzopt_label_burstGovernor: Horde first sight: lighter work in heavy frames
UI_pzopt_tip_burstGovernor: When a horde first comes into view, dozens of frames in a row run late. A frame that started late for its slot or followed a frame that used nearly all of its time now creates fewer queued zombies and gives fewer zombies their 3D model; that work moves to the lighter frames right after. Changes only when zombies appear, not which or where. Acts at a frame cap, on the zombie creation queue and on the 3D model budget (both on by default since 2026-10-15).
UI_pzopt_label_burstLateUs: Horde first sight: a frame this late is heavy (us)
UI_pzopt_tip_burstLateUs: A frame that starts more than this many microseconds after its slot under the frame cap counts as heavy.
UI_pzopt_label_burstWorkPct: Horde first sight: a frame after this much work is heavy (%)
UI_pzopt_tip_burstWorkPct: A frame whose previous frame worked for more than this share of the cap's frame time counts as heavy.
UI_pzopt_label_zombieSpawnBurstUs: Horde first sight: zombie creation in a heavy frame (us)
UI_pzopt_tip_zombieSpawnBurstUs: The time a heavy frame may spend creating queued zombies.
UI_pzopt_label_zombieModelAddBurstUs: Horde first sight: 3D models given in a heavy frame (us)
UI_pzopt_tip_zombieModelAddBurstUs: The time a heavy frame may spend giving zombies their 3D model.
UI_pzopt_label_zombieModelAddHeavyEvery: Horde first sight: 3D models only every Nth heavy frame
UI_pzopt_tip_zombieModelAddHeavyEvery: In a run of heavy frames only every Nth one gives zombies their 3D model; in the others they stay flat sprites a frame longer.
UI_pzopt_label_zombieSpawnSlackBudgetUs: Zombie creation queue: use the frame's spare time (us kept free)
UI_pzopt_tip_zombieSpawnSlackBudgetUs: At a frame cap, queued zombies are created in the time the last frame left unused before the cap, less this margin, instead of a fixed time a frame. Only with the zombie creation queue on.
UI_pzopt_label_zombieSpawnHeavyMin: Zombie creation queue: zombies a heavy frame creates at least
UI_pzopt_tip_zombieSpawnHeavyMin: A heavy frame creates at least this many queued zombies. Only with the zombie creation queue on.
UI_pzopt_tip_zombieSpawnMaxAgeMs: A queued zombie waits at most this long, so a slow machine's small per-frame time never thins the horde. Only with the zombie creation queue on.
UI_pzopt_label_zombieSpawnAgedCapUs: Zombie creation queue: time a frame for zombies that waited too long (us)
UI_pzopt_tip_zombieSpawnAgedCapUs: The queued zombies past the longest wait are created within this much time a frame instead of all in one frame (all at once after three times the longest wait). Only with the zombie creation queue on.
UI_pzopt_label_frameQueue: Frame queue: every frame on the cap's beat (adds input delay)
UI_pzopt_tip_frameQueue: With a frame cap, every frame is held back until a fixed time after the moment of game time it shows, long enough that almost every frame is ready by then (the 99th percentile of the last 2 seconds, GPU time included). A frame whose update or drawing takes longer than usual then still reaches the screen on the beat instead of late, and the frames around it absorb it. The price is input delay: what you do reaches the screen about 3-7 ms later at a 120 fps cap, more in a big horde. Driving at 120 km/h with a 120 fps cap, frames within 9 ms rose from 92 % to 97.5 %, and to 99.5 % with the GPU's time counted (below). Only while you play a world with a frame cap: never uncapped, in the menus, the pause menu or the loading screen, with vsync on a fixed-refresh display (vsync already sets the beat), on macOS, or with the just-in-time input sleep. Replaces "Even frame delivery" while it acts. Off = present pacing as before.
UI_pzopt_label_frameQueueGpu: Frame queue: count the GPU's drawing time
UI_pzopt_tip_frameQueueGpu: The frame queue's holding time also covers how long the GPU still draws after the game has handed a frame over (measured with GPU timestamps a few frames later). Without it a frame whose GPU work runs long is swapped on the beat but shown late. Louisville horde at a 120 cap: frames within 9 ms 96.6 to 98.7 %, for 3-5 ms more input delay.
UI_pzopt_label_frameQueueMinPct: Frame queue: shortest holding time (% of a frame)
UI_pzopt_tip_frameQueueMinPct: The frame queue holds each frame for a time between this and the longest holding time below, in percent of the cap's frame time, following the slowest recent frames. At 260 with the longest at 260 (the default since 2026-10-15) the holding time is fixed at 2.6 frames, 21.7 ms at a 120 fps cap: it never has to grow after a slow frame, which is when the frames after one came late. Louisville horde at a 120 cap: about 0.4 points more frames within 9 ms than the adaptive holding time, for about 2.5 ms more input delay on average. Lower = less input delay, more late frames. Applies at frame caps from the setting "fixed holding time from (fps)" up; below it the shortest holding time for low caps is used.
UI_pzopt_label_frameQueueMaxPct: Frame queue: longest holding time (% of a frame)
UI_pzopt_tip_frameQueueMaxPct: The longest the frame queue holds a frame, in percent of the cap's frame time. Above about 2.5 frames the game thread starts to wait for a free frame slot.
UI_pzopt_label_frameQueueFixedMinFps: Frame queue: fixed holding time from (fps)
UI_pzopt_tip_frameQueueFixedMinFps: The shortest holding time above (2.6 frames by default, a fixed holding time) applies only at frame caps of this many fps or more. 2.6 frames are 21.7 ms at a 120 fps cap but 43 ms at 60 and 87 ms at 30, a delay you feel; below this cap the queue follows the slowest recent frames instead, from the shortest holding time for low caps below (10 ms at 60 fps, 20 ms at 30), and starts there again after a load, a menu or a cap change, settling within a few seconds (the low-cap entries below).
UI_pzopt_label_frameQueueLowCapMinPct: Frame queue: shortest holding time at low caps (% of a frame)
UI_pzopt_tip_frameQueueLowCapMinPct: Below the cap set in "fixed holding time from (fps)", the frame queue holds each frame for at least this share of the cap's frame time and otherwise as long as the slowest recent frames need, up to the longest holding time. Lower = less input delay, more late frames.
UI_pzopt_label_frameQueueLowCapCalmMs: Frame queue at low caps: start from the shortest holding time (ms of steady frames)
UI_pzopt_tip_frameQueueLowCapCalmMs: Below the cap set in "fixed holding time from (fps)": after a world loads, a menu or the pause menu closes or the cap changes, the frame queue starts at its shortest holding time and learns from the frames only once they have been ready within one frame of their beat for this long (at most 10 s). Without it the slow frames of a world's first seconds set the holding time to its longest, 43 ms at a 60 fps cap and 87 ms at 30, and it took 20 s and over a minute to come down: that much more input delay.
UI_pzopt_label_frameQueueLowCapDecayPct: Frame queue at low caps: how fast the holding time falls (% of a frame per second)
UI_pzopt_tip_frameQueueLowCapDecayPct: Below the cap set in "fixed holding time from (fps)", after a burst of slow frames the holding time comes down by at most this share of the cap's frame time a second: 25 % is 4.2 ms a second at 60 fps and 8.3 ms at 30 (the fixed 1 ms a second of high caps took over a minute at 30). Lower = steadier after a burst, more input delay.
UI_pzopt_label_frameQueueLowCapMarginPct: Frame queue at low caps: safety margin (% of a frame)
UI_pzopt_tip_frameQueueLowCapMarginPct: Below the cap set in "fixed holding time from (fps)", the holding time is the slowest recent frames' time plus this share of the cap's frame time (20 %: 3.3 ms at 60 fps, 6.7 ms at 30). With the holding time coming down within seconds, the margin is what keeps a frame that is a little slower than the recent ones on the beat: replayed on a Louisville horde route, 20 % had no more late frames than the old slow-falling holding time, which stayed at 50-87 ms at a 30 fps cap. Lower = less input delay, more late frames.
UI_pzopt_label_workerQosMac: Priority of the game's helper threads (Mac)
UI_pzopt_tip_workerQosMac: The macOS priority class of the helper threads that update and draw the zombies with the game thread every frame. At the old background class (utility) they lost their cores whenever a virtual machine, a build or Spotlight was busy beside the game, and the game slowed down while stock did not. User-initiated (the default) lets them keep their cores. No effect on Windows or Linux. Applies on the next launch.
UI_pzopt_tip_gcG1Tuned: With G1 (the default collector), the next launch also gets the settings measured on the Louisville horde: a small young generation collected often in short pauses, objects that survive moved straight to the old generation instead of being copied back and forth, the old generation cleaned up in many small steps, and a larger space for compiled code so it no longer starts extra collection cycles. Written into the game's launcher file only on the Java version it was tested with, and left out when you set any of these G1 options yourself; the uninstallers take them out again. Applies on the next launch.
UI_pzopt_label_gcSlack: Garbage collection in the frame cap's spare time
UI_pzopt_tip_gcSlack: With a frame cap, the collection of short-lived objects that would land in the middle of a frame is started a few frames early, at the end of a frame that has time to spare before the cap, so it no longer makes a frame late. It fills the rest of the young generation with throwaway memory to start the collection at that moment; the game itself is untouched. Needs G1 (the default); without a cap nothing changes.
UI_pzopt_label_gcSlackQueue: Spare-time garbage collection under the frame queue
UI_pzopt_tip_gcSlackQueue: Where the collection above runs while the frame queue holds frames. In the game thread's spare time it could overlap the end of a hold and make that frame late (8 of 28 collections in a Louisville run); slack waits for a frame whose swap leaves room for the collection: 35 of 35 collections without a late frame.
UI_pzopt_label_handoffRecalcFast: Chunk joining: border recalc without repeats
UI_pzopt_tip_handoffRecalcFast: When a loaded chunk joins the world, its border squares are recalculated against the neighbours (collision, pathfinding, sight). The game recomputed each square's tile properties about fifteen times and its walkable-neighbour links dozens of times in that pass; now once each, with the same result.
UI_pzopt_tip_propIdCache: Questions like 'does this tile carry a fuel amount' looked the property up by name in a table every time; the answer's id is now kept per property type. Same answers.
UI_pzopt_tip_chunkHandoffCost: How the spare-time scheduler guesses whether the next chunk's joining fits the time left in a frame. chunk (the default): the running mean of whole joinings. square (until 2026-10-15): a learned cost per square, which one heavy chunk kept pessimistic for a long time.
UI_pzopt_label_chunkHandoffSlackMaxWait: Chunk joining: longest wait for spare time (frames)
UI_pzopt_tip_chunkHandoffSlackMaxWait: A loaded chunk that does not fit a frame's spare time joins after this many frames anyway, in a light frame, so a queue never builds behind one heavy chunk. A world load or a teleport keeps the stock count. 0 = 600 frames, as until 2026-10-15.
UI_pzopt_label_chunkHandoffForceAnyFrame: Chunk joining: an overdue chunk joins in the next spare time
UI_pzopt_tip_chunkHandoffForceAnyFrame: A chunk past its longest wait joins in the next frame's spare time, light frame or not (still one such chunk a frame).
UI_pzopt_label_chunkHandoffFrameBudgetUs: Chunk joining: time a frame may spend on a backlog (us)
UI_pzopt_tip_chunkHandoffFrameBudgetUs: When chunks queue up while you move, a frame joins them only until this much time is used (at least one); the rest join in the next frames' spare time. A world load or a teleport keeps the stock count. 0 = stock: the whole count.
UI_pzopt_label_aotNoIndy: Warm-start cache: save it without lambda linking (makes it work)
UI_pzopt_tip_aotNoIndy: With the game's Java (Zulu 25.0.1) the warm-start cache was never written: Java crashed while saving it at the end of the recording launch (an hs_err file in the game folder after every second quit), so the next launch found no cache and recorded again, forever. Saved without Java's pre-linked lambda calls (-XX:-AOTInvokeDynamicLinking) the cache is written and keeps the loaded classes and all method profiles. Needs the warm-start cache on. Written into the game's launcher file for the next launch; the uninstallers take it out again.

UI_pzopt_note_72ada64502: default: none unless they waited too long

UI_pzopt_note_1dc242c4fe: default: follow the recent frame times
UI_pzopt_note_81cb423375: learn from the first frame (round 11: the loading bursts set it to the longest)
UI_pzopt_note_9f40fb8b91: 1 ms a second, as at high caps
UI_pzopt_note_cecd861244: work the player waits for: keeps its cores when other programs are busy
UI_pzopt_note_e18919a490: background work: the efficient cores first, gives way to other programs
UI_pzopt_note_4c38a4f775: the game and render threads' own class
UI_pzopt_note_09e7d34c3e: default: in the spare time, only while the held frame's swap is far enough away
UI_pzopt_note_2cdc37d52f: the spare-time rule as without the queue

UI_pzopt_label_godRaysDoorLeaf: God rays: open doors block the light
UI_pzopt_tip_godRaysDoorLeaf: An open door stands in its doorway's light: the shaft and its sunlit patch on the floor lose the part the door shades, and a glass door lets its share through.
UI_pzopt_tip_godRaysDoorSwingMs: When a door opens the light sweeps in through the widening gap over this long, and it is cut off the same way as the door shuts (0: the light comes and goes the moment the door does).
UI_pzopt_label_godRaysCharShadows: God rays: people's shadows in the shafts
UI_pzopt_tip_godRaysCharShadows: The player, other people and zombies standing in a shaft of light cast their shadow into the lit dust and onto the sunlit patch on the floor.
UI_pzopt_label_godRaysDoorDustPct: God rays: dust stirred by doors (%)
UI_pzopt_tip_godRaysDoorDustPct: A door opening stirs up the dust in its shaft: thicker swirls drift in with the draft and settle over a few seconds.
UI_pzopt_label_godRaysSpill: God rays: lamplight spilling out at night
UI_pzopt_tip_godRaysSpill: At night a lit room's light spills out through its open doors and windows into the fog and the rain, shaped by the opening.
UI_pzopt_tip_godRaysSpillPct: How bright the light spilling out of lit rooms is.
UI_pzopt_label_godRaysBouncePct: God rays: light bounced off the sunlit floor (%)
UI_pzopt_tip_godRaysBouncePct: The sunlit patch a shaft lays on the floor bounces a little of its light onto the walls and furniture around it. Subtle next to the game's own room light, so off by default.
UI_pzopt_label_godRaysRoofExact: God rays: sun under porch roofs
UI_pzopt_tip_godRaysRoofExact: Off (the default): a window or doorway under a porch roof or a floor above lets no light in. On: the sun comes in under the roof's edge as its height allows, so a low morning or evening sun reaches in under a porch and a high midday one does not. Applies on the next launch.
UI_pzopt_tip_voxelLight: Street lamps, house lamps and room lights are traced through the world's walls, windows, doorways, fences, floors and tree crowns: they cast real shadows (a fence, a stair, a building's corner), light reaches a room through its windows, walls facing a lamp catch more of it, and the sky lights rooms from their windows and doorways instead of a flat indoor darkening. Each chunk picture keeps its own light layer, worked out again only when a light or the buildings change. Needs a graphics card with OpenGL 4.3 (not macOS). Applies on the next launch.
UI_pzopt_tip_voxelLightTorchShadows: A torch you carry casts shadows of walls, fences, floors and crowns too (traced again only when the torch moves).
UI_pzopt_tip_voxelLightSkyMethod: How the sky's light reaches into rooms. Flood: spread from the open sky through windows and doorways. Cascades: rays towards the sky from every square, shared between neighbours (the sky through a window comes from where it faces). Cones: the same with every ray traced.
UI_pzopt_tip_voxelLightBounce: Lit floors and walls light their surroundings a little: a lamp pool fills the area round it, a lit window spills warm light outside.

UI_pzopt_tip_translucentGridsPerFrame: Translucent furniture made of several tiles (picnic tables, large metal shelves, animal-hide rugs) is drawn every frame as in the stock game. Baked, the ground showed through it in wedges along the seams between its tiles.
UI_pzopt_label_luaZombieLod: Mod scripts on zombies: every frame only near you
UI_pzopt_tip_luaZombieLod: Some mods run a Lua function for every zombie in every frame (the OnZombieUpdate event): with 20 such functions and a big horde that was most of the frame (650-mod list, Louisville horde: 65 ms a frame, 5.6 fps). With this on, the zombies near you (12 squares) still run every mod function every frame; the others on screen run them 10 times a second and those off screen 4 times, spread so every frame carries the same share. A function that runs less often is told the time that passed since its last call (GameTime's multiplier), so mod timers keep their pace, and a function that just changed a zombie keeps running every frame on it for a second. Mods known to need every frame are left alone. On by default since 2026-10-25, with the time per frame below. Applies on the next launch.
UI_pzopt_label_luaZombieBudgetUs: Mod scripts on zombies: time per frame (us)
UI_pzopt_tip_luaZombieBudgetUs: The time per frame the mod functions of the zombies not near you may take. Above it, their interval grows (up to the longest gap below) until they fit; below it, it shrinks back to the rates above. Keeps the frame time steady however big the horde, and the rate high when there are few zombies. 0 = the fixed rates only. Applies on the next launch.
UI_pzopt_label_luaZombieMaxGapMs: Mod scripts on zombies: longest gap (ms)
UI_pzopt_tip_luaZombieMaxGapMs: The time per frame never stretches a zombie's mod functions further apart than this. Applies on the next launch.
UI_pzopt_label_luaZombieHz: Mod scripts on zombies: fixed rate (without the near / far tiers)
UI_pzopt_tip_luaZombieHz: Without "every frame only near you": every zombie's mod functions run at most this many times a second, spread over the frames. 0 = every frame, stock. Applies on the next launch.
UI_pzopt_label_luaZombieLodNear: Mod scripts on zombies: near distance (squares)
UI_pzopt_tip_luaZombieLodNear: The distance to you under which a zombie's mod functions run every frame. Applies on the next launch.
UI_pzopt_label_luaZombieLodHz1: Mod scripts on zombies: on-screen rate
UI_pzopt_tip_luaZombieLodHz1: How often a second the mod functions of a zombie on screen but not near you run. Applies on the next launch.
UI_pzopt_label_luaZombieLodHz2: Mod scripts on zombies: off-screen rate
UI_pzopt_tip_luaZombieLodHz2: How often a second the mod functions of a zombie off screen run. Applies on the next launch.
UI_pzopt_label_luaZombieWriters: Mod scripts on zombies: functions that change zombies
UI_pzopt_tip_luaZombieWriters: What happens to a mod function that changes zombies. watch = every mod function runs at the rate, but every frame on a zombie it changed in its last call (it called a setter of that zombie: setTarget, setUseless, setHealth ... or changed its mod data), for a second; learn = the same, only for the functions whose code names such a setter; full = those functions always every frame; stagger = at the rate like the others. Applies on the next launch.
UI_pzopt_label_luaZombieTimeComp: Mod scripts on zombies: tell skipped time
UI_pzopt_tip_luaZombieTimeComp: A mod function that runs less often than every frame reads the time since its last call from GameTime's multiplier and time delta, so a mod counting time (bleeding, burning, timers) keeps its pace. Without it, such a mod runs slower in proportion. Applies on the next launch.
UI_pzopt_label_luaZombieCaptureDue: Mod scripts on zombies: no record when nothing is due
UI_pzopt_tip_luaZombieCaptureDue: A zombie updated on another core whose mod functions are not due in this frame is not recorded for the game thread's replay. Applies on the next launch.
UI_pzopt_label_luaZombieCheapUs: Mod scripts on zombies: cheap functions every frame (us)
UI_pzopt_tip_luaZombieCheapUs: A mod function that takes less than this per call on average keeps running every frame (deferring it saves little). 0 = off. Applies on the next launch.
UI_pzopt_label_luaZombieCostShare: Mod scripts on zombies: costly functions less often than cheap ones
UI_pzopt_tip_luaZombieCostShare: With the time per frame above: a mod function that costs more per call runs less often than a cheap one (its interval grows with the square root of its cost, 1 to 8 times the cheapest one's, never past the longest gap), and the time this frees runs the cheap ones more often. For the same time per frame the mod functions run, on average, closer to every frame. Applies on the next launch.
UI_pzopt_label_luaZombieDirtySkip: Mod scripts on zombies: skip unchanged zombies (risky)
UI_pzopt_tip_luaZombieDirtySkip: A zombie whose position, state, target, health and mod data did not change since its mod functions last ran is skipped when they come due. A mod that reacts to something else (the time, the player, the weather) misses those calls: off by default. Applies on the next launch.
UI_pzopt_label_luaZombieBatchApi: Mod scripts on zombies: batch event for mod authors
UI_pzopt_tip_luaZombieBatchApi: Adds Events.OnZombieUpdateBatch(zombies, elapsed): once a frame, the list of zombies whose turn it is (all of them without a rate) and for each the seconds since its last batch call. A mod written for it runs one Lua call a frame instead of one per zombie. Applies on the next launch.
UI_pzopt_label_luaCollideDedupe: Mod scripts: one collision event per pair a frame
UI_pzopt_tip_luaCollideDedupe: The game fires OnCharacterCollide / OnObjectCollide for every collision test that touches, and a pair pushing into each other is reported several times a frame. With this on, each (object, other) pair fires once a frame; both directions stay separate events. Applies on the next launch.
UI_pzopt_label_luaJit: Lua: hot functions compiled to Java code
UI_pzopt_tip_luaJit: Lua functions the game and mods call often are compiled to Java bytecode on a background thread, so the Java JIT runs them like Java code. The same results, errors, stack traces and mod profiler entries as the interpreter; functions it cannot compile keep running interpreted.
UI_pzopt_label_luaJavaFast: Lua: game functions called without reflection
UI_pzopt_tip_luaJavaFast: A Java method Lua calls often (getPlayer, square:getObjects, ...) gets a small generated caller: the same argument checks, conversions and error reports as the stock path, without Java reflection.
UI_pzopt_tip_luaFastTable: Lua tables are stored in a compact map with the same iteration order, which the compiled Lua code reads directly.
UI_pzopt_tip_luaPatternFast: string.find, match, gmatch and gsub run the game's own pattern matcher rewritten on plain positions: the same steps and the same answers and errors. A pattern with a back-reference (%1) keeps the stock matcher.
UI_pzopt_label_luaStringFast: Lua: text patterns without the shared pool
UI_pzopt_tip_luaStringFast: The stock pattern matcher takes its position objects from a plain allocation instead of a locked pool shared by all text calls. Applies to the patterns the faster matcher leaves to it (or all of them with it off).
UI_pzopt_tip_luaEventDispatchFast: The game walks an event's whole handler list after every handler to see whether it is still listed (with 600 mod OnTick handlers that is 360,000 compares a frame) and builds the profiler's label for each call even with the profiler off. This loop asks the slot it just called first. Exactly the same handlers in the same order, whatever a handler adds or removes. Applies on the next launch.
UI_pzopt_label_luaEventSkipEmpty: Mod events: empty handlers not called
UI_pzopt_tip_luaEventSkipEmpty: An event handler that is an empty Lua function is not called. Exact. Applies on the next launch.
UI_pzopt_tip_luaTickHz: Mods' OnTick, OnPlayerUpdate and OnTickEvenPaused handlers run at most this many times a second instead of every frame, spread over the frames so no frame takes them all; below this frame rate nothing changes. The game's own handlers and those that read the keyboard, mouse or pad, place windows, read the camera or move a character stay every frame. A handler that was skipped reads the time of every frame it missed (getMultiplier, getTimeDelta, ...), so timers, fuel and needs advance as before. Never on a server, not while everyone sleeps. Applies on the next launch.
UI_pzopt_label_luaTickAdaptive: Mod OnTick / OnPlayerUpdate when the game is slow
UI_pzopt_tip_luaTickAdaptive: When the game thread is the limit and the frame rate is under the cap, mods' heavy per-frame handlers are called less often (never less than every 4 frames or every quarter second), the heaviest first, each handler getting a fair share. The same exceptions and time catch-up as the rate above. Applies on the next launch.
UI_pzopt_label_luaTickInputWake: Mod key and mouse polls follow the rate too
UI_pzopt_tip_luaTickInputWake: A mod handler that only polls the keyboard, mouse or pad (and does nothing else that needs every frame) normally stays every frame under the rate above. With this on it follows the rate, and also runs in every frame where a key, a mouse button or the wheel changed, so it still sees every key press and release in the frame it happens; while a controller is in use it stays every frame. Applies on the next launch.
UI_pzopt_tip_luaErrorThrottle: A mod handler that fails every frame prints the same Java and Lua stack trace every frame. With 3 or 10, the same error from the same handler is printed that many times, then counted (a line every 100 repeats). The error count, the error popup and the debug error list still see every error. Applies on the next launch.
UI_pzopt_tip_luaLoadStream: A chunk joining the world runs every mod's LoadGridsquare handler on each of its squares, then the loot and the LoadChunk handlers. Stock does a chunk's whole joining in one frame; this runs it square by square over the next frames, in the stock order, a little each frame and more while chunks queue up. The chunk is not drawn until all of it has run. Off = stock.
UI_pzopt_label_luaLoadBudgetUs: Chunk joining in time slices: least time a frame (us)
UI_pzopt_tip_luaLoadBudgetUs: The least a frame spends on a joining chunk's slices; while chunks queue up it spends more, to keep up with them. Lower keeps each frame lighter and readies chunks later; 2000 cost tails on a light mod list.
UI_pzopt_label_luaLoadNearestFirst: Chunk joining in time slices: nearest first
UI_pzopt_tip_luaLoadNearestFirst: The next chunk to join is the queued one nearest the point you reach in 0.75 s instead of the oldest (a chunk that waited over a second still goes first). Off by default: it changes the order mods see the chunks in (the order check found mods keeping lists and flags across chunks), for no measured gain on the routes tried.
UI_pzopt_label_luaLoadChunkSplit: Chunk joining in time slices: LoadChunk handlers one at a time
UI_pzopt_tip_luaLoadChunkSplit: A chunk's LoadChunk handlers (mods that look at the whole chunk at once) run one per slice instead of all in the slice that ends the chunk, still before it is drawn.
UI_pzopt_label_luaLoadSlack: Chunk joining in time slices: in the frame cap's spare time
UI_pzopt_tip_luaLoadSlack: With a frame cap, slices also run in the time the frame would wait anyway, while their learned cost fits.
UI_pzopt_label_luaLoadPrefilter: Mods' square handlers: skip the proven no-ops
UI_pzopt_tip_luaLoadPrefilter: A mod's LoadGridsquare handler is left out on a square when it already ran on an identical square (the same level, room, objects, sprites, mod data) without changing anything, while reading nothing but those and its own Lua values, and none of what it read has changed since. Same result by construction; one skip in 32 still runs and is checked.
UI_pzopt_label_luaLoadSigProject: Mods' square handlers: compare only what a handler reads
UI_pzopt_tip_luaLoadSigProject: With the skipping, two squares count as identical for a handler when the parts it ever read are equal (its signature leaves out the rest), so more squares match.
UI_pzopt_label_luaLoadBatch: Mods' square handlers: handler by handler
UI_pzopt_tip_luaLoadBatch: A chunk's LoadGridsquare handlers run one handler over all its squares, then the next, instead of every handler on each square in turn. It changes what mods see: the order check found Fence Sheets reading squares that stock had not loaded yet when it ran (213,000 calls on the 54-mod spin) and Total Weight Rebalance and Fence Sheets touching the same squares in the other order. Off by default, no measured gain.
UI_pzopt_label_luaLoadNoopSkip: Mods' square handlers: skip learned no-ops (risky)
UI_pzopt_tip_luaLoadNoopSkip: Like the proven skipping, but also for handlers that read more than the square's signature (coordinates, the cell, other squares), after four calls that did nothing. A handler that acts on one particular square would then be skipped there: about 1 call in 22,000 on a 650-mod list. Off by default.
UI_pzopt_label_mapObjectsFast: Map object callbacks: only where one can run
UI_pzopt_tip_mapObjectsFast: The game's sprite callbacks (OnNewWithSprite / OnLoadWithSprite) are looked up for every object of every joining square; this asks first whether any object of the square has a registered sprite. Same result.
UI_pzopt_label_sunShadowStaticLights: Shadows from street lamps, lamps and fires
UI_pzopt_tip_sunShadowStaticLights: At night (and in dark places), characters, animals and cars standing in the light of a street lamp, a lamp, a wall light or a fire cast soft shadows away from it: short and dark right under the lamp, long and faint at the edge of its light. Each one takes the shadows of the two lights that light it most. A light only shades who it really reaches, as the game lights it: the same floor, a clear line from the light (walls and closed doors block it, windows do not), a building's own lights only inside it.
UI_pzopt_tip_sunShadowRoomLights: With the shadows from lamps on: a room lit by its ceiling light (the switch on and the power on) gives the people, animals and cars in it soft shadows from the light above, short and dark round the feet, long and faint towards the walls; a long hallway has its light in two or three places. A room's light only shades who stands in that room, and the shadow stops at its walls.
UI_pzopt_tip_reflectionsFlow: The reflection moves with the water instead of sitting on it like a still picture: the waves that carry the river's current and the wind carry the mirrored image too, on the water's own clock. Calm water is nearly a mirror; a fast river, wind and rain break it into streaks stretched along the current. Puddles ripple with the wind and the rain (they have no current). It reuses the waves the water already computes: no measurable cost. Applies at once.
UI_pzopt_tip_reflectionsFlowPct: How much the current, the wind and the rain bend and break the reflection (0: a still mirror whatever the weather; 200: twice the default).
UI_pzopt_tip_groundHexTiling: Lawns, fields, dirt and sand lose their visible tile repeat: each natural square takes its painted ground from the art at its own place in the world (hex-tiling, Mikkelsen 2022) instead of repeating the same few painted variants, so a big field no longer reads as a diamond quilt when you zoom out. Crop rows, paving and anything players build stay as they are. Baked into the cached chunk pictures: nothing extra per frame.
UI_pzopt_tip_groundMacroPct: Grass and dirt drift slowly in colour and dryness over tens of squares, as real ground does, instead of one even tone. Baked into the chunk pictures.
UI_pzopt_label_groundHeightBlend: Ground: grass grows over the dirt edge
UI_pzopt_tip_groundHeightBlend: Where grass meets dirt or sand, the taller material wins texel by texel (height blending), so grass blades grow over the edge and sand fills the cracks, instead of the even alpha fade the game paints. Baked into the chunk pictures.
UI_pzopt_tip_groundScatter: The ground collects what the season leaves: leaves under the trees and in the gutters in autumn, flowers in spring, litter by the roads, frost in the shade on a cold morning. Placed by rules from the world itself (trees, roads, the month, the wind), always the same leaf in the same place. Baked into the chunk pictures; a season step re-bakes them slowly in the background.
UI_pzopt_tip_groundScatterDensityPct: How much ground cover there is.
UI_pzopt_label_glints: Glints on frost, snow and wet asphalt
UI_pzopt_tip_glints: Frost, snow and wet roads sparkle: tiny flakes catch the sun, a torch, headlights or a street lamp, and the sparkle moves with the light (Deliot and Belcour 2023). Only where a frost, snow or wet surface and a light meet.
UI_pzopt_tip_glintPass: Particles: each frosty, snowy or wet square holds a counted number of tiny ice facets; only the ones that mirror the light into your eye are drawn, as points that stay put on the ground while the camera moves. Compact: the same flakes, sorted out by a compute pass first. Diamonds: the light is worked out for every pixel of the square (the Deliot and Belcour model), the most detailed and the most expensive.
UI_pzopt_label_glintAsync: Glints: worked out beside the game
UI_pzopt_tip_glintAsync: Which frosty, snowy or wet squares catch a light is worked out on a thread of its own while the game draws the rest of the frame, instead of on the game's main thread.
UI_pzopt_tip_glintHdrPct: With HDR output on, glints shine past the white of a normal picture, as the sun's glitter on the water does. Off: they stop at white.
UI_pzopt_tip_groundCoverFrost: After a cold, clear night the grass and the dirt turn white with rime in the shade, and it melts where the sun has been shining. Prints and ruts show dark through it.
UI_pzopt_label_groundCoverWind: Ground cover: leaves in the wind
UI_pzopt_tip_groundCoverWind: In autumn wind a few leaves lift off the ground and tumble downwind, hopping and spinning, and settle again. More wind and more fallen leaves, more of them; none when it is calm, wet or out of season.
UI_pzopt_tip_groundCoverPlacement: How leaves, petals and litter are spread inside a square: blue noise keeps every piece apart from the next at any amount, a jittered grid lets pieces bunch up.
UI_pzopt_tip_groundCoverAssets: Which art the ground cover uses: shapes drawn by the shader (leaves, petals, paper), the game's own leaf-clump and litter decals, or both.
UI_pzopt_tip_groundTracks: Cars leave tyre ruts in mud and snow, people leave footprints, a horde wears a path across a lawn. Grass flattens and recovers over a couple of game days, mud keeps its ruts, snow refills while it snows. The ground's relief lights them like the rest of the art.
UI_pzopt_tip_groundTracksLook: bake: drawn into the ground's textures when a chunk is redrawn, over the snow too (with Tracks: show at once, the fresh ones also each frame until then). patch: inside the ground tiles' own drawing (no extra draw, but snow covers the tracks). composite: drawn over the picture every frame (fresh tracks show at once, costs a little every frame where tracks are on screen).
UI_pzopt_tip_groundTracksRealtime: A print or a rut shows the frame it is pressed: what changed since its chunk was last redrawn is drawn over the picture every frame until the redraw takes it over (Tracks: how they are drawn = bake). Off: tracks show when their chunk is next redrawn, a moment later (seconds under a horde). Trodden grass plants follow at the redraw either way.
UI_pzopt_tip_groundTracksWater: After rain, water stands in mud and snow ruts. auto: puddles when Puddle ripples is on, else bake. bake: drawn with the tracks (still water). puddles: the game's puddles fill the ruts, with their ripples, raindrop rings and reflections (needs Puddle ripples on). off: no water in the ruts.
UI_pzopt_tip_groundTracksPom: The near wall of a rut hides part of its floor, as seen from the camera (relief offset sampling): ruts and prints read as cut into the ground instead of painted on it.
UI_pzopt_tip_groundTracksAo: The floor of a rut sees less sky and is a little darker.
UI_pzopt_tip_groundTracksShadowSteps: A rut's wall shades its floor when the sun is low: steps of the shadow test.
UI_pzopt_tip_groundTracksStrengthPct: How deep wheels and feet press into the ground.
UI_pzopt_tip_groundTracksVehicles: Cars leave tyre tracks, deeper and smeared where a wheel slips.
UI_pzopt_tip_groundTracksFeet: Players, zombies and animals leave footprints; a horde wears a path.
UI_pzopt_tip_groundTracksBodies: Bodies on the ground and dragged bodies leave their imprint.
UI_pzopt_tip_groundTracksGrass: The tall grass and plants over a path, a rut or a print lie flat and go to straw, then stand up again as the ground recovers.
UI_pzopt_label_groundTracksRebakesPerSec: Tracks: redraws a second under a crowd
UI_pzopt_tip_groundTracksRebakesPerSec: A horde over many chunks redraws them at most this often a second in all: their tracks show a little later instead of costing frame time.
UI_pzopt_label_groundTracksPersist: Tracks: keep them when you leave
UI_pzopt_tip_groundTracksPersist: Tracks are kept per save in Zomboid/pzopt/ground/ (never inside the save itself) and are still there when you come back. Off: they are forgotten once you leave the area.
UI_pzopt_tip_groundTracksDays: Game days trodden grass takes to stand up again. Each ground keeps its own pace around it: sand blows smooth sooner, mud keeps its ruts about five times longer (rain softens them within a day), packed snow lasts until it thaws or new snow fills it.
UI_pzopt_tip_grassBlades: Near you, at zoom 1 or closer, the grass becomes real blades in clumps: wind waves roll across them, a low sun shines through, and they stay trampled where people walked. Further out the painted grass with foliage sway stays. Each blade takes its colour from the painted grass under it.
UI_pzopt_tip_grassBladeRadius: How far round you the grass has blades.
UI_pzopt_tip_grassBladeTorchShadows: With "Per-pixel lighting: torch shadows" on, each blade near you also casts its own shadow into your torch's beam. Off (the default), the blades cast none, so the beam on a lawn stays clean; they still sit in the shadows of fences, walls and furniture. Does nothing while torch shadows are off.
UI_pzopt_tip_pplShadowFilter: Soft: sharp where an object touches the ground and softer further away, as a real torch's lens draws them. pcf: crisp edges everywhere, a little cheaper. Applies at the next launch.

UI_pzopt_v5_why_enabled_cpu: The world is baked into chunk textures instead of drawn tile by tile, and the lighting, cutaway, rain and zombie work is trimmed or cached: on the desktop's spinning route 336 to 472 fps uncapped.
UI_pzopt_v5_why_enabled_render: Rain, puddles and sprites are packed once and sent in large batches, so the render thread issues far fewer draw calls (in a stock thunderstorm the rain alone is 73 % of the render thread).
UI_pzopt_v5_why_enabled_cores: The zombies' bone math, action checks, lighting reads, character draw preparation and the boot's loading run on worker threads, beside the game thread.
UI_pzopt_v5_why_enabled_gpu: Fog is drawn into a quarter-size buffer in one pass, puddles skip hidden pixels and chunk textures re-bake less often.
UI_pzopt_v5_why_enabled_ram: Chunk textures' puddle vertices, the lighting and sprite caches and the worker threads' scratch memory stay in the Java heap.
UI_pzopt_v5_why_enabled_disk: Boot caches (precompiled Lua, animation clips, texture pack indexes) are written under Zomboid/pzopt the first time.
UI_pzopt_v5_why_enabled_load: The boot loads sound, animations and scripts on parallel threads and reads the caches: launch to menu 7.4 to 5.0 s, Continue to the world 6.5 to 4.0 s on the desktop.
UI_pzopt_v5_why_enabled_chunks: New chunks are read, decoded and baked on workers and under a per-frame budget, so they appear sooner without a hitch while you move.
UI_pzopt_v5_why_treesInChunkTexture_cpu: Every tree went through the per-frame translucent pass, 35 % of the game thread at max zoom; baked, it is no longer walked and prepared each frame (frame mean 6.2 to 5.2 ms on the desktop's max-zoom route).
UI_pzopt_v5_why_treesInChunkTexture_rend: Far fewer sprites are handed to the GL each frame: render thread 35 to 32 % busy on the same route (the persistent sprite buffer had already taken most of its load).
UI_pzopt_v5_why_treesInChunkTexture_gpu: One chunk composite replaces thousands of overlapping tree sprites drawn every frame: GPU busy 84 to 61 % on the desktop's max-zoom route.
UI_pzopt_v5_why_treesInChunkTexture_chun: Each new chunk texture also bakes its trees, so an arrival costs more; on a 4-core laptop at 120 km/h that was more than drawing them (see Trees: bake only below this chunk rate).
UI_pzopt_v5_why_windSpriteSway_cpu: The stock option takes every plant out of the bake and the game thread prepares each one per frame, sheared, with a lighting query per tree; kept baked, that walk is gone.
UI_pzopt_v5_why_windSpriteSway_render: The option's path is one draw call and its uniforms per plant sprite every frame; with the plants baked the render thread issues the chunk composite instead.
UI_pzopt_v5_why_windSpriteSway_gpu: On the desktop the stock option costs about 370 us of GPU a frame at zoom 1; the sway shader that bends the baked plants costs about 20 us.
UI_pzopt_v5_why_treeBakeMaxChunksPerSec_: Baking a short-lived texture's trees, their copies in the neighbours and the 5x5-chunk scan cost the game thread more than drawing them: a 4-core laptop at 120 km/h ran 42.7 fps with trees per frame, 19.5 baked.
Above the rate the trees are drawn every frame, as in the stock game, so the GPU draws them again instead of reading them from the chunk texture.
Above the rate a new chunk texture bakes without trees and without the tree pass, so each arrival costs less while you drive fast.
UI_pzopt_v5_why_luaTickHz_cpu: At ~300 fps (a 55-mod list, 60 a second = a call every 5 frames) the mods' tick handlers fell from 0.28 to 0.16 ms a frame and the frame time 3 to 8 %; on a 650-mod list with the cap at 4 frames a call, mod OnTick fell from 30.6 to 8.2 ms a frame.
UI_pzopt_v5_why_luaZombieLod_cpu: Only the zombies near you run every mod function every frame: with the 26 mods that listen, in the Louisville horde (2,400 zombies) the mod functions took 84 ms a frame in stock and 6.5 ms with the 2 ms budget below.
UI_pzopt_v5_why_luaLoadStream_cpu: No frame carries a whole chunk's mod handlers: on the 54-mod list's spinning route frames over twice the median fell from 118-147 to 40-43 (those by LoadGridsquare / LoadChunk 46-70 to 5-6), p99 17.3-20.6 to 13.1-14.8 ms.
UI_pzopt_v5_why_luaLoadStream_chunks: Chunks are ready to draw sooner, as none waits behind the stock pace: queued to drawable p99 0.9 s to 0.3 s on the spin, 0.3 to 0.1 s on the drive.
UI_pzopt_v5_why_sunShadowStaticLights_gp: One more shadow area per lit character, at most two lights each: the same cost as a torch's shadow for each.
UI_pzopt_v5_why_sunShadowStaticLights_cp: A line test from each light to the squares the characters stand on, kept for about a second: at most 48 a frame.
UI_pzopt_v6_leaf_presentPacing_tip: What each frame's hold is timed against: the GPU's completion, the CPU's end of the frame, or both.
UI_pzopt_v6_leaf_vrr_tip: Follow what the display reports, or always act as if it runs variable refresh.
UI_pzopt_v6_leaf_borderlessFullscreen_ti: On Linux only (the platform whose desktops need it for variable refresh), or on every platform.
UI_pzopt_v6_leaf_vehicleSmooth_tip: How a vehicle is placed between physics steps: drawn between the last two (10 ms behind) or the last one carried forward.
UI_pzopt_v6_leaf_bloodBake_tip: Who draws the floor splats into the chunk pictures: the GPU in the bake, or the CPU before it.
UI_pzopt_v6_leaf_hordeBatch_tip: Batches that keep the stock drawing order to the pixel, or the fastest order with the zombies after the other moving objects.
UI_pzopt_v6_leaf_modCompat_tip: What happens to a setting a Java mod also patches: switched off (max compatibility) or kept on and reported (max performance).
UI_pzopt_v6_leaf_luaTickAdaptive_tip: How the mods' per-frame time is set: a budget from the frame's headroom, or one that halves when a frame is late and grows when it is on time.
UI_pzopt_v6_leaf_corePlacement_tip: Which cores take which threads while the switch is on.
UI_pzopt_v6_leaf_gpuPstate_tip: The fixed clock to hold, or the lowest one whose frame time still fits the cap.
UI_pzopt_v6_leaf_gcSlackQueue_tip: When the spare-time collection runs under the frame queue.
UI_pzopt_v6_leaf_upscaler_tip: Which upscaler renders the world smaller and scales it back up. Its render size is the next setting.
UI_pzopt_v6_leaf_spriteFilter_tip: How the world's art is sampled when it is drawn at a size other than its own.
UI_pzopt_v6_leaf_carOccupant_tip: How the people inside a car are drawn behind its glass.
UI_pzopt_v6_leaf_darknessFloorPct_tip: How much light a seen square keeps at least, in % of full light.
UI_pzopt_v6_leaf_overlayStats_tip: How much the statistics block shows.
UI_pzopt_v6_leaf_overlayTree_tip: How many sub-phases each phase of the game-thread tree lists.
UI_pzopt_v6_leaf_overlayVerdict_tip: The short verdict, or with the two biggest game-thread sub-phases.
UI_pzopt_v6_leaf_overlayGraph_tip: How many frames the graph spans (and so its width).
UI_pzopt_v6_leaf_overlayFlame_tip: Where the flame graph sits and how wide it is.
UI_pzopt_v6_leaf_consoleLog_tip: Which PZ Optimization lines reach the console.
UI_pzopt_v6_leaf_groundTracksWater_tip: Who draws the water standing in the ruts: the game's puddles (with their ripples) when Puddle ripples is on, the tracks' own bake (still water), or always the puddles.
UI_pzopt_v6_why_presentPacing_render: The render thread waits out each frame's hold before the swap (parked, the last part spun) and reads back a GPU timestamp query per frame, a few frames later.
UI_pzopt_v6_why_frameQueue_render: The render thread holds every capped frame's swap until its slot plus the holding time: parked, then spinning the last millisecond.
UI_pzopt_v6_why_vrr_cpu: With your cap Uncapped or above the display's maximum, the game caps itself just inside the range (157 fps at 165 Hz), so the game thread prepares fewer frames a second.
UI_pzopt_v6_why_vrr_gpu: The GPU draws only the frames the display can show inside its range instead of every frame it can.
UI_pzopt_v6_why_chunkGridWidth_cpu: Chunk bakes, arriving chunks and the world's update scale with the grid's area; on 4-core machines it is the one lever (the low-end preset uses 9).
UI_pzopt_v6_why_chunkGridWidth_cores: The native lighting thread lights every loaded chunk: at 13 it used 44 % of a core instead of 70 %.
UI_pzopt_v6_why_chunkGridWidth_gpu: Fewer chunk levels to bake into textures and draw.
UI_pzopt_v6_why_chunkGridWidth_vram: Each loaded chunk level keeps its baked texture in GPU memory; fewer chunks, fewer textures.
UI_pzopt_v6_why_chunkGridWidth_ram: Fewer chunks, squares and objects held in memory.
UI_pzopt_v6_why_chunkGridWidth_load: Fewer chunks to load and light before the world appears (vanilla's 19 x 19 grid is 361).
UI_pzopt_v6_why_chunkGridWidth_chunks: A row of chunks you cross is shorter, so each arrival is less work: at 9 most of the +11 ms that late drive frames spent on arriving chunks (bakes, square loading, new-chunk lighting) went.
UI_pzopt_v6_why_luaTickAdaptive_cpu: Only while the game thread is the limit: the mods' heaviest per-frame handlers run every second to fourth frame.
UI_pzopt_v6_why_zombieLodDynamic_cpu: Fewer zombies get model draw data and animation blending each frame.
UI_pzopt_v6_why_zombieLodDynamic_render: Fewer model draws for the render thread to issue.
UI_pzopt_v6_why_zombieLodDynamic_gpu: Fewer 3D models to draw: in the Louisville horde with a floor of 32 models, the GPU-bound seconds (6 ms of 3D zombie draws) went and uncapped play rose from 141 to 172 fps.
UI_pzopt_v6_why_fogPass_cpu: The game thread no longer walks every square on screen per level to place the fog rows; it reads per-chunk fog masks instead: about 0.4 to 0.1 ms a frame on a laptop.
UI_pzopt_v6_why_fogPass_render: One draw call for every fog row (their values sent as vertex data) instead of about 190 draw calls a frame, each with three uniform updates.
UI_pzopt_v6_why_fogPass_gpu: Stock shades each pixel with up to 12 screen-wide rows (7 noise reads each, depth written per pixel, so nothing is rejected early): 1.5 ms a frame at 5K. The pass costs about 0.3 ms.
UI_pzopt_v6_why_fogPass_vram: The reduced-size fog buffer and its depth textures (a quarter of the screen per axis by default).
UI_pzopt_v6_why_rainTiles_cpu: The game thread walked the 1,024-particle cell once per screen cell (13x7 cells at 5K, max zoom), now once: the weather draw went from 1.76 to 0.10 ms a frame in a desktop thunderstorm (111 to 188 fps).
