UI_pzopt_v6_why_rainTiles_render: The render thread uploads the cell once and issues one draw per screen cell instead of sending about 100,000 rain quads: its submission went from 5.5 to 2.9 ms a frame in the same storm.
UI_pzopt_v6_why_hordeBatch_render: A run of zombies needs one shader and buffered per-draw records instead of a state save and restore, ~25 uniform writes and a palette upload per model.
UI_pzopt_v6_why_hordeBatch_gpu: Most of the stock cost was per-draw state and uniform traffic, not pixels: in a 450-zombie horde the zombies' GPU time drops from about 6.5 to 1.2 ms a frame.
UI_pzopt_v6_why_upscaler_gpu: The world's per-pixel work (fog, rain, water, lights) follows the render size: in a static storm with the stock fog at 5K, FSR 1.0 at quality ran 54 % faster than off, bicubic 73 %. On a fast drive the gain is small: chunk bakes do not shrink.
UI_pzopt_v6_why_upscaler_vram: The smaller world picture and the upscaler's own images sit beside the screen-sized one; taau and DLSS also keep a history picture at the output size.
UI_pzopt_v6_why_gpuPstate_gpu: Most of the game's GPU work waits on memory, not on the clock: a Radeon 890M held its 120 fps cap at 640 MHz instead of bursts at 2.7-2.9 GHz, 1.2 W less at 1 GHz. Each frame's GPU work takes a little longer (3.4 to 4.2 ms at 1 GHz).
UI_pzopt_v7_verdict_cost: Costs frame rate on your PC
UI_pzopt_v7_verdict_neutral: Little change to your frame rate
UI_pzopt_v7_verdict_help_end: and this takes work off it.
UI_pzopt_v7_verdict_cap: your PC held its frame cap in
UI_pzopt_v7_verdict_none: it does not change what limits your PC's frames
UI_pzopt_v7_why_modCompat_load: The mods' jars are read at launch to find the methods they patch: 24 ms with no Java mod, 163 ms with ZombieBuddy and Ultimate ZBetterFPS. Off skips the scan.
UI_pzopt_v7_why_uiRetained_cpu: Kept windows are replayed instead of running their Lua: at 240 fps the UI's share of the frame 4 to 0.9 % with the HUD, 9.8 to 1.4 % with the inventory open, 16.6 to 2.2 % with crafting, 40 to 4 % with the map.
UI_pzopt_v7_why_uiTickStagger_cpu: The updates no longer land in one frame: the worst UI-update frame 711 to 435 us with the inventory, 1.34 to 1.14 ms with crafting; the average is the same.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_enabled_cpu: The world is baked into chunk textures instead of drawn tile by tile, and the lighting, cutaway, rain and zombie work is trimmed or cached: on the desktop's spinning route 336 to 472 fps uncapped.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_enabled_render: Rain, puddles and sprites are packed once and sent in large batches, so the render thread issues far fewer draw calls (in a stock thunderstorm the rain alone is 73 % of the render thread).
UI_pzopt_v8_why_enabled_cores: The zombies' bone math, action checks, lighting reads, character draw preparation and the boot's loading run on worker threads, beside the game thread.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_enabled_gpu: Fog is drawn into a quarter-size buffer in one pass, puddles skip hidden pixels and chunk textures re-bake less often.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_enabled_ram: Chunk textures' puddle vertices, the lighting and sprite caches and the worker threads' scratch memory stay in the Java heap.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_enabled_disk: Boot caches (precompiled Lua, animation clips, texture pack indexes) are written under Zomboid/pzopt the first time.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_enabled_load: The boot loads sound, animations and scripts on parallel threads and reads the caches: launch to menu 7.4 to 5.0 s, Continue to the world 6.5 to 4.0 s on the desktop.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_enabled_chunks: New chunks are read, decoded and baked on workers and under a per-frame budget, so they appear sooner without a hitch while you move.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_treesInChunkTexture_cpu: Every tree went through the per-frame translucent pass, 35 % of the game thread at max zoom; baked, it is no longer walked and prepared each frame (frame mean 6.2 to 5.2 ms on the desktop's max-zoom route).
UI_pzopt_v8_why_treesInChunkTexture_rend: Far fewer sprites are handed to the GL each frame: render thread 35 to 32 % busy on the same route (the persistent sprite buffer had already taken most of its load).
UI_pzopt_v8_why_treesInChunkTexture_gpu: One chunk composite replaces thousands of overlapping tree sprites drawn every frame: GPU busy 84 to 61 % on the desktop's max-zoom route.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_treesInChunkTexture_chun: Each new chunk texture also bakes its trees, so an arrival costs more; on a 4-core laptop at 120 km/h that was more than drawing them (see Trees: bake only below this chunk rate).
UI_pzopt_v8_why_windSpriteSway_cpu: The stock option takes every plant out of the bake and the game thread prepares each one per frame, sheared, with a lighting query per tree; kept baked, that walk is gone.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_windSpriteSway_render: The option's path is one draw call and its uniforms per plant sprite every frame; with the plants baked the render thread issues the chunk composite instead.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_windSpriteSway_gpu: On the desktop the stock option costs about 370 us of GPU a frame at zoom 1; the sway shader that bends the baked plants costs about 20 us.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_treeBakeMaxChunksPerSec_: Baking a short-lived texture's trees, their copies in the neighbours and the 5x5-chunk scan cost the game thread more than drawing them: a 4-core laptop at 120 km/h ran 42.7 fps with trees per frame, 19.5 baked.
Above the rate the trees are drawn every frame, as in the stock game, so the GPU draws them again instead of reading them from the chunk texture.
Above the rate a new chunk texture bakes without trees and without the tree pass, so each arrival costs less while you drive fast.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_treeBakePass_cpu: Each bake scans the 5x5 chunks around it for crowns that reach in and draws copies of them, and a changed tree re-bakes the neighbours holding its copy (bakes +9 % on the spinning route).
UI_pzopt_v8_why_treeBakePass_gpu: The copies and the extra neighbour re-bakes are GPU work in the bakes (about 0.2-0.3 ms per bake on the desktop); the frame rate stayed within noise (280 vs 281.5 fps).
UI_pzopt_v8_why_treeAppend_cpu: On the 120 km/h desktop drive 60 % of all bakes were these neighbour re-bakes, each a full bake prepared on the game thread; now only the new trees' quads are listed.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_treeAppend_gpu: Each neighbour re-bake was about 300 us of GPU, 2.9 a frame on the 120 km/h desktop drive; drawing only the new trees into the finished texture removes about half of them.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_treeAppend_chunks: A chunk arriving next to baked ones no longer re-bakes their textures, so each arrival while driving costs less.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_treeRebakeLazy_cpu: Fewer re-bakes means fewer bake preparations on the game thread: neighbour re-bakes 20k to 7k on the desktop's 120 km/h drive with Trees: only trees reaching the cutaway.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_treeRebakeLazy_gpu: Each tree passed re-dirtied its chunk and about 7 neighbour textures up to four times; with the reach rule, bakes fell 31k to 21k on the desktop's drive (320 to 430 fps, GPU-bound).
UI_pzopt_v8_why_edgeTestFast_cpu: The written-out test skips the predicate calls: 154 instead of 181 ns a call, under 1 % of the game thread in the Louisville horde.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_driveTreeCutaway_cpu: Trees leaving and rejoining the bake add re-bakes prepared on the game thread: 17.4k to 21.6k bakes on the desktop's 120 km/h drive, with every tree fix on.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_driveTreeCutaway_gpu: Every see-through tree is drawn each frame in three passes and its chunk re-bakes: the rule added 0.37 ms of per-frame trees and 0.18 ms of bakes a frame on the desktop's drive (514 to ~430 fps).
UI_pzopt_v8_why_treeCutawayReach_cpu: A kept tree skips the re-bakes of its chunk and its neighbours; only its fade is stepped each frame, a few sums per tree.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_treeCutawayReach_gpu: Most see-through trees never reach a marked pixel yet left the bake and were drawn every frame in three passes; kept baked they cost neither (with the lazy re-bakes 320 to 430 fps on the desktop's drive).
UI_pzopt_v8_why_bloodBake_cpu: A bake no longer walks nine chunks' splat queues: blood per bake 122-131 to 35 us, its game-thread time 21 to 8.7 ms a second in a fight on the desktop (cpu mode: 66 us, 13.6 ms).
UI_pzopt_v8_why_bloodBake_render: The per-splat shader, depth-test and blend changes are gone: the blood's render-thread time 74-79 to 17 us a frame in the same fight (cpu mode: 43 us).
UI_pzopt_v8_why_bloodBake_gpu: One instanced draw per chunk replaces a state change and a quad per splat: bake GPU time 76 to 68 us a frame in that fight.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_bloodBake_chunks: At 1,000 splats a chunk blood doubled the cost of every chunk bake, so arrivals hitched longer; the worst second's blood time fell 33 to 6.4 ms.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_bloodAppend_cpu: With 20 new splats a second, blood-only re-bakes fell 465 to 30 in 15 s on the desktop, and the blood's game-thread time 8.7 to 2.1 ms a second.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_bloodAppend_gpu: A splat quad drawn into a finished texture replaces a full floor re-bake: bake GPU time 68 to 53 us a frame in the same fight.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_bloodSettleSec_cpu: One extra re-bake per floor that took appended blood, this long after its first splat; shorter shows the exact order sooner, 0 skips the re-bake.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_bloodFadeFix_cpu: The pushed-out list only grows (6,800 splats in a test fight) and every bake of the chunk and its neighbours walks it; dropping them keeps the walk short.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_bloodFadeFix_gpu: Those old splats are no longer drawn into each re-bake of the floor.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_bloodRebakeCoalesceMs_cp: The splats of one hit share a re-bake: 413 to 199 re-bakes in a 15 s fight on the desktop. Longer gathers more but shows the new blood later.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_bloodRebakeCoalesceMs_gp: Every re-bake saved is a floor texture the GPU does not redraw (about 0.2 ms of GPU a bake on the desktop).
UI_pzopt_v8_why_bloodAppendPlants_cpu: By a road most splats land near grass: blood-only re-bakes fell 441 to 38 in a 15 s fight on the desktop, 146 of 383 splats appended under plants.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_bloodAppendPlants_gpu: The plants are drawn once more into a small layer instead of the whole floor re-baking; that pass is below the profiler's resolution.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_bloodAppendVegetation_cp: Those splats no longer re-bake their floor at all; the remaining re-bakes of a fight go too.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_fliesToggleFix_cpu: Each toggle forced an immediate re-bake next to the car, prepared on the game thread: 430+ of them on the 120 km/h Rosewood drive, now none.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_fliesToggleFix_gpu: Those forced re-bakes were about 0.2 ms of GPU each and never waited for the bake budget.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_windowsInChunkTexture_cp: The 30-130 windows and doors a frame leave the per-frame pass; on the desktop's max-zoom route that stayed within the run-to-run noise.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_translucentTilesInChunkT: The per-frame pass drew 1,500-3,600 such tiles a frame at max zoom, now 50-120: frame mean 5.0 to 4.5 ms, p99 16.4 to 13.8 ms on the desktop's max-zoom route.
Thousands fewer sprites a frame to submit: render thread 31 to 19 % busy on the same route.
The tiles come with the chunk composite instead of one quad each: GPU busy 62 to 59 %.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_bakeScheduler_cpu: Arrivals, cutaways and lighting no longer stack in one frame: a heavy frame used to prepare 12-120 level bakes on the game thread.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_bakeScheduler_render: Each bake is about 0.03 ms of render-thread submit; spread over frames, the render thread's heavy frames are no longer piled with dozens of them.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_bakeScheduler_gpu: The bakes were the GPU's burst (3.5 ms mean in heavy frames, about 0.2 ms a bake); spread out, GPU busy fell 61 to 47 % on the Rosewood drive with the rest of the set.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_bakeFrameBudget_cpu: Caps how much bake work lands on one frame. Lower keeps frames shorter but leaves levels waiting longer; on the Rosewood drive a ceiling of 4 was no better than 8.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_bakeBudgetAdaptive_cpu: A long frame is followed by fewer bake preparations, so slow frames do not stack one on the next.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_bakeBudgetAdaptive_gpu: Bakes are mostly GPU work (about 0.2 ms each on the desktop); after a slow frame half as many are queued, so the GPU's bursts stay smaller.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_occlusionGrantedOnly_cpu: The hidden-level pass skips the levels still waiting: on the Rosewood 120 km/h drive p99.9 17.0 to 15.9 ms and the worst frame 45 to 27 ms.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_bakeNoSync_render: Each question to NVIDIA's threaded driver made the render thread wait for every bake queued before it: in the Louisville horde with every Enhancement on, the bake time per frame p99 8.3 to 1.9 ms, worst 25 to 9 ms.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_bakeMipLevels_gpu: Building 3 levels instead of 11 after every bake: 0.062 to 0.020 ms, a whole bake 0.20 to 0.16 ms of GPU on the desktop. More levels cost more for nothing visible.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_renderChunkTopUp_render: A fresh chunk texture costs the render thread about 1 ms of GL allocation; made ahead, a burst of arrivals no longer pays it in one frame (210 of 210 on the Rosewood drive).
UI_pzopt_v8_why_renderChunkTopUp_vram: The spare textures sit in GPU memory ready for use, 32 by default at the current zoom's texture size.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_bakeBudget_cpu: A new chunk row at max zoom baked dozens of textures in one frame (26 % of slow frames); 8 a frame, with the lighting budget, took p99 13.8 to 8.3 ms on the desktop. Lower spreads more, new chunks fill in later.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_rebakeBudget_cpu: Re-bakes past the budget wait a few frames instead of piling onto one; lower holds more stale images, higher allows longer frames.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_lightingRebakeBudget_cpu: A lightning strike dirtied every texture on screen at once: five 50-90 ms frames per strike. Spread at 8 a frame, the storm drive's p99.9 fell 57 to 12.5 ms.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_lightingRebakeBudget_gpu: The flash's re-bakes reach the GPU a few per frame instead of all in one frame.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_lightingRebakeMaxFrames_: A longer window spreads a flash's re-bakes thinner, for shorter frames, but leaves light stale longer; 30 frames is an eighth of a second at 240 fps.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_lightingRebakeMs_cpu: Daylight drift moves every square a step at a time, which dirtied every texture on screen; holding them 250 ms bakes far fewer. Longer saves more but the light catches up later (1,000 measured no better).
UI_pzopt_v8_why_zoomRetain_cpu: Stock bakes every level a zoom-out reveals in the frame it appears, hundreds for a full spin; here they are spread 4-12 a frame over the next 20-40 frames.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_zoomRetain_gpu: Kept textures that come back unchanged need no bake, and the rest reach the GPU a few per frame instead of all at once.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_zoomRetain_vram: Textures off screen stay in GPU memory while their chunk is inside the widest zoom's view: at most what stock itself holds at the widest zoom.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_zoomRebakeBudget_cpu: Caps the zoom's bakes in one frame; lower spreads the fill over more frames (old images or gaps for longer), higher fills faster with longer frames.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_lightingStrongDelta_cpu: Strong changes skip the hold, so a moving torch or headlight re-bakes the few levels in its beam each frame; a lower threshold marks more of them.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_lightingStrongDelta_gpu: Those immediate re-bakes are GPU work (about 0.2 ms each); in a horde, turning can mark nearly every exterior level strong, which the budget below caps.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_lightingStrongBudget_cpu: Fewer bake preparations a frame on the game thread while you turn among tall buildings.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_lightingStrongBudget_gpu: Without a cap, turning in downtown Louisville baked 100+ tall chunk textures a frame: 10.8 fps with the GPU 97 % busy; a cap of 8 ended that.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_lightingStrongFrameMs_gp: In a slow frame the out-of-sight fade moves further and marks more levels strong; halving their bakes keeps that GPU work from growing frame after frame.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_lightingGlobalDeltaPct_c: A flash would otherwise count as a strong change on every exterior square and re-bake everything in one frame; lower spreads more such events, higher lets more land at once.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_lightingBudget_cpu: Refreshing the light info of a new chunk row was 12 % of the slow frames' game thread; 8 a frame, with the bake budget, took p99 13.8 to 8.3 ms on the desktop's max-zoom route.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_lightingFlush_cpu: The chunks still queued are refreshed in the frame the lighting pass lands, so that frame carries the rest of the budget's work.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_visBlurReduce_gpu: The 25 texture reads per pixel (about 340 million a frame at the widest zoom) become one: about 0.13 ms less GPU time a frame on a laptop. The pass's full-screen blend itself stays.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_cutawayFast_cpu: The per-square occluder test only runs for chunk levels that changed; an unchanged level copies its stored mask, a few bit operations instead of 64 square tests a level each frame.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_cutawayRadius_cpu: Fewer chunks to walk in each cutaway visit, which runs almost every frame while you move through a town: with the scan interval below, about 8 fps more at about 200 fps on the desktop's Rosewood route. A smaller radius walks less.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_gridStackInterval_cpu: While you stand in one square facing one way, the points-of-interest, collapsing-building and hidden-floor scans run one frame in 8 (the default) instead of every frame. A higher number skips more.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_lightSwitchCheckFrames_c: The lighting asks every light source's switch for power every frame (grid, generators, the 3x3x2 squares around it): 2.3 % of the game thread on the Rosewood route, 0.3 % with the default 15.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_rainTiles_cpu: The game thread walked the 1,024-particle cell once per screen cell (13x7 cells at 5K, max zoom), now once: the weather draw went from 1.76 to 0.10 ms a frame in a desktop thunderstorm (111 to 188 fps).
UI_pzopt_v8_why_rainTiles_render: The render thread uploads the cell once and issues one draw per screen cell instead of sending about 100,000 rain quads: its submission went from 5.5 to 2.9 ms a frame in the same storm.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_rainSplashesFast_cpu: Skipping straight to the next square that splashes replaces a random roll for every idle square on screen each frame: about 2.6 % of the frame on a laptop in a storm.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_puddleCache_cpu: Stock re-packed every wet square of every chunk level on screen each frame: 4.5 ms of a 13 ms thunderstorm frame at max zoom on the desktop, now 0.96 ms (70 to 109 fps with the profiler on).
UI_pzopt_v8_why_puddleCache_ram: The packed puddle vertices (32 numbers per wet square) are kept on each loaded chunk.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_puddleCacheFrames_cpu: At 60 about 4 batches a frame are rebuilt as a backstop on a storm route; a lower number rebuilds more often (1 = every batch every frame, the stock cost), a higher one less.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_puddleEarlyZ_gpu: Without a per-pixel depth write the graphics card rejects hidden puddle pixels before the ~200-step shader: puddles 0.29 to 0.10 ms a frame on the desktop's 120 km/h storm drive (357 to 390 fps).
UI_pzopt_v8_why_puddleVbo_render: The render thread no longer streams every wet square through the sprite buffer each frame: 93 to 38 % busy on the desktop's 120 km/h storm drive (232 to 325 fps).
UI_pzopt_v8_why_puddleVbo_gpu: The graphics card had been starving on the streamed puddle data; drawn from its own buffers with one draw per chunk level, puddles went from 1.3 to 0.29 ms a frame on the same drive.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_puddleVbo_vram: One vertex buffer per chunk level with puddles, kept while the chunk is loaded.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_weatherMaskIdleSkip_cpu: Stock rasterised the whole view every frame, testing each outdoor square for an interior: the weather pass went from 2.6 to 0.5 % of the game thread outdoors and from 6.6 to 2.4 % on the spinning Rosewood route.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_weatherMaskIdleSkip_gpu: With nothing to cut, the mask's draw into its screen-sized buffer is skipped as well.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_weatherFxScalePct_gpu: Fewer pixels to fill in the weather buffers. At 5K the full-size pass was about 11 % of the uncapped frame, but 50 % measured no faster on the desktop's spinning route, so the gain is small.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_weatherFxScalePct_vram: The mask and particle buffers shrink with the square of the percentage: 50 % is a quarter of the memory.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_fogPass_cpu: The game thread no longer walks every square on screen per level to place the fog rows; it reads per-chunk fog masks instead: about 0.4 to 0.1 ms a frame on a laptop.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_fogPass_render: One draw call for every fog row (their values sent as vertex data) instead of about 190 draw calls a frame, each with three uniform updates.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_fogPass_gpu: Stock shades each pixel with up to 12 screen-wide rows (7 noise reads each, depth written per pixel, so nothing is rejected early): 1.5 ms a frame at 5K. The pass costs about 0.3 ms.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_fogPass_vram: The reduced-size fog buffer and its depth textures (a quarter of the screen per axis by default).
UI_pzopt_v8_why_fogScalePct_gpu: Fog work scales with the buffer's area (50 a quarter, 25 a sixteenth): on the 5K desktop about 0.8 ms a frame at 100, 0.39 ms at 50, 0.18 ms at 25.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_fogScalePct_vram: The fog buffers shrink with the area too: a sixteenth of the screen at 25.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_fogMaskFrames_cpu: Reading the masks instead of the squares: the fog row walk went from 215 to about 35 us per level a frame on a laptop. A higher number refreshes the masks less often; 0 walks every square.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_cutawayVisitPrefilter_cp: Most walls on screen cannot cut, so their square lookups are skipped: 454 to 466 fps on the desktop's uncapped spinning Rosewood route.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_cutawayInvalidateChanged: Far fewer chunk textures are re-baked while you move: with the sound-zone and light-info changes of the same step, 374 to 442 fps on the desktop's uncapped spinning Rosewood route.
Every re-bake skipped is a chunk-level texture the graphics card does not redraw.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_occlusionSkipLightingOnl: Daylight drift dirties chunk levels nearly every frame, and stock rebuilt the whole occlusion grid each time: with the chunk hand-off budget of the same step, 442 to 454 fps uncapped on the desktop.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_lightInfoChunkGate_cpu: One call instead of 64 per unchanged chunk level, each a call into the native lighting library: 466 to 500 fps on the desktop's uncapped spinning Rosewood route.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_lightInfoOncePerFrame_cp: Each square is read from the native lighting library at most once a frame; part of the 374 to 442 fps step on the desktop's uncapped spinning Rosewood route (with two other changes).
UI_pzopt_v8_why_soundZoneCache_cpu: Seven ambient parameters each scanned the zones of an 80x80 area every frame; part of the 374 to 442 fps step on the desktop's uncapped Rosewood route (with two other changes).
UI_pzopt_v8_why_worldSoundFast_cpu: A ringing house alarm adds its 600-tile sound every frame: 0.4 ms a frame in stock, 0.007 ms with this (242 to 290 fps in the desktop's alarm storm). At 2000 tiles stock took 4.4 ms a frame.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_animBonesParallel_cpu: The bone math was 9 % of the game thread in the Louisville horde; the game thread now does only its share of the batch.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_animBonesParallel_cores: The blending of every zombie's bones is split across the frame worker threads (8 by default).
UI_pzopt_v8_why_frameThreads_cores: More threads split each batch finer: on a Ryzen AI 9 HX 370 handheld 11 ran a horde frame about 5 % faster than 8; on the 16-core desktop 12 was no faster than 8.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_actionEvalParallel_cpu: The rule tests were 7-10 % of the game thread in the Louisville horde; it now only applies the results.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_actionEvalParallel_cores: The evaluations run on the frame worker threads, a share each.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_animatorParallel_cpu: The animators were 12 % of the game thread in a horde. With the bone batch and pipeline settings the zombies' postupdate fell from about 3.0 to 0.6 ms a frame in the Louisville horde (90 to 105 fps).
UI_pzopt_v8_why_animatorParallel_cores: Each zombie's animator is a task on the frame workers; about 15 of ~800 zombies a frame fall back to the game thread.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_headOnWorker_cpu: That step leaves the game thread's postupdate loop: about 0.1 ms a frame less in the Louisville horde.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_headOnWorker_cores: It runs inside each zombie's decision-rule task on the frame workers.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_lazyPose_cpu: Most of the 60 keyframe searches per track per frame are never made: a far-sprite zombie reads one or two bones, and a modelled zombie's searches happen in the bone batch on the workers.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_animatorPipeline_cpu: The game thread no longer waits for the whole batch before applying: it starts with the first finished zombie and runs an unstarted task itself while it waits.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_animatorPipeline_cores: The decision rules and the animators run on the workers alone, overlapping the game thread's apply loop.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_animBatchAsync_cpu: The game thread stops waiting for the bone batch at the end of the loop: on its own this took the zombies' postupdate from 18 to 10 % of the game thread in the Louisville horde.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_animBatchAsync_cores: The bone batch keeps running on the workers while the game thread goes on, until the game's own animation join point.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_guardedCallbacks_cpu: The game thread no longer reads these eight values for every zombie before a batch, and every zombie animation state can now be evaluated on the workers.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_guardedCallbacks_cores: The eight rules are read in the zombies' tasks on the frame workers; only the rare case comes back to the game thread.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_modelLockPerInstance_cpu: The game thread, which applies the animator results and takes part in the batch, waits less for it.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_modelLockPerInstance_cor: The animator tasks on the workers run side by side instead of one at a time: each had run 2.4x slower in parallel, and the workers' animator time went from 5.3 to 2.7 ms a frame.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_poolStatsBatched_cores: The workers stop retrying the same shared counter update against each other (a compare-and-set loop per pooled object), so the batches scale across the cores.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_ecsLookupFast_cpu: These lookups run many times per zombie per frame: 5 % of the game thread in the Louisville horde before.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_lookupMemo_cpu: A burst of new zombies or new 3D models spent 8-20 ms a second of game thread in these lookups; a remembered name is one hash probe.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_actionConditionFast_cpu: No text formatting and parsing per rule test, across the thousands of rule tests a horde makes each frame.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_skinTransformsPrecompute: The render pass on the game thread no longer multiplies the skin matrices: 3 % of the game thread in a horde.
The multiplications run in each zombie's bone task on the frame workers.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_skinPalettePrecompute_cp: Building each model's draw data copies the bone palette in one bulk copy instead of storing 16 numbers per bone.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_skinPalettePrecompute_co: Storing the palette is added to each zombie's bone task on the frame workers.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_shadowPrep_cpu: Three bone-to-world transforms and three ground projections per zombie leave the game thread's render pass.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_shadowPrep_cores: They run in the zombie's bone task on the frame workers.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_boneIndexCache_cpu: A search of the skeleton's bone names per bone, per drawn character, per frame becomes a cache hit.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_lightingReadParallel_cpu: These reads were 12 % of the game thread in the Louisville horde; it now takes one share and runs the room hooks.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_lightingReadParallel_cor: Each queued chunk level is read on a frame worker; the native lighting reads are pure reads, so the levels do not interfere.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_zombieCullSortFast_cpu: Each zombie's score is computed once instead of twice per comparison of the sort: the sort was 1.4 % of the game thread in a Louisville horde.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_vehicleCull_cpu: Downtown Louisville has hundreds of parked cars; the exact test (two matrix multiplies per car per zombie) was 6 % of the game thread there, 0.7 % with this.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_nearVehicleGrid_cpu: Downtown most of those 16 chunk lookups found an empty car list: 2.4 % of the game thread in the Louisville horde, now one rectangle query on the frame's table.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_playerLosFast_cpu: The player's sight pass was 16 % of the game thread in the Louisville horde, 12 of it this search; with the spot early-out below it fell to 3.7 %.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_playerLosParallel_cpu: The player's sight pass went from about 1.1 to 0.4 ms a frame in the Louisville horde on a laptop (74-80 to 82-84 fps over whole runs).
UI_pzopt_v8_why_playerLosParallel_cores: The reads run in chunks of 64 objects on the frame workers: about 2.4 ms more CPU time a frame across the workers on the desktop.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_zombieSpotFast_cpu: Most of a horde cannot see you, so their spot test stops at the first zero; with the spotted-list change above the player's sight pass went from 16 to 3.7 % of the game thread in Louisville.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_charDrawPrep_cpu: The characters draw went from 13 % of the game thread to under 5 % in the Louisville horde; the game thread keeps the visibility test and the per-square light refresh.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_charDrawPrep_cores: About 480 zombies' draw data a frame are built on the pass's own thread pool (14 threads on a 16-core machine), overlapping the chunk bakes.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_hordeBatch_render: A run of zombies needs one shader and buffered per-draw records instead of a state save and restore, ~25 uniform writes and a palette upload per model.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_hordeBatch_gpu: Most of the stock cost was per-draw state and uniform traffic, not pixels: in a 450-zombie horde the zombies' GPU time drops from about 6.5 to 1.2 ms a frame.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_hordeBatchVao_render: No new vertex setup per mesh: each had made the render thread wait about 1 ms for the driver, the 5-26 ms render-thread spikes when the horde came into view.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_atlasBatch_render: One persistent vertex buffer and a run of draws instead of a full sprite-batch setup per far zombie.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_atlasBatch_gpu: Each far zombie was its own short sprite batch, about 1.3 ms of GPU a frame in the horde seconds; drawn in runs, far fewer state changes separate them.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_hordeBatchOrder_render: About a fifth as many batch flushes for the render thread to set up.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_hordeBatchOrder_gpu: About 50 batches a frame instead of ~245, each with its own state push and pop: the horde's GPU time in the densest seconds of the Louisville route went from about 7 to 4 ms a frame.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_hordeBatchUnits_render: About a sixteenth as many texture binds to issue.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_hordeBatchUnits_gpu: Fewer texture switches stall the graphics card between draws: the bind before every draw had cost about 0.9 ms of GPU a frame in the Louisville horde seconds.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_renderPrewarm_render: The horde's first sight no longer makes them: on the Louisville route that frame had taken 27 ms and the first clothing picture 12-17 ms (now 2.1-3.3 ms).
UI_pzopt_v8_why_renderPrewarm_load: About 0.2 s more at the end of loading, while the world appears.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_renderPrewarmOutlines_re: No 10-11 ms render-thread frame at the first outline (measured on the Louisville route).
UI_pzopt_v8_why_renderPrewarmOutlines_vr: The three screen-sized outline framebuffers take their video memory from the start of the session instead of from the first outline.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_hordePaletteMismatch_ren: The slow compare cost about 0.6 ms of render thread a frame when a horde first came into view.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_charDrawThreads_cores: More threads finish the ~480 zombies' draw data sooner, so the game thread does not wait for it; on a 16-core machine 14 keep it from waiting.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_zombieAtlasFast_cpu: About 1,100 such zombies a frame in a Louisville horde, each now one flat call; part of the characters draw falling from 13 to under 5 % of the game thread.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_renderLastFast_cpu: About 2,500 zombie inventories a frame on the Louisville horde are no longer walked: 0.05 ms of the frame.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_actionSnapshotFilter_cpu: The per-frame snapshot was 7.6 % of the game thread in the Louisville horde; it now visits only the handful of variables with side effects.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_emitterParamSkip_cpu: The footstep material walk and the room lookup per zombie per frame were 1.6 % of the game thread in the Louisville horde.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_separateFast_cpu: The push-apart pass was 3.2 % of the game thread in the Louisville horde; zombies on a few hundred squares recomputed the same wall answers three to eight times a frame.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_separateParallel_cpu: With it the zombies' share of the game thread went from 16 to 12 % in the Louisville horde.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_separateParallel_cores: The push-apart computes run on the frame workers at the top of the update.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_ragdollGate_cpu: About 60,000 questions a frame each looked up the body model: 1.2-2.2 % of the game thread in the Louisville horde, now close to 0; with the body model cache below, about 3 % more fps.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_bodyModelCache_cpu: Getting a character's animation player went from 1.6 to 0.2 % of the game thread in the Louisville horde, and working out its body model from 0.7 to 0 %.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_sleepCheckMemo_cpu: The player list was walked tens of thousands of times a frame for this answer: 0.7 % of the game thread in the Louisville horde.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_stateParamMemo_cpu: Each read went through the component map, a class-keyed map and a new capturing lambda; now one probe. The state-param maps were 0.9 % of the game thread in the Louisville horde.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_actionGroupCache_cpu: Two lower-cased copies of the group name and two map probes per zombie per frame are gone.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_profilerThreadMemo_cpu: Two scans of a list of names per probe, and the zombie update and postupdate each have a probe: 0.7 % of the game thread in the Louisville horde.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_zombieSimLodTiles_cpu: Fewer zombie updates a frame: with 8 tiles, two steps and the thump spread the zombies' game-thread time went from 1.9 to 0.85 ms a frame in the Louisville horde. A closer distance saves more.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_zombieSimLodSteps_cpu: Each further step halves the update rate of the zombies past it once more; three steps made the Louisville test scene unstable.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_zombieCheckSpread_cpu: Each zombie's door-and-window grid test runs on one frame in N instead of every frame; part of the set that took the zombies from 1.9 to 0.85 ms a frame in the Louisville horde.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_zombieLodDynamic_cpu: Fewer zombies get model draw data and animation blending each frame.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_zombieLodDynamic_render: Fewer model draws for the render thread to issue.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_zombieLodDynamic_gpu: Fewer 3D models to draw: in the Louisville horde with a floor of 32 models, the GPU-bound seconds (6 ms of 3D zombie draws) went and uncapped play rose from 141 to 172 fps.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_zombieLodFixed3d_cpu: Fewer zombies get model draw data and animation blending each frame.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_zombieLodFixed3d_render: Fewer model draws for the render thread to issue.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_zombieLodFixed3d_gpu: Only this many 3D models are drawn instead of the game's 510; the rest are flat sprites, which cost far less to draw.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_zombieLodFadeMs_gpu: While a zombie crossfades, both its 3D model and its sprite are drawn.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_zombieFirstSightSprite_r: At the horde's first sight on the Louisville route the clothing pictures a frame drop from 29-34 (13-17 ms of render thread) to 9-10 (about 3 ms).
UI_pzopt_v8_why_entityUpdateParallel_cpu: The update loop is the only part of the frame that grows with the whole zombie population; the calm zombies leave it: -0.9 ms a frame in a steady horde on the desktop, -2 to -4 ms on the Louisville horde.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_entityUpdateParallel_cor: The calm zombies' updates run on the eight frame workers: about 2.3 ms more process CPU a frame in a steady horde, spread over cores that were idle.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_entityUpdatePipeline_cor: The zombie batch goes to the workers before the game thread updates the animals, vehicles and busy zombies, so the workers run while the game thread works instead of waiting for it to reach the batch.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_entityUpdateMoreStates_c: About 300 more zombies a frame leave the game thread's inline phase in downtown Louisville; most of that time is now spent waiting at the batch's join, so the update section gains only ~0.05 ms.
The sitting and default-state zombies run the idle zombies' generic update on the frame workers.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_postupdateParallel_cpu: Each calm zombie's move (push, wall and fence slides, stairs, landing square) is no longer computed in the game thread's movement loop: the postupdate section 2.44 to 2.08 ms a frame in the horde.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_postupdateParallel_cores: The moves are computed in one task per zombie on the frame workers.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_postupdateNoopSkip_cpu: One list search per zombie per frame is skipped for zombies that stayed on their square: the movement loop about 0.06 ms a frame shorter in the Louisville horde.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_postupdateEligibleOnWork: The game thread no longer scans every zombie before the batch (its first touch of each zombie's animation player, a cache miss each): about -0.08 ms a frame in the Louisville horde.
The eligibility test runs at the start of each zombie's own movement task on a worker.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_postupdateVehicleOnWorke: The 32-54 zombies a frame that come near Louisville's parked cars no longer fall back to the game thread's stock movement.
Their car collision (the game's own resolveCollision, under its lock) runs in their movement task on the workers.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_postupdateFuse_cpu: The game thread no longer waits after its loop for these zombies' decisions and animators: the postupdate 1.97 to 1.60 ms a frame in the Louisville horde.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_postupdateFuse_cores: A target-less zombie's animation-state decision, and when nothing changes its animator, run on the workers while the movement loop is still going.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_postupdateClean_cpu: The movement loop passes over a clean zombie without reading it: the loop 0.76 to 0.32 ms a frame in the Louisville horde.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_postupdateClean_cores: The rest of a clean zombie's postupdate (attack variables, balance, sight flag) is finished in its movement task on a worker.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_separateEdgeCache_cpu: The separation batch, which the game thread shares and waits for, finishes sooner: the wall test was 39 % of its time.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_separateEdgeCache_cores: Each wall answer is worked out once a frame and kept on the square for all workers; before, every worker asked the grid again.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_luaSilentSkip_cpu: No empty event is recorded on the workers and replayed on the game thread for every batched zombie: the replay about 0.04 ms a frame shorter in the Louisville horde.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_luaZombieLod_cpu: Only the zombies near you run every mod function every frame: with the 26 mods that listen, in the Louisville horde (2,400 zombies) the mod functions took 84 ms a frame in stock and 6.5 ms with the 2 ms budget below.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_luaZombieBudgetUs_cpu: The zombie mod functions' time per frame stays near this however big the horde: Louisville horde with 26 such mods, game-thread frame 106 to 20 ms (p99 151 to 97 ms) at 2 ms.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_luaZombieMaxGapMs_cpu: A longer gap lets the budget stretch further in a big horde, so less time per frame; a shorter one keeps mod functions closer to every frame.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_luaZombieHz_cpu: Each zombie's mod functions run at most this often a second instead of every frame; it only helps while the frame rate is above the rate.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_luaZombieLodNear_cpu: A larger near distance runs more zombies' mod functions every frame.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_luaZombieLodHz1_cpu: A higher rate runs the on-screen zombies' mod functions more often.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_luaZombieLodHz2_cpu: A higher rate runs the off-screen zombies' mod functions more often.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_luaZombieCaptureDue_cpu: A zombie updated on another core is not recorded and replayed on the game thread when none of its mod functions is due.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_luaZombieDirtySkip_cpu: Mod functions are not run on a zombie whose watched state did not change since their last call.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_randPerWorker_cpu: The batch finishes sooner, so the game thread waits less at its join: 0.59 to 0.46 ms a frame.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_randPerWorker_cores: The workers no longer queue at the one locked generator (about 7 % of the batch's samples): the batch's worker CPU 4.95 to 3.81 ms a frame in the Louisville horde.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_animalLosFast_cpu: An animal's sight call for each zombie beyond 10 squares is folded into its exact bookkeeping: with 60 cows near a horde the animals' sight 2.62 to 1.74 ms a frame on the desktop.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_renderPrepParallel_cpu: Two world walks per on-screen character leave the game thread's character draw: 0.57 to 0.22 ms a frame in Louisville on the desktop.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_renderPrepParallel_cores: Each character's sun share and water proximity are worked out on the frame workers while the game thread draws the ground.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_pplPackParallel_cpu: The light-map packing leaves the game thread: with the torch test per chunk, its preparation 0.56 to 0.17 ms a frame in Louisville on the desktop, 1.04 to 0.35 ms on the laptop's drive.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_pplPackParallel_cores: Each changed piece of the light map is packed in its own task on the frame workers.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_pplTorchNearChunk_cpu: One reach test per 8x8 chunk replaces 64 square tests where no torch reaches; measured together with the light map on other cores (above).
UI_pzopt_v8_why_schedulerClassifyParalle: The per-object decisions leave the game thread: the scheduler's start 0.28 to 0.17 ms a frame in a steady horde on the desktop, -0.34 ms on a Mac.
Each object's update rate (its simulation level) is computed on the frame workers; the game thread only files the results.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_schedulerFillParallel_cp: The game thread fills the schedule from arrays the workers wrote, without touching each object (a cache miss each before): the scheduler's start 0.43 to 0.32 ms a frame in the Louisville horde.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_schedulerFillParallel_co: The square test and every per-object read the fill needs are made in the workers' classification tasks.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_zombieStatsFold_cpu: About 2,000 statistics-map additions and achievement checks a frame in a horde become three: roughly -0.4 ms a frame in a steady horde on the desktop.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_visPolyAsync_cpu: The cone's shape is no longer built on the game thread; with the shading data on other cores, the laptop's tile drawing -0.41 ms a frame on a 120 km/h drive.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_visPolyAsync_cores: The shape is built on a thread of its own from the start of the tile drawing, while the game thread draws the ground.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_aoContextParallel_cpu: A chunk redraw no longer gathers its neighbourhood's grass, tree, wall and roof masks itself; with the vision cone on its own thread, the laptop's tile drawing -0.41 ms a frame on a drive.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_aoContextParallel_cores: The masks of all the chunks a frame redraws are gathered in one batch on the frame workers.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_translucentOrderCache_cp: The level-by-level merge and sort runs only when a level changes: the laptop's tile drawing -0.30 ms a frame on a 120 km/h drive.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_losLightPrefetch_cpu: Handing the squares out and waiting for the batch costs more than the sight check's own reads (~130 ns a square): the check +0.12 to 0.14 ms a frame.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_losLightPrefetch_cores: The light refresh of the sight squares runs on the frame workers ahead of the check.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_zombieSpawnSpread_cpu: Dressing and animating dozens of new zombies no longer lands in one frame of several milliseconds; the same work is spread over the next frames within a small budget a frame.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_zombieModelAddBudgetUs_c: Model and clothing builds past the budget move to the next frames instead of piling into one 4 ms frame: in the Louisville horde frames over 12 ms halved (4.7 to 2.4 %). Lower spreads more, higher gives models sooner.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_burstGovernor_cpu: In a run of late frames the zombie creation and model building get the smaller heavy-frame budgets below, so that work lands in the lighter frames after them instead of on the late ones.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_persistentVbo_render: Stock orphaned and re-mapped a GL buffer for every 64 KB of sprites, ~25 % of the render thread at max zoom: its busy time 63 to 35 % on the max-zoom route, about 2.7x the uncapped frame rate there.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_persistentVboFrameSync_r: Each fence check is a round trip to NVIDIA's driver thread (~1 ms under load), even for a long-signalled fence; one fence a frame removes nearly all of them.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_persistentVboSlots_rende: With more slots a wrap of the 128-buffer ring rarely meets a batch the GPU still reads, so the render thread waits on a fence less often (within the run noise on the town drive).
UI_pzopt_v8_why_persistentVboSlots_vram: Each sprite buffer keeps this many storage slots instead of one: at 4, four times the ring's buffer memory.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_vboBatchKb_render: Stock uploaded and drew every 28 quads, 73 % of the render thread in a thunderstorm at 5K; with 1024 KB and single-advance quads the storm's submission 8.7 to 6.1 ms a frame.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_vboBatchKb_vram: The batch's vertex and index buffers are created at this size (up to 1.5 MB) instead of 4 KB.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_vboFastQuads_render: Four vertices, four indices and one position advance are written in one step instead of four checked calls; part of the storm's 8.7 to 6.1 ms submission with the larger batch.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_reflexBoost_gpu: With the clocks held up each frame's GPU work finishes sooner: 3.9 to 1.3 ms at a 60 fps cap on an RTX 4090, for about 28 W more power.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_reflexCapFps_cpu: With vsync the game makes a few percent fewer frames than the refresh (157 instead of 165 at 165 Hz), so the game thread prepares fewer frames a second.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_reflexCapFps_gpu: The GPU draws those few percent fewer frames too.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_uiRetained_cpu: Kept windows are replayed instead of running their Lua: at 240 fps the UI's share of the frame 4 to 0.9 % with the HUD, 9.8 to 1.4 % with the inventory open, 16.6 to 2.2 % with crafting, 40 to 4 % with the map.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_uiRetainedChildren_cpu: Unchanged buttons and panels are replayed instead of redrawn: the map's share of the frame 6.4 to 4.1 % (its symbol buttons).
UI_pzopt_v8_why_uiVerify_cpu: Each kept window's read set (Lua fields, game getters, the mouse) is re-checked every frame and changed windows drawn at once: e.g. the inventory with a 200-item stack 1.8 to 2.3 % of the frame at 240 fps.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_uiAnimate_cpu: A moving window runs its Lua every frame while it moves: scrolling a 200-item stack 8 to 15 % of the frame at 240 fps, taken from the frame's spare time.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_uiSlack_cpu: Optional redraws are granted only from the frame's spare time (uncapped a fifth of it), so they never push the game thread past the cap: 240 fps held in every UI scene measured.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_uiMoveReplay_cpu: A dragged window's kept picture is shifted to its new place instead of its Lua running every frame of the drag.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_uiTickStagger_cpu: The updates no longer land in one frame: the worst UI-update frame 711 to 435 us with the inventory, 1.34 to 1.14 ms with crafting; the average is the same.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_uiLuaFast_cpu: A hidden inventory skips its 70-100 us button re-arrange ten times a second and the item list one pass: the HUD's element updates ~30 to ~20 us a frame.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_hotsaveWarmup_cpu: The first save pass after a transfer runs warm code: its map records 16.5 to 5.8 ms, the one-off stutter gone.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_hotsaveWarmup_load: The three warm-up passes add about 36 ms to the loading screen.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_mapStreetMemo_cpu: Street lengths and translated names are worked out once per view and language, and the sort uses one index pass: the map's UI 6.4 to 3.8 ms a redraw.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_mapStreetCache_cpu: The label layout is not redone while the view, streets, options, style and language stay the same: the map's UI 3.8 to 1.4 ms a redraw.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_mapVisitedFast_cpu: Each texture row is built in an array and copied at once instead of four checked writes per pixel: the first map open's long frame 97 to 67 ms.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_luaJit_cpu: Lua registers stay in Java locals and numbers unboxed instead of every instruction writing the shared Lua stack: the Lua VM benchmark's kernels 4.4 times faster (geomean, 513 to 117 us), a mod LoadGridsquare handler 5.4 times, an OnTick handler 7.7 times.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_luaJavaFast_cpu: No reflective invoke and no pooled argument objects per call: with the compiler on, the benchmark's LoadGridsquare kernel 899 to 351 us.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_luaFastTable_cpu: Compiled field reads find a key's slot by one identity compare and array-like tables are read by index: the Lua VM benchmark 140 to 117 us (geomean) with the compiler on.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_luaPatternFast_cpu: No position object per matching step: the string benchmark of the patterns mods run every frame (a per-mod gsub, a list gmatch, item-type matches) 9.5 to 3.2 us.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_luaStringFast_cpu: No locked pool per position object: the same benchmark on the stock matcher 9.5 to 4.4 us.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_modProfile_cpu: Performance keeps every optimisation in the methods Java mods patch and reuses the windows mods draw in; Compatibility switches those off, so the game thread does the stock work there.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_modCompat_load: The mods' jars are read at launch to find the methods they patch: 24 ms with no Java mod, 163 ms with ZombieBuddy and Ultimate ZBetterFPS. Off skips the scan.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_uiRetainedMods_cpu: Mod-drawn windows are replayed like the game's own instead of running their Lua 60 times a second.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_luaEventDispatchFast_cpu: With ~800 mod handler calls a frame the loop's own cost fell from 0.17 to 0.10 ms a frame (650-mod list).
UI_pzopt_v8_why_luaTickHz_cpu: At ~300 fps (a 55-mod list, 60 a second = a call every 5 frames) the mods' tick handlers fell from 0.28 to 0.16 ms a frame and the frame time 3 to 8 %; on a 650-mod list with the cap at 4 frames a call, mod OnTick fell from 30.6 to 8.2 ms a frame.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_luaTickAdaptive_cpu: Only while the game thread is the limit: the mods' heaviest per-frame handlers run every second to fourth frame.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_luaTickInputWake_cpu: The mods' key and mouse pollers run at the rate above instead of every frame, plus the frames where input changed.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_physicsStepHz_cpu: Bullet runs more vehicle steps a second on the game thread (120-240 instead of 100), each a full physics step.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_physicsStepMode_cpu: Above 100 fps every frame runs its own physics step, so the game thread runs more steps a second than stock's fixed 100.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_vrr_cpu: With your cap Uncapped or above the display's maximum, the game caps itself just inside the range (157 fps at 165 Hz), so the game thread prepares fewer frames a second.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_vrr_gpu: The GPU draws only the frames the display can show inside its range instead of every frame it can.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_vrrCap_cpu: Uncapped, the game thread prepares only the frames the display can show (157 a second at 165 Hz) instead of as many as it can.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_vrrCap_gpu: The GPU draws those frames only, not the ones above the display's range.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_presentPacing_render: The render thread waits out each frame's hold before the swap (parked, the last part spun) and reads back a GPU timestamp query per frame, a few frames later.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_frameQueue_render: The render thread holds every capped frame's swap until its slot plus the holding time: parked, then spinning the last millisecond.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_frameQueueGpu_render: A GPU timestamp query per frame, read back a few frames later, puts the GPU's drawing time into the holding time.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_macPresent_render: Each frame is handed from OpenGL to Metal by Java calls into the Objective-C runtime, and the render thread waits for a free Metal drawable.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_macPresent_gpu: An extra copy of every frame into a shared IOSurface, then a GPU upscale (MPS bilinear) from the game's resolution to the panel's native size.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_macPresent_vram: Three IOSurface textures at the game's resolution plus Metal drawables at the panel's native size (3024x1898 on the 14-inch MacBook Pro).
UI_pzopt_v8_why_limiterSleep_cpu: The game thread sleeps through its wait instead of spinning: about half a core less at a 120 fps cap (VRR test: the game's CPU 406 to 340 % of a core, busiest core 46 to 36 %).
UI_pzopt_v8_why_corePlacement_cores: The background threads run on the efficient cores, which cost a fraction of the power for the same work (one busy thread: 9.2 W on a Zen 5 core, 2.2 W on a Zen 5c). Ayaneo Flip at a 120 fps cap: 37 to about 30 W, same frame rate.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_workerQosMac_cpu: The game thread no longer waits at its per-frame joins for helpers that lost their cores: Louisville horde on an M1 Pro with four busy cores beside the game, 20.5 ms a frame instead of 34.7 (55 fps instead of 35).
UI_pzopt_v8_why_workerQosMac_cores: The helper threads hold their cores against other programs' work: under that load the game used 4.4-4.8 cores instead of 3.2. Quiet, the horde also ran a little faster (59.5 fps instead of 55.5).
UI_pzopt_v8_why_gpuPstate_gpu: Most of the game's GPU work waits on memory, not on the clock: a Radeon 890M held its 120 fps cap at 640 MHz instead of bursts at 2.7-2.9 GHz, 1.2 W less at 1 GHz. Each frame's GPU work takes a little longer (3.4 to 4.2 ms at 1 GHz).
UI_pzopt_v8_why_jitSteady_cores: The compiler threads stop recompiling thrown-away code: a 100 s walk threw it away ~2,000 times and compiled 16,600 times; the compiler fell from 0.83 to 0.43 cores on the Ayaneo Flip, 1.4-2.1 W less.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_lightingSyncPark_cores: LWJGL's timer slept in 1 ms steps and then spun the last millisecond of every wait on a core; the lighting thread now stays asleep until its next update.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_gcHeap_cpu: With room to spare Java never has to stop the game for a full clean-up: 3 GB ran 95 % full in the Louisville horde (2 GB froze it for 205 ms), and with 132 mods 4 GB froze it for 150-280 ms at a time where 8 GB never did.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_gcHeap_ram: The game may take 4 GB instead of 3 (8 GB with 30+ mods), never more than half your RAM. It grows into what it gets: the horde settles at 3.6-3.9 GB, 132 mods used 4.2-6.2 GB of an 8 GB heap.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_luaGcNoop_cpu: Each such call froze the game thread for 120-140 ms in a vanilla game (more with a bigger heap); Java's concurrent mode was worse, 270-320 ms, because the game thread waits for the whole cycle.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_gcHeapFixed_ram: The whole heap is taken from the system at boot: 4,096 MB from the start, where a growing 4 GB heap held 2.9-3.6 GB on the spinning route and in the horde.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_gcPreTouch_ram: Every page of the heap is backed by real memory from boot, not only once the game first uses it.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_gcPreTouch_load: Writing every page of the heap takes a moment at boot, longer with a bigger heap (not measured on its own).
UI_pzopt_v8_why_gcMode_cpu: In a horde ZGC's 3 GB ran 95 % full and fell behind: the game thread stalled up to 12.8 ms waiting for it, 66 fps against 72-90 with G1; uncapped on the spinning route ZGC was 3 % slower too.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_gcMode_cores: ZGC's collector threads run alongside the game all the time; on a 4-core laptop they took cycles straight from the game thread (with G1, no allocation stalls there).
UI_pzopt_v8_why_gcG1Tuned_cpu: The game thread's collection pauses went from 7-12 ms to typically 3-5 ms at the same heap size.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_gcSlack_cpu: The few-millisecond pause moves into time the frame would spend waiting for the cap anyway: on the Louisville horde at 120 fps a scheduled collection cost the frames 1-3 ms instead of 10-14.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_soundTickHz_cpu: Above the rate, frames skip a refresh the sound engine would not have applied. Together with \"Skip silent zombies' sound emitters\" the game thread's sound work fell from 5.3 % to 2.8 % in a horde with a storm and alarms.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_emitterIdleSkip_cpu: Stock checked every zombie's three emitters every frame: 2.8 % of the game thread in a horde of 2,000, 0.7 % with the skip.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_worldSoundCleanupFast_cp: Stock swept every loaded chunk's list each frame and shifted the list once per expired entry: 0.35 % of the game thread with alarms, thumps and gunfire, now 0.17 %.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_hearingHoist_cpu: The repeated lookups were 0.33 % of the game thread in the sound test scene (horde, storm, alarms, gunfire), now 0.10 %.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_chunkGridWidth_cpu: Chunk bakes, arriving chunks and the world's update scale with the grid's area; on 4-core machines it is the one lever (the low-end preset uses 9).
UI_pzopt_v8_why_chunkGridWidth_cores: The native lighting thread lights every loaded chunk: at 13 it used 44 % of a core instead of 70 %.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_chunkGridWidth_gpu: Fewer chunk levels to bake into textures and draw.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_chunkGridWidth_vram: Each loaded chunk level keeps its baked texture in GPU memory; fewer chunks, fewer textures.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_chunkGridWidth_ram: Fewer chunks, squares and objects held in memory.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_chunkGridWidth_load: Fewer chunks to load and light before the world appears (vanilla's 19 x 19 grid is 361).
UI_pzopt_v8_why_chunkGridWidth_chunks: A row of chunks you cross is shorter, so each arrival is less work: at 9 most of the +11 ms that late drive frames spent on arriving chunks (bakes, square loading, new-chunk lighting) went.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_chunkGridFollowView_chun: Upstairs the grid loads the chunks under the ground the camera shows, so the ones at the top screen corners are there instead of missing (at level 4 the corners lay 7 tiles outside the grid before).
UI_pzopt_v8_why_parallel_cores: The recalculation, about 71 % of the streamer's work, runs on up to 4 workers, at about 0.4 ms more CPU per chunk (the workers share the caches).
UI_pzopt_v8_why_parallel_ram: Each worker keeps its own square getter, and finished chunks wait in memory until it is their turn to be handed over.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_parallel_chunks: With the streamer's wake-up, the median chunk is ready in 9.3 ms instead of 20 and p90 in 84 ms instead of 184 on the car-speed route (stock: 166 / 310 ms).
UI_pzopt_v8_why_workers_cores: Each worker is a thread recalculating chunks. On 4 cores or fewer they took time from the game thread (a 4-core laptop's drive ran at half the frame rate), hence 1 there.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_workers_chunks: A wider pool finishes a row of chunks sooner: p90 chunk latency 103 ms with 2 workers, 84 with 4; 8 bought nothing.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_loadWorkers_cores: The initial chunk recalculation spreads over more threads only during the load (about 5.4 thread-seconds on 8 workers on the desktop).
UI_pzopt_v8_why_loadWorkers_load: The first chunks are ready sooner. More than half the cores bought nothing: with 15 workers each chunk took longer, as the threads contend until Java has compiled the code.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_wake_chunks: A chunk no longer waits for the next 140 ms check: median chunk latency 166 to 20 ms on its own on the car-speed route, 8x.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_chunkHandoffDivisor_cpu: Each joining rolls the chunk's loot and erosion on the game thread; fewer per frame means no frame carries a whole row of them.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_chunkHandoffDivisor_chun: Chunks of a big row wait a few frames longer to appear. A higher divisor spreads them further and makes them wait longer.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_handoffRecalcFast_cpu: The border pass is about half of a chunk's joining time on the game thread: 207-299 us a chunk instead of 416-459 us in the Louisville horde.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_handoffRecalcFast_chunks: Cheaper joinings fit a frame's spare time sooner, so waiting chunks join earlier.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_propIdCache_cpu: The name lookups were 0.8 % of the game thread in the Louisville horde and 10 % of a chunk's joining, and run while tiles are drawn too.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_slackWork_cpu: Joinings of 1-50 ms each downtown and far loot rolls move into time the frame would wait anyway: the chunk map's p99 a frame fell from 2.8 to 0.2 ms in the Louisville horde.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_slackWork_chunks: A chunk may wait a few frames for spare time before it appears (at most \"Chunk joining: longest wait\", 6 frames by default).
UI_pzopt_v8_why_chunkHandoffCost_cpu: With the per-square guess chunks waited, the queue grew, and a few frames a run then joined the backlog at once, each over 4 ms; the whole-chunk mean keeps them flowing into spare time.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_chunkHandoffCost_chunks: Chunks no longer wait behind one heavy chunk's estimate (up to 600 frames before).
UI_pzopt_v8_why_chunkHandoffSlackMaxWait: No backlog builds up, so no frame later has to join many waiting chunks at once (such frames took over 4 ms).
A chunk joins within 6 frames instead of waiting up to 600 for spare time. Lower joins sooner, more often in a busy frame.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_chunkHandoffForceAnyFram: An overdue chunk no longer waits on for a light frame, which in a busy scene may not come for a while.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_chunkHandoffFrameBudgetU: A backlog no longer lands in one frame: such frames took over 4 ms of the game thread, now about 1.5 ms. Lower spreads it further, higher clears the queue sooner.
The rest of a backlog joins over the next frames instead of all in one.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_hotsaveStaged_cpu: The save's serialisation, a 2-5 ms game-thread stall while driving, is split over nine streamer updates, so no single frame carries all of it.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_hotsaveIntervalSec_cpu: Stock saved after every drained chunk-save queue, a 2-5 ms game-thread stall about twice a second while driving; at 30 s it is rare. Higher saves less often.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_hotsaveIntervalSec_disk: Those files are rewritten every 30 s at most instead of about twice a second while driving.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_luaLoadStream_cpu: No frame carries a whole chunk's mod handlers: on the 54-mod list's spinning route frames over twice the median fell from 118-147 to 40-43 (those by LoadGridsquare / LoadChunk 46-70 to 5-6), p99 17.3-20.6 to 13.1-14.8 ms.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_luaLoadStream_chunks: Chunks are ready to draw sooner, as none waits behind the stock pace: queued to drawable p99 0.9 s to 0.3 s on the spin, 0.3 to 0.1 s on the drive.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_luaLoadNearestFirst_chun: The chunks ahead of you join before the ones behind or far to the side.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_luaLoadChunkSplit_cpu: A chunk's last slice no longer carries every LoadChunk handler at once.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_luaLoadSlack_cpu: Joining work moves into time the frame waits anyway: with it off on the drive frames over twice the median went 26 to 56.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_luaLoadPrefilter_cpu: Handlers that do nothing on most squares cost nothing there: LoadGridsquare time 21 % lower on the 54-mod drive, 47 % on a 650-mod list (29.0 to 15.3 ms a frame).
UI_pzopt_v8_why_luaLoadSigProject_cpu: Fewer signatures to learn and hash per handler, so more skips and less bookkeeping.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_luaLoadNoopSkip_cpu: More handlers skipped than the proven skipping can.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_fmodAsync_cores: FMOD's start-up (about 1.6 s) runs on a boot thread; the main thread waited 0 s for it.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_fmodAsync_load: Launch to main menu 6.57 to 5.20 s on the desktop.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_preloadAnimSets_cores: The 1.1 s parse runs on a boot thread.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_preloadAnimSets_load: Creating the player in the world load fell from 0.35 to 0.05 s: Continue to world 5.11 to 4.54 s on the desktop.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_bootPump_cores: The file threads decode during boot instead of sitting idle for its first 4 s.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_bootPump_ram: Decoded textures and animations are in memory from boot on, earlier than in stock.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_bootPump_load: Less is left to decode at Continue: the world load's wait for its files fell from 0.85 to 0.36 s, and to none with \"Register models early\".
UI_pzopt_v8_why_bootFileThreads_cores: More threads decode textures and animations at once during boot (10 by default on 16 threads).
UI_pzopt_v8_why_bootFileThreads_load: Boot decoding finishes sooner. Too many slow the boot's Lua: with 16 threads all busy the boot took 7.55 s instead of about 6.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_earlyModels_load: The animations are imported by the main menu, so the world load no longer waits for them (its file wait 0.36 to 0.01 s).
UI_pzopt_v8_why_luaPrecompile_cores: 1,419 Lua files compile on up to 14 threads during boot.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_luaPrecompile_load: Boot 6.04 to 5.58 s on the desktop; at Continue the server Lua (0.9 s of compiling) and the map zones come from the cache.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_animClipCache_cores: Importing the 2,209 .X animation files cost the file threads 14-17 thread-seconds a boot; reading the cache costs 2.9.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_animClipCache_disk: About 89 MB of clips (2,161 files) under Zomboid/pzopt/anims, written on the first boot.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_animClipCache_load: Continue to world 4.89 to 4.02 s on the desktop once the cache is warm.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_packIndex_disk: Seven small index files under Zomboid/pzopt/packs, written on the first boot.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_packIndex_load: The byte-by-byte scan of 526 MB of packs is gone from every later boot (the pack headers were 0.64 s of the boot's main thread).
UI_pzopt_v8_why_scriptParserFast_ram: Stock rewrote the multi-MB script text once per comment and copied the rest of it once per token; those throwaway copies are gone.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_scriptParserFast_load: The stock passes cost 1.8 s of boot (1.56 s of it stripping comments): boot 7.35 to 6.57 s on the desktop.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_itemParamSwitch_load: The comparison chain was about 0.9 s of the boot's main thread.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_fileThreads_cores: Texture, model and depth-map decoding spread over more threads (8 on the desktop's 16).
UI_pzopt_v8_why_fileThreads_load: The world load no longer waits for decoded files (3.5 s in stock). Many more threads slowed the game's own map loaders (1.5 to 4.0 s beside 14 file threads), hence half the cores.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_fileInflight_ram: More files can be read and decoded at the same time, each holding its buffers.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_fileInflight_load: The file threads always have a next task waiting, so none sits idle during the load.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_textureBufferMb_render: Larger values pile uploads onto one frame: with 256 MB one frame a few seconds into the world took 5.05 s.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_textureBufferMb_ram: Up to this many MB of decoded textures wait in memory for their upload (256 instead of 50).
UI_pzopt_v8_why_textureBufferMb_load: The decoders pause less often while the loading screen is up.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_parallelDepthMaps_cores: The decodes spread over the file threads instead of queuing behind one lock.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_parallelDepthMaps_load: The depth maps are ready earlier in the world load.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_loaderCpuFixes_cores: The loader thread stops repeating work: vehicle zones checked once (11 checks over 9,690 zones were 0.6 s), lot headers looked up per cell instead of per chunk, rooms indexed instead of searched.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_loaderCpuFixes_load: Collision data 0.52 to 0.13 s and the map-zone phase 1.52 to 1.29 s of the world load on the desktop.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_shaderCache_render: The render thread builds each shader once instead of once per model.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_shaderCache_load: On a laptop whose loading-screen frame took 220 ms, 73 animal models waited 16.5 s of a 31 s load; now only the first model per shader waits.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_shaderWarmup_render: The builds happen in the loading screen instead of mid-play, where the first burnt car's vehicle program took the render thread 428 ms and a foliage-sway variant 144 ms.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_mipmapArrays_cores: The file threads build mip levels with bulk row copies instead of byte-by-byte buffer access, a few percent faster (a 2048 x 2048 texture's first level 13.5 ms instead of 14.3).
UI_pzopt_v8_why_texCompress_render: The render thread no longer compresses inside each upload: about 26 s a boot on a Radeon 890M in stock, about 0.1 s with Auto.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_texCompress_cores: The file threads copy each texture into a 128 MB staging buffer (Auto), or compress it on the CPU (Worker: about 46 s of file-thread time a boot on the Ayaneo Flip).
UI_pzopt_v8_why_texCompress_gpu: With Auto, compute shaders build each texture's mip levels and its BC3 compression on the GPU while the textures load.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_texCompress_load: The main menu runs at 60 fps from 4 s after boot instead of 25-34 fps for 10-16 s.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_tileDefPreload_cores: Parsing the tile-definition files and building ~61k sprites runs on a boot thread.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_tileDefPreload_load: The tile-definition step of the world load fell from 0.76 to about 0.2 s.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_skipIdChecks_load: The six walks over every building and room cost about 0.37 s of CPU per world load.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_voronoiFast_cores: The noise was 89 % of the eight map-loader threads' work.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_voronoiFast_load: The map loaders finish in 0.7 s instead of 1.5 s, so the world load no longer waits for them.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_earlyTilePacks_load: Removes the 0.2-0.6 s wait for tile textures at the end of a warm world load.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_aotCache_disk: A cache of about 127 MB is written at the end of the recording launch.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_aotCache_load: Continue to world 2.64 to 2.02 s and launch to main menu about 0.6 s shorter on the desktop.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_noLoadFade_load: The loading screen's 350 ms fade and the main menu's 250 ms fade are skipped: leaving the menu takes 0.15 s instead of 0.51.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_noIntroWait_load: Up to 33 s less before you can start a new game.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_noClickToStart_load: No wait for your click once the world is ready: you are in as soon as it is loaded.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_noLoadingScreen_load: The fade from black played in full before the world appeared (0.36 s of renders and sleeps); now it is skipped.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_resumeShot_disk: Each quit writes a 1920-pixel-wide JPEG and its position file into the save folder.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_resumeShot_load: The load takes as long, but you see the place you left from its first frame instead of a loading screen.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_centerFirstLoad_load: You enter once the chunks within 3 of you are loaded and lit instead of all of them: the world shows 3.02 s after Continue instead of 3.51 on the desktop.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_centerFirstLoad_chunks: The first chunks load and light nearest you first instead of in no particular order (stock lit them in rows, so the world appeared in diagonal bands).
UI_pzopt_v8_why_upscaler_gpu: The world's per-pixel work (fog, rain, water, lights) follows the render size: in a static storm with the stock fog at 5K, FSR 1.0 at quality ran 54 % faster than off, bicubic 73 %. On a fast drive the gain is small: chunk bakes do not shrink.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_upscaler_vram: The smaller world picture and the upscaler's own images sit beside the screen-sized one; taau and DLSS also keep a history picture at the output size.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_upscalerQuality_gpu: Fewer world pixels to shade: performance draws a quarter of them, quality 44 %. DLSS's own cost follows its output size instead, so with dlss the levels move the frame rate by about 10 % only.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_upscalerScalePct_gpu: A lower percentage shades fewer world pixels (they fall with its square: 50 is a quarter) for a softer picture; 0 follows the quality preset.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_dlssPreset_gpu: The network runs on the GPU every frame: at 5120x2160 on an RTX 4090 preset E takes 0.64-0.74 ms, the transformer K 1.54 ms (the 120 km/h drive at 327 fps with E, 249 with K). At 1440p and below a third or less.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_dlssOutputPct_gpu: DLSS costs time per pixel it writes, not per pixel it reads: in a heavy storm with fog at 5K on an RTX 4090, DLSS E at quality gained 22 % over no upscaler with a 67 % output, 17 % at 75 %, 10 % at the full size.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_dlssOutputFilter_gpu: rcas is one small sharpen pass at the DLSS output's size (the stock-fog scene ~3 % slower than the plain bicubic finish); fsr1 adds a full-screen EASU pass, about 0.2 ms a frame at 4K; bicubic is free.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_dlssWaterCurrent_gpu: One more pass each frame mixes the water pixels of the frame just drawn into DLSS's picture, masked to the water (rivers, lakes) on screen.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_dlssWaterCurrent_vram: Two textures at the output size, made the first time water is on screen, hold the mixed picture and the last frame's water.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_dynRes_gpu: In a GPU-bound scene the world renders smaller until the GPU fits the cap: on the desktop under a heavy per-pixel load late frames fell from 28 % to 3-8 % at about 60 % size.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_dynRes_vram: With the upscaler off the temporal upscaler (taau) keeps a 16-bit history picture at the screen size.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_dynResTargetPct_gpu: A lower share leaves the GPU more idle time each frame by rendering the world smaller; a higher one keeps more resolution and misses the cap more often.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_dynResMinPct_gpu: A lower floor lets a heavy scene shed more pixels (50 % is a quarter of them); a higher one keeps the picture sharper and holds the cap less firmly.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_dynResMaxPct_gpu: Below 100 the world never renders at full size, so the GPU shades fewer pixels even in light scenes, for a softer picture all the time.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_dynResFps_gpu: A rate above your cap renders the world smaller and leaves the GPU idle time; a lower one lets the world use more of each frame at a larger size.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_spriteFilter_gpu: The world picture is sampled by a variant of the same program, picked once a frame for the zoom: nothing measurable zoomed in, cheaper zoomed out; up to ~0.07 ms a frame on the desktop's town drive at 5K.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_spriteFilterMin_gpu: One copy of the art read a few times costs less than the game's blend of two: with the default two adaptive samples the 5K composite is 59 us cheaper at zoom 1.75 and 147 us at 2.5; four adaptive samples cost about what the game's blend does.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_hdrAuto_render: On Linux HDR runs in a native Wayland window, where NVIDIA's GL driver has no worker thread of its own: its work lands on the render thread (38 to 90 % of a core on the desktop's town drive).
UI_pzopt_v8_why_hdrAuto_cores: The map of which squares lamps, torches and fires light is built on its own worker thread (about 0.2 ms a frame), not on the game thread.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_hdrAuto_gpu: On an HDR screen the world is drawn into a 16-bit float picture and encoded for it at the end of each frame: about 0.25 ms a frame at 5K (none on KDE, which takes the picture as it is). Nothing on an SDR screen.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_hdrAuto_vram: The 16-bit float frame buffers at the screen's size.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_hdr_render: On Linux HDR runs in a native Wayland window, where NVIDIA's GL driver has no worker thread of its own: its work lands on the render thread (38 to 90 % of a core on the desktop's town drive).
UI_pzopt_v8_why_hdr_cores: The map of which squares lamps, torches and fires light is built on its own worker thread (about 0.2 ms a frame), not on the game thread.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_hdr_gpu: The world is drawn into a 16-bit float picture and encoded for the HDR screen at the end of each frame: about 0.25 ms a frame at 5K (none on KDE, which takes the picture as it is).
UI_pzopt_v8_why_hdr_vram: The 16-bit float frame buffers at the screen's size.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_hdrBloomPct_gpu: The bright parts are blurred in smaller copies and added back each frame (skipped at 0): 0.065 ms at 4K on its own, ~0.1 ms of the HDR set on the desktop's town drive at 5K.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_hdrGlintPct_gpu: Water and puddles are drawn once more into a glint target and car bodies write their speculars beside their colour (skipped at 0): ~0.07 and ~0.1 ms a frame on the desktop's town drive at 5K.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_ambientOcclusion_gpu: Computed once when a chunk's picture is drawn (~25-35 us a picture) and kept, so a still or moving camera pays nothing more: ~1.3 % of the GPU's time in the worst streaming, ~0.1 ms a frame on a town drive.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_ambientOcclusion_vram: Each chunk picture keeps its shading as a one-byte image beside it, at the AO resolution (half its size per axis by default).
UI_pzopt_v8_why_aoScalePct_vram: Every chunk picture's shading is kept at this size: 100 holds four times what 50 does, 25 a quarter. The GPU time hardly changes, it follows the number of pictures, not their texels.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_sunShadows_render: Every character, animal and car is drawn once more from the sun, and the far-field heights are uploaded for each baked picture: about 25 us a model on a laptop's render thread.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_sunShadows_gpu: The static shadows are baked into the chunk pictures with the AO (a picture a frame re-shaded when the sun moves); characters and cars are shaded every frame. The dearest Visual: +0.7 ms GPU on the desktop's town drive at 5K.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_sunShadows_vram: A 2048 x 2048 depth atlas for the casters' shapes, the far-field height map and the sun term kept beside each chunk picture's shading.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_sunShadowCharacters_gpu: One instanced pass after the world shades the ground round each character: ~10 us of GPU for 70 characters on the desktop, 125-200 us for 16 on a laptop's integrated GPU.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_sunShadowMeshes_render: Every caster is drawn a second time by the render thread, at most 32 a frame: about 25 us a model on a laptop.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_sunShadowMeshes_gpu: Each caster's pose is drawn from the sun into its own tile and the shadow pass filters it softly: ~50 us a frame for 40 zombies, 8 animals and a car on the desktop, against ~30 for the rounded shapes.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_sunShadowMeshes_vram: The 2048 x 2048 32-bit depth atlas the casters' 128 x 128 tiles live in (16 MB).
UI_pzopt_v8_why_sunShadowRate_render: Each renewed pose is one more model draw on the render thread (about 25 us on a laptop), up to 32 a frame instead of 12 in bursts.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_sunShadowRate_gpu: Every pose is drawn again each frame: with 40 characters on screen about 0.09 ms a frame on an RTX 4090, against 0.03 ms at 15 a second.
UI_pzopt_v8_why_entityShadows_render: Two more uniform uploads per model draw: about 15 us a frame of render thread for that crowd.
